title: The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: What God Wants Has Never Been Merely a Job Done
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a true scene. There was a brother who had served in his church for eighteen years. He was the coordinator of the worship team, a small-group leader, the general organiser of every conference. Wherever someone was missing, there he was. One year, at year’s end, the church held an appreciation evening for him. From the platform the pastor counted off, one by one, all the things he had done, and the congregation applauded again and again. When it was over, he sat alone in the emptied sanctuary and did not get up for a long time. Later he said something to the pastor: “Pastor, in these eighteen years I’ve done so many things. But suddenly I’m not so sure whether God and I still really know each other.”

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is like a needle. What it pierces is not only that brother’s heart, but the hearts of many of us.

It is very easy for us to understand “doing God’s will” as a task list: finish a job, hit a target, run a ministry well. As the items on the list are crossed off one by one, we assume we are drawing closer and closer to God. Yet from beginning to end the Bible shows us a deeper truth —

God’s will is not just about doing things; God’s will is about building relationships.

Look at Genesis. God made the heavens, the earth, the light, the sea, the birds and the beasts, and only last of all did he make man. When God made man, he did not first hand Adam a work schedule; he first breathed his own breath into him, and then walked with him himself in the garden. The first charge God gave Adam was not “This is how much you must get done”; it was that he should live in relationship. And the first thing God called “not good” was this: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). God made man not for work but for relationship; not to complete tasks, but to walk with him and to be connected with others.

Now look at the first thing God did after man fell. He did not begin by pronouncing a sentence. In “the cool of the day” he walked in the garden and called to the man, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). Brothers and sisters, this is the first question God asks in the whole Bible, and it is a question about relationship. Of course God knew which tree Adam was hiding behind. God was not asking for coordinates. He was asking: How did things between us come to this?

Revival is the same. What is revival? We often think revival means lively meetings, packed sanctuaries, impressive numbers, visible results. But the revival the Bible speaks of has at its core “relationships restored” — our relationship with God, our relationship with ourselves, our relationships with one another, all established anew. In the last verse of the Old Testament, the prophet Malachi foretells the Elijah who is to come: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers” (Malachi 4:6). Do you see? God’s own definition of end-time revival is the repair of relationships.

So this morning we are going to enter together into a truth that lies at the very centre:

The centre of God’s will is building relationships.

In this lesson we will take three steps. First, we will see that doing God’s will is the starting point of building relationships. Second, we will see that doing God’s will brings our lives into eternal value. Third, we will learn the three levels of doing God’s will — living in it, dying in it, and passing it on.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html:
To receive today’s message accurately, we first need to know where our three theme passages come from. They come from three entirely different scenes, yet they point to the same centre.

The first is John 15:14.

The author of John’s Gospel is generally held to be John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. It was written around AD 80 to 90, to believers scattered far and wide who were already into their second generation. Chapter 15 belongs to the “Farewell Discourse” (John 13–17); the setting is after the Last Supper, on the way to the Garden of Gethsemane. The Lord Jesus knew that the hour for him to leave the world had come. He did not lay down a constitution for an organisation, nor did he hand out job assignments. He spoke of a vine: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Notice what the Lord says next: “You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you” (John 15:14). And straight after, in verse 15, the Lord says: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Brothers and sisters, see this key point: the Lord ties “doing” and “friends” together. The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much each one does; it is whether he knows his master’s heart. A servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions. The Lord says that if you do what he commands, you are raised from servants to friends — doing his will is the door into the relationship.

The second is Matthew 12:50.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, by Matthew, the tax collector who once sat at the tax booth. The scene in chapter 12 is Jesus teaching the crowds in a house, when someone tells him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.” Jesus answers, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples he says, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:48–50).

What a staggering statement. The Lord Jesus was not denying natural family ties — on the cross he still remembered to entrust his mother to John. The Lord was declaring a deeper truth: in the kingdom of God, the closest relationships rest not on blood but on “doing the Father’s will together”. Doing his will turns a crowd of strangers into one family.

The third is 1 John 2:17.

First John was written at about the same time as John’s Gospel, to the churches around Asia Minor. False teachers had already arisen, early Gnostic ideas were having their influence, and believers were wavering between “loving the world” and “loving the Father”. In the previous verse John speaks of “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life”, and then he says: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:17).

Three scenes, three identities: friends, family, people who remain forever. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? All three verses are about relationships, not performance.

sections.heading: 1. Doing God’s Will Is the Starting Point of Building Relationships
sections.html:
“You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.” (John 15:14)

“For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50)

From Genesis to the New Testament, God keeps repeating one thing: he wants people to listen to his word.

Look at this clear thread running through it all —

Adam failed because he did not listen to God. God said to him, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake.” (Genesis 3:17)

Abraham was blessed because he listened to God. “So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him.” (Genesis 12:4) A man of seventy-five left his country, his relatives and his father’s house, and set out for a place whose name he had not yet been told.

Israel was chosen in order to listen to God. “Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine.” (Exodus 19:5)

Saul was rejected because he did not listen to God. Samuel said to him, “But now your kingdom will not continue. Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which Yahweh commanded you.” (1 Samuel 13:14) Later Samuel put it even more plainly: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: it wasn’t that Saul did nothing. He did a great deal — he fought battles, he offered sacrifices, he kept back the best of the sheep and cattle to offer to God. His ministry report looked splendid. What he failed at was not ministry but relationship. He would rather do “things that are good for God” according to his own judgement than do what God actually said. That is the self-centred life.

At the heart of all this history is not “right and wrong” but “relationship”.

To listen is to trust. To obey is to connect.

We need to see this clearly. How far a person is willing to listen to someone usually shows how far he trusts that person. You don’t hand the steering wheel to someone you don’t trust. So when a person is willing to do God’s word, he is not completing an order; he is responding to a relationship. He is saying: Lord, I trust you.

It is like a child listening to his father. A five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say, “Don’t move,” and he stops. He stops not because he has understood the traffic laws, but because he knows that voice, and he knows that voice loves him. Love and trust are the real fuel of obedience.

Turn it the other way round: the root of disobedience has never been a lack of information; it has been a broken relationship. In the Garden of Eden, it wasn’t that Eve didn’t know what God had said — she could recite God’s words. What the serpent did was first to shake her “trust” in God — “Has God really said …?” The serpent was hinting: God is hiding something from you; God doesn’t really have your good at heart. Once trust collapsed, obedience collapsed with it.

Psychology offers a fascinating piece of corroborating evidence here. In the 1950s and 1960s the British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and later his colleague Mary Ainsworth tested it with her “Strange Situation” experiment. A child who has formed a secure attachment with a caregiver is actually more willing to leave the mother and explore the world, and also more willing to respond when the mother calls. By contrast, insecurely attached children are not more obedient; they are more resistant and more disorganised. So it turns out that the capacity to obey grows out of a secure relationship. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order of the gospel: it is not that we obey first and then God loves us; it is that God first loved us, and so we are able to obey.

In 1995 the American psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary published their well-known paper on “the need to belong” in Psychological Bulletin, arguing that forming and maintaining relationships is one of the most fundamental human drives, no less powerful than the need for food. They studied human beings from a secular angle; the Bible had long since explained the reason at its source — man was made in the image of God, and God himself is a God in relationship: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, in perfect love from all eternity.

And here a 321 insight comes into view.

Obey God with the heart and you build the relationship; analyse God with the brain and you lose the relationship.

Brothers and sisters, many people “know a great deal” yet are “far from God”, because relying on the brain is not the same as relying on the heart. When the person who relies on the brain hears God’s word, the first reaction is to assess it: Is it reasonable? Is it worth it? What will others think? By the time the assessment is finished, the prompting of the Holy Spirit has passed. When the person who relies on the heart hears God’s word, the first reaction is to respond: Lord, I am willing.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be joyful, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Obedience is not a conclusion of the brain; obedience is a response of the heart. This morning, let me ask you one question: in recent days, has God said something to you that you are still “studying” but have never actually “gone and done”?

sections.heading: 2. Doing God’s Will Brings Our Lives into Eternal Value
sections.html:
“The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

This verse lays bare a staggering fact: everything in the world will pass away; only one thing is eternal — doing God’s will.

Why?

Because doing God’s will is not merely behaving correctly; it is “being connected in God”.

Notice that John’s wording here is unusual. He does not say “the deeds of doing God’s will remain forever”; he says that the “person” who does God’s will remains forever. In the original, the reference here is to the person, not the work. In other words, eternity is not stuck onto your results; eternity is stuck onto you as a person. It is not because what you do is so great, but because you yourself are connected to the Eternal One.

It is like a tree. A branch joined to the root has life and bears fruit; a branch cut off from the root withers and dies. When a branch has just been cut, it looks exactly like the branches still on the tree — just as green, just as leafy, perhaps even still in flower. The difference only shows after a few days. Brothers and sisters, our spiritual condition is like that too. A life cut off from God doesn’t wither at once; for a while it “seems fine”. That is exactly where the danger lies. The Lord could not have put it more clearly: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

A life connected to God endures; a life cut off from God is short-lived.

How did Jesus himself see this? By the well of Sychar he said to his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34)

That day the Lord Jesus had walked a long road; he was tired and thirsty. The disciples came back from the town with food and urged him to eat. Yet the Lord said these words. Brothers and sisters, weigh this carefully: the Lord did not say “doing the Father’s will is my job”, nor “it is my responsibility”. He said, “my food”.

That means: doing God’s will is not a burden; it is life’s supply.

It is just like eating — eating isn’t pressure; eating is what sustains life. No one wakes up in the morning sighing, “Oh dear, three meals again today.” We don’t put meals on our to-do list as a chore, because eating is itself a pleasure, itself a source of strength. Brothers and sisters, if obeying God has always felt like a chore in your heart, that usually means one thing: we are still treating it as work, and we haven’t yet tasted that it is food.

Here is a spiritual comparison; keep it in your heart:

If a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.

In 2010 a team led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University in the United States published a large meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine. It brought together 148 studies and more than 300,000 participants, and found that people with strong social connections had roughly a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period than those with weak connections. Meanwhile the Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and running now for more than eighty years, has followed the health and happiness of several hundred men across their whole lives. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up in that now widely known conclusion: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.

Brothers and sisters, even these perishable bodies of ours were made according to the principle of “relationship” — when relationships are good, people live longer; when relationships break, people wither faster. How much more our souls? How much more our relationship with the everlasting God?

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine says: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Those words were spoken sixteen hundred years ago, and they are still accurate today. The human heart was made to God’s measurements; put anything else in there and it will work loose, it will leak.

The 321 insight here is also very clear:

Doing God’s will is food for the spiritual life; not doing God’s will is famine for the spiritual life.

And the 321 vision speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. First John 2:17 is the summary of all four shifts. The world and its lusts are earthly, temporary and worldly; the one who does God’s will is heavenly, eternal and godly. Brothers and sisters, the thing keeping you busy this morning — set it a hundred years from now, set it before the Lord’s judgement seat — how much of it will remain?

Here is a very practical test: spread out your diary for this week, and beside each item ask one question — “Does this connect me to God and to people, or does it pull me away from God and from people?” No need to rush to delete anything; first, mark it honestly. Simply seeing honestly is already the beginning of change.

sections.heading: 3. Three Levels of Doing God’s Will: Living in It, Dying in It, Passing It On
sections.html:
“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

The Lord Jesus spoke these words in Passion Week. Some Greeks had come asking to see him, the disciples went to tell him, and the Lord answered, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” (John 12:23) Then he spoke of this grain of wheat. Brothers and sisters, the Lord put “being glorified” and “dying” in the same breath. It is the most counter-intuitive sentence in the world, and the most powerful.

Doing God’s will is not something you “do once”; it has three levels: living in it, dying in it, and passing it on.

The first level: living in God’s will

Living in God’s will means beginning to obey God, being willing to do what God says.

This is the starting point. Without this step, nothing that follows exists. But at this stage we often meet difficulty, struggle, and the challenge of circumstances.

Why? Because the moment obedience touches the ground, it runs into a cost. When Abraham heard God say, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house,” if he had merely agreed in his heart, nothing would have happened. The moment he set out, his tents, his livestock, his servants, his kinsmen, his standing, his sense of security — all of it had to move with him. Obedience has never been completed in the head; obedience is completed with the feet.

Moses was the same. Before the burning bush at Horeb he said “but” to God five times — Who am I? What shall I tell them your name is? They will not believe me. I have never been eloquent. Lord, please send someone else. Brothers and sisters, when we read it we think Moses was terribly long-winded, but to be honest, which of us isn’t like that? When God’s call comes, the first visitors to arrive in our hearts are often not joy but excuses.

So the most practical exercise in “living in God’s will” is to put “I am willing” before “I understand”. The Lord Jesus in Gethsemane gives us the best example: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) He understood fully how bitter that cup was, and still he said, “yours, be done”.

The second level: dying in God’s will

Dying in God’s will means holding on to the end, not giving up because of circumstances.

Jesus on the cross is the most complete example. He did not merely “begin to obey”; he was “obedient to the end, even to death on a cross”. Paul describes it like this: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:8)

Notice the words “to the point of death”. If our obedience has a bottom line, that bottom line is our real master. Very often this is how we obey: I’ll obey, so long as it doesn’t affect my income; I’ll obey, so long as it doesn’t hurt my reputation; I’ll obey, so long as my family doesn’t object. Brothers and sisters, those “so long as” clauses are the parts of us that have not yet died.

Hebrews gives us a very deep sentence: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” (Hebrews 5:8) Even the Son of God had to “learn” obedience, and learn it in suffering. How could we be the exception?

Psychologists have observed something similar in the secular sphere. In 2007 Angela Duckworth of the University of Pennsylvania and her colleagues published their research on “grit”. They followed new cadets at West Point through an extremely gruelling summer of training, and found that what predicted who would make it through was not their fitness scores, nor their academic entry scores, but “grit” — passion and unrelenting perseverance towards long-term goals. Brothers and sisters, even worldly training works this way: what decides the outcome is often not the ability to start, but the will to stay. How much more the road of the kingdom of heaven?

The German martyr-pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote that famous line in The Cost of Discipleship: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Bonhoeffer was not theorising on paper. In April 1945 he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, at only thirty-nine. He signed that sentence with his life.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person obeys up to a certain point and then stops, because going any further would touch the “self”. The selfless person can go all the way to the end, because there is no longer a “self” inside to protect.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) When that grain of wheat falls into the ground and “dies”, it is not the end; it is the moment it can at last become a whole field of wheat.

The third level: passing on God’s will

Passing on God’s will means not only living it out yourself but also helping others to live it out.

Moses raised up Joshua. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.” (Numbers 27:18) Joshua was not parachuted in. He was the one who had followed Moses all through the forty years in the wilderness, who kept watch at the tent of meeting for Moses, who went up the mountain with Moses. Passing on is not handing over a post; passing on is handing over a life.

Jesus raised up disciples. “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” (Mark 3:14) Look at the order: first “that they might be with him”, then “send them out to preach”. Relationship first, ministry after. This is exactly what the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. For three and a half years the Lord Jesus was not running a training course; he was living life with them — walking together, eating together, getting into boats together, facing the wind and the waves together.

Paul raised up Timothy. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) There are four generations in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. The nature of the gospel has never been one generation’s firework display; it is a relay, one baton after another.

This is life influencing life, life multiplying life.

And this is the key truth: true revival means life multiplying life. Not one person on fire, but a whole company of people raised up.

Let us come back to that grain of wheat. Sow one grain in the soil; it sprouts and comes into ear, and a single ear can usually yield thirty to fifty grains. And the original grain? You can no longer find it. Its husk has rotted in the soil; its nourishment has become root, become stalk, become new grain. Brothers and sisters, this is both the cost and the glory of passing it on: if you want to keep that one grain, you will only ever have that one grain; if you are willing to be buried, God will grow a whole field out of you.

In the 1960s the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward social learning theory, and with his famous “Bobo doll” experiment he showed that children learn behaviour not mainly from being lectured but from observing and imitating the role models they see. In the early 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma in Italy discovered “mirror neurons” in the monkey brain — when a monkey watches another perform an action, the area activated in its brain is the very same as when it performs that action itself. When God made us, he built this “imitation” circuitry into us. No wonder Paul dared to say, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)

This is precisely why passing it on cannot be done by courses but only by life: people can’t learn what you say; people can learn what you live.

The 321 insight is sharpest of all here:

Only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.

The self-centred person cares only about what he gains; the selfless person is willing to let his life be used to build others up. The self-centred person is afraid of others overtaking him, so he holds something back; the selfless person longs for others to overtake him, so he empties out everything he has. Brothers and sisters, if you want to see whether someone is truly selfless, there is a very accurate test: see whether he can sincerely rejoice in someone else’s success.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Placing This Lesson Back within the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s message back within the framework of the 321 vision, we see it even more clearly.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me”; he obeyed to the end, even to death on the cross; he raised up twelve disciples. Living in it, dying in it, passing it on: the Lord himself walked all three levels to the end. The Bible is my standard — we do not judge by feelings what God’s will is; we first go back to God’s word: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) The Holy Spirit is my guide — God’s will is not worked out by analysis; it is confirmed within us by the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the battle over obedience is, in the end, a battle over the throne. It is not me sitting on the throne issuing orders and keeping God on as a consultant; it is letting Jesus truly reign as King. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when that grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, the field of wheat that grows up is not there to prove itself; it is there to glorify the God who made it grow.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, God’s system is not piled up out of organisational charts; it grows out of one healthy relationship after another. Living in his will is our relationship with God; dying in his will is our relationship with ourselves; passing on his will is our relationship with others. This is exactly the priority of relationships the 321 vision speaks of: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The fivefold change is here too. When the mindset changes, I no longer see God’s will as a task list but as a road of relationship. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes naturally. The order must never be reversed. The mistake we have so often made is trying to use ministry to drive relationships, and busyness to prove life. The result: the bigger the ministry, the emptier the person.

Then there is the 920 practice. 920 means this: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before that person we practise living the selfless life, which is the “0”; and what grows from it is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, if this lesson’s practice is to touch the ground, the most natural place is 920: today, whom has God placed in front of you? That person is your “2”. Are you living out the “0” towards him or her?

Then there are the 235 relationships. Becoming a “2” with someone selfless is having a spiritual companion; building a “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Today’s third level, “passing it on”, is in fact 235 put into practice — Moses and Joshua are a “3”; Jesus and the Twelve are a “5”; Paul and Timothy are both a “3” and a “5”.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Saul’s failure was exactly a leaving of his originally intended position; the Lord Jesus’ victory was exactly a returning to it. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: From Doing Things to Building Relationships
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We will set them within “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they are not just three good ideas but can truly grow into our lives.

Exercise 1: Every day, ask yourself one question — right now, am I doing a task, or building a relationship?

In ministry, at home, at work, stop and ask yourself: is my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing right now drawing the relationship closer, or pushing it further away?

How to practise: every evening, take one minute to look back over three things, and check whether they “made the relationship better”.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: first, remember today’s sentence — the centre of God’s will is building relationships. Put it on your phone’s home screen or on the dinner table.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you “see” in one concrete situation — so the way I answered just now was doing a task, not building a relationship. Information is knowing; revelation is being illuminated.

Conviction: sincerely acknowledge that “people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things” — no longer just agreeing with your lips.

Implementation: start that one-minute review this very evening; don’t wait until next Monday.

Evaluation: after a week, look back — which day was the most distant? What was I busy with at the time?

Correction: identify the one time of day when you most easily “let the task replace the person”, and adjust it.

Repetition: do it for forty days in a row. A change of mindset has never been a one-off decision; it is formed by repetition.

Multiplication: bring this one-minute exercise to your family or your small group, and do it together with someone.

Exercise 2: Practise “obeying with the heart” rather than “analysing with the brain”

When God’s word comes to you, don’t first analyse whether it is “reasonable or not”; first respond: Lord, I am willing.

How to practise: each day choose one verse, and that day deliberately live it out. For example, “be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19): deliberately practise listening in your conversations.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: each morning choose one verse, copy it onto paper and carry it with you.

Revelation: don’t ask, “What does this verse mean?” Ask, “Lord, in which matter today do you want me to live this out?”

Conviction: admit that in the past you have often substituted analysis for obedience, and confess it to the Lord.

Implementation: that same day, find the person you find hardest to listen to, and practise being “swift to hear, slow to speak”.

Evaluation: in the evening, write down honestly: today, did I keep quiet when I should have kept quiet?

Correction: if you failed, try again tomorrow with the same verse; don’t change the subject.

Repetition: one verse can be practised for a whole week. Depth matters more than quantity.

Multiplication: share this week’s verse and your story with one person, and invite them to choose a verse too.

Exercise 3: Deliberately build a relationship rather than complete a task

Today, reach out to one person: a phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear. The aim is not to “solve the problem” but to “let the other person feel loved”.

How to practise: every day, show care to at least one person — a family member, a co-worker or a friend.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: write down three names — the “2”s God has placed on your heart.

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see that person’s real need right now, not the need you assume they have.

Conviction: believe that “letting the other person feel loved” is itself ministry, not extra work on top of ministry.

Implementation: make that phone call today. Don’t send a message — phone; a voice carries warmth.

Evaluation: was I in a hurry to give advice? Did I really listen to the end?

Correction: next time, listen for three minutes before you speak.

Repetition: take turns caring for those three names, and keep it up for a whole season.

Multiplication: when that person is touched by God’s love, invite them to go and care for someone too — this is life multiplying life.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, many people work hard all their lives doing a great many things, yet neglect the most important thing — relationships.

Don’t lose people for the sake of tasks; don’t lose connection for the sake of getting things done.

What God values is not how much you have done, but whether you walk with him in love and stay connected with others.

There is a saying generally attributed to Mother Teresa: “We cannot do great things, only small things with great love.” The reason it moves people is that it shifts the focus from “the size of the task” to “the depth of the love”.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

God’s will is not a task list; it is a road of relationship.

When you truly grasp this, your whole life will change —

The focus is no longer “how much I do”, but “how deeply I love”.

The focus is no longer “what I complete”, but “whom I connect with”.

Let us think once more about the brother in our introduction. Eighteen years of service were not in vain; God will surely remember every bit he offered. What he truly needed was not to stop serving, but to put the order back in place: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When he is connected to the Lord again, everything he did in those eighteen years will turn from “performance” into “fruit”; from the earthly and temporary into the heavenly and eternal.

The Lord Jesus said, “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) The definition of eternal life is “knowing” — it is relationship.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let Jesus be King over your obedience. No longer do I decide whether to obey only after I’ve finished assessing; he speaks, and I go.

Second, let Jesus be King over your perseverance. No longer do I keep walking only when circumstances allow; I am that grain of wheat, willingly falling into the ground.

Third, let Jesus be King over your passing it on. No longer caring only about what I gain, but entrusting what I have received to faithful people who will be able to teach others.

May our whole lives be not merely about completing a mission, but about building eternal relationships in God, living out Christ, and becoming overcomers.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ.

“For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50)
“The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)
declarations: Lord!
I will no longer be just someone who gets things done; I will be someone who builds relationships.
I choose to obey you with my heart, and no longer to analyse you with my brain.
I will live in your will, die in your will, and pass on your will.
Let my life be not merely about getting things done, but about being connected to you, influencing others, and bearing eternal fruit.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Deliberately build a relationship rather than complete a task
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we are still before you.

Lord, please forgive us — we have so often substituted busyness for closeness, results for obedience, and ministry for relationship. We have done a great many things, yet grown like strangers before you. Lord, we want to turn back.
Give us a heart that obeys with the heart, and take away our habit of analysing you with our brains. When you speak a word, let us answer with a word: Lord, I am willing.
Help us to live in your will and not draw back in difficulty; help us to die in your will and not turn aside before the cost; help us to pass on your will, handing our lives on to the next person.
Lord, make us that grain of wheat that willingly falls into the ground. May every person we care for today come a little closer to you because of us.
Your will be done; your name be glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50) Looking back over this year, in what area have you been “doing a lot, yet far from God”? What has made you treat God’s will as a task list rather than a road of relationship?

“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Of the three levels — living in it, dying in it, passing it on — which one have you reached so far? Is there a specific person to whom God wants you to begin passing on your life?

blog.title: He Had Served for Eighteen Years

blocks.x: Yet he wasn’t sure whether he and God still really knew each other
There was a brother who had served in his church for eighteen years.

Coordinator of the worship team, small-group leader, general organiser of every conference — wherever someone was missing, there he was. One year, at year’s end, the church held an appreciation evening for him. From the platform the pastor counted off, one by one, all the things he had done, and the congregation applauded again and again.

When it was over, he sat alone in the emptied sanctuary and did not get up for a long time. Later he said to the pastor: “In these eighteen years I’ve done so many things. But suddenly I’m not so sure whether God and I still really know each other.”
That sentence is like a needle. And what it pierces is not only that brother’s heart.
1. God did not make us for work

It is very easy for us to understand “doing God’s will” as a task list: finish a job, hit a target, run a ministry well. As the items on the list are crossed off one by one, we assume we are drawing closer and closer to God.
But from beginning to end, the Bible is saying something else.

Look at Genesis. When God made man, he did not first hand Adam a work schedule; he breathed his own breath into him, and then walked with him himself in the garden. The first thing God called “not good” was not “not done well enough”, but “It is not good for the man to be alone.”
After man fell, the first thing God did was not to pronounce a sentence either. He walked in the garden and called out, “Where are you?”
This is the first question God asks man in the whole Bible, and it is a question about relationship. God was not asking for coordinates. He was asking: How did things between us come to this?
God’s will is not just about doing things; God’s will is about building relationships.
2. To listen is to trust; to obey is to connect
On the way to the Garden of Gethsemane, the Lord Jesus said:
“You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.” (John 15:14)

The Lord ties “doing” and “friends” together. The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much each one does; it is whether he knows his master’s heart. A servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions.
So when a person is willing to do God’s word, he is not completing an order; he is responding to a relationship.

It is like a child listening to his father. A five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say, “Don’t move,” and he stops. He stops not because he has understood the traffic laws, but because he knows that voice, and he knows that voice loves him.

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and later his colleague Mary Ainsworth tested it with her “Strange Situation” experiment: children who have formed a secure attachment with a caregiver are actually more willing to leave the mother and explore, and also more willing to respond when the mother calls. So it turns out that the capacity to obey grows out of a secure relationship.
This is exactly the order of the gospel: it is not that we obey first and then God loves us; it is that God first loved us, and so we are able to obey.
This is also the 321 insight: obey God with the heart and you build the relationship; analyse God with the brain and you lose the relationship.
3. Living in it, dying in it, passing it on
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)
Doing God’s will is not something you “do once”; it has three levels.
Living in God’s will: beginning to obey. Obedience has never been completed in the head; obedience is completed with the feet.
Dying in God’s will: holding on to the end. If our obedience has a bottom line, that bottom line is our real master.
Passing on God’s will: not only living it out yourself but also helping others to live it out. Moses raised up Joshua, Jesus raised up disciples, Paul raised up Timothy.

Sow one grain of wheat in the soil, and a single ear can usually yield thirty to fifty grains. And the original grain? You can no longer find it. If you want to keep that one grain, you will only ever have that one grain; if you are willing to be buried, God will grow a whole field out of you.
True revival means life multiplying life. Only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.
Three things you can do today
First, every evening take one minute to look back over three things, and ask yourself: today, was I doing tasks, or building relationships?
Second, each day choose one verse and deliberately live it out that day. Don’t first analyse whether it is reasonable; first respond: Lord, I am willing.
Third, every day deliberately show care to at least one person. A phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear. The aim is not to solve the problem but to let the other person feel loved.

Don’t lose people for the sake of tasks; don’t lose connection for the sake of getting things done. What God values is not how much you have done, but whether you walk with him in love and stay connected with others.
The focus is no longer “how much I do”, but “how deeply I love”; no longer “what I complete”, but “whom I connect with”.
Reflection: Looking back over this year, in what area have you been “doing a great deal, yet far from God”? Today, who is the one person God wants you to connect with first?

brief12.title: The Centre of God’s Will Is Building Relationships
notes: Slide text:
Live in his will, die in his will, pass on his will
“He who does God’s will
remains forever.”
1 John 2:17
Key points:
1. Greet the congregation; announce the lesson title and theme verse: 1 John 2:17.
2. Point out the subtitle: living in his will, dying in his will, passing on his will.
3. Set the tone in one sentence: God’s will is not just about doing things; it is about building relationships.
4. Preview the three points, and ask everyone to listen with one question in mind: am I doing tasks, or building relationships?

brief12.title: Introduction: Tasks or Relationship?
notes: Slide text:
God’s will is not just about doing things;
it is about building relationships.
God did not make us for work,
but to walk with him.
Key points:
1. Example: a brother who served eighteen years sat in the empty sanctuary after his appreciation evening and said, “I’m not sure whether God and I still really know each other.”
2. Point out that we often treat God’s will as a task list, assuming that crossing items off brings us closer to God.
3. Go back to Genesis: the first thing God called “not good” was “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18).
4. God called in the garden, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) — the first question God asks man in the Bible is a question about relationship.
5. Definition of revival: our relationships with God, with ourselves and with one another restored.

brief12.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Slide text:
“You are my friends,
if you do whatever I command you.”
John 15:14
A servant follows orders; a friend understands
Key points:
1. Background: John 15 is part of the Farewell Discourse, on the Lord’s way to the Garden of Gethsemane.
2. The Lord did not lay down an organisational constitution; he spoke of the vine and the branches (John 15:5).
3. “Doing” and “friends” are tied together; in the next verse the Lord says, “I have called you friends.”
4. Contrast: a servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions. Obedience is the door into the relationship.

brief12.title: Point 1: Obedience Begins the Relationship
notes: Slide text:
“Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven,
he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”
Matthew 12:50
Obedience turns strangers into family
Key points:
1. Read Matthew 12:50 and describe the scene: his mother and brothers standing outside.
2. The Lord was not denying family ties; on the cross he still entrusted his mother to John.
3. Main point: the closest relationships in God’s kingdom rest not on blood but on doing the Father’s will together.
4. Close with one line: obedience turns a crowd of strangers into one family.

brief12.title: To Listen Is to Trust
notes: Slide text:
Adam didn’t listen — and lost the relationship
Abraham listened — and was blessed
Saul didn’t listen — his kingdom didn’t last
Obey God with the heart, don’t analyse him with the brain
Key points:
1. Move quickly through four figures: Adam (Genesis 3:17), Abraham (Genesis 12:4), Israel (Exodus 19:5), Saul (1 Samuel 13:14).
2. Add “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22).
3. Remind them: Saul’s ministry report looked splendid; what he failed at was not ministry but relationship.
4. Illustration: a five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say “Don’t move” — not because he understands the law, but because he knows the voice that loves him.
5. 321 insight: obeying with the heart builds the relationship; analysing with the brain loses it. “Out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

brief12.title: Point 2: Only the One Who Obeys Remains Forever
notes: Slide text:
“The world is passing away with its lusts,
but he who does God’s will
remains forever.”
1 John 2:17
Key points:
1. Read 1 John 2:17 and explain the background: false teachers had arisen, and believers were wavering between loving the world and loving the Father.
2. Key: the verse says the “person” who does God’s will remains forever, not the “deeds”.
3. Eternity is not stuck onto your results; it is stuck onto you as a person.
4. Optional: Holt-Lunstad’s team’s 2010 meta-analysis found that people with strong social connections had roughly a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival.

brief12.title: Doing God’s Will Is Food for the Spirit
notes: Slide text:
“My food is to do the will
of him who sent me.”
John 4:34
No food, the body weakens; no obedience, the spirit dries up
Key points:
1. The scene: the Lord had walked a long road, tired and thirsty, sitting by the well of Sychar (John 4:34).
2. The Lord did not call it a job or a responsibility; he called it “food”.
3. Illustration: no one wakes up in the morning sighing, “Three meals again today.”
4. Spiritual comparison: if a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.

brief12.title: Point 3: Living in God’s Will
notes: Slide text:
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies,
it remains by itself alone.”
John 12:24
Begin to obey; do what God says
Key points:
1. Read John 12:24 and explain the setting: Passion Week, when some Greeks came asking to see the Lord.
2. The Lord put “being glorified” and “dying” in the same breath.
3. The first level, “living in it”: beginning to obey, being willing to do what God says.
4. Mention the cost: the moment Abraham set out, his tents, livestock, standing and sense of security all had to move with him.
5. Key line: obedience is never completed in the head; it is completed with the feet.

notes: Slide text:
Dying in his will: holding on to the end
“To the point of death” (Philippians 2:8)
Passing it on: helping others live it out
True revival is life multiplying life
Key points:
1. The second level, “dying in it”: Philippians 2:8 — notice the words “to the point of death”.
2. Name our “so long as” clauses: so long as it doesn’t affect my income, doesn’t hurt my reputation, my family doesn’t object — those are the parts not yet dead.
3. Optional: quote Bonhoeffer, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” He was executed in a concentration camp in 1945.
4. The third level, “passing it on”: Moses and Joshua, Jesus and the disciples, Paul and Timothy (2 Timothy 2:2).
5. 321 insight: only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.

Key points:

2. The first thing God called “not good” was “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18).
3. After the fall, God’s first words were “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) — a question about relationship.
4. Optional: Malachi 4:6, turning the hearts of the fathers to the children — God’s definition of end-time revival is the repair of relationships.
5. Conclusion: revival is not lively meetings, but three kinds of relationship restored.

brief21.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Slide text:
“You are my friends,
if you do whatever I command you.”
John 15:14
The Farewell Discourse: the vine and the branches
Key points:
1. Background: John 13–17 is the Farewell Discourse, on the Lord’s way to the Garden of Gethsemane.
2. The book is generally thought to have been written around AD 80 to 90, by the apostle John.
3. The Lord did not lay down an organisational constitution or hand out job assignments; he spoke of the vine (John 15:5).
4. It is in this setting that the Lord speaks verse 14.

brief21.title: Point 1a: Friends and Family
notes: Slide text:
“I have called you friends.”
John 15:15
“Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven,
he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”
Key points:
1. Read on into verse 15: “I have called you friends.”
2. Contrast: a servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions. Obedience raises us from servants to friends.
3. The scene in Matthew 12: his mother and brothers standing outside; the Lord points to his disciples as he speaks.
4. The Lord was not denying family ties — on the cross he still entrusted his mother to John.
5. Conclusion: obedience turns a crowd of strangers into one family.

brief21.title: Point 1b: From Adam to Saul
notes: Slide text:
Adam didn’t listen — the relationship broke
Abraham listened — and was blessed
Israel listened — and became his people
Saul didn’t listen — his kingdom didn’t last
Key points:
1. Move quickly through four figures, reading each verse aloud: Genesis 3:17, Genesis 12:4, Exodus 19:5, 1 Samuel 13:14.
2. Add “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22).
3. Stress that Abraham set out at seventy-five, for a place whose name he had not yet been told.
4. Saul’s ministry report looked splendid; what he failed at was not ministry but relationship.

brief21.title: Point 1c: To Listen Is to Trust
notes: Slide text:
Listening = trust
Obeying = connection
Not completing an order,
but responding to a relationship
Key points:
1. The core: listening = trust; obeying = connection.
2. Illustration: you don’t hand the steering wheel to someone you don’t trust.
3. Illustration: a five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say “Don’t move”; he knows the voice that loves him.
4. The reverse: the serpent said to Eve, “Has God really said …?” — first shake trust, and obedience collapses with it.

brief21.title: Point 1d: The Heart, Not the Brain
notes: Slide text:
Obey God with the heart — build the relationship
Analyse God with the brain — lose the relationship
“Out of it is the wellspring of life”
Proverbs 4:23
Key points:
1. John Bowlby’s attachment theory and Mary Ainsworth’s “Strange Situation” experiment.
2. Securely attached children are more willing to explore and more willing to respond when called — obedience grows out of a secure relationship.
3. The order of the gospel: it is not that we obey first and then God loves us; God first loved us.
4. 321 insight: obeying with the heart builds the relationship; analysing with the brain loses it.
5. Quote Proverbs 4:23: out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

brief21.title: Point 2a: Only the One Who Obeys Remains Forever
notes: Slide text:
“The world is passing away with its lusts,
but he who does God’s will
remains forever.”
1 John 2:17
Key points:
1. Read 1 John 2:17 and give the background: false teachers had arisen, and believers were wavering between loving the world and loving the Father.
2. The previous verse speaks of the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.
3. Key: the verse says the “person” who does God’s will remains forever, not the “deeds”.
4. Eternity is not stuck onto your results; it is stuck onto you as a person.

brief21.title: Point 2b: The Branch and the Root
notes: Slide text:
“He who remains in me
bears much fruit.”
John 15:5
A cut branch withers only after a few days
Key points:
1. Illustration: a branch joined to the root bears fruit; a branch cut off from the root withers.
2. Go further: a freshly cut branch is just as green and leafy; the difference only shows after a few days.
3. Application: a life cut off from God doesn’t wither at once; for a while it “seems fine” — that is exactly the danger.
4. Close with John 15:5.

brief21.title: Point 2c: This Is My Food
notes: Slide text:
“My food is to do the will of him who sent me
and to accomplish his work.”
John 4:34
Not a burden, but life’s supply
Key points:
1. The scene: the Lord had walked a long road, tired and thirsty, sitting by the well of Sychar, and the disciples came back with food.
2. The Lord did not call it a job or a responsibility; he called it “food”.
3. Illustration: no one wakes up in the morning sighing, “Three meals again today.”
4. A reminder: if obedience has always felt like a chore, it means we haven’t yet tasted that it is food.

brief21.title: Point 2d: Food and Famine
notes: Slide text:
Doing God’s will = food for the spiritual life
Not doing God’s will = famine for the spiritual life
From the temporary to the eternal
From the worldly to the godly
Key points:
1. Spiritual comparison: if a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.
2. Data: Julianne Holt-Lunstad’s team’s 2010 meta-analysis — 148 studies, more than 300,000 people; those with strong connections had roughly a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival.
3. Optional: quote Augustine’s Confessions — our heart is restless until it rests in you.
4. The 321 fourfold shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

brief21.title: Point 3a: A Grain of Wheat
notes: Slide text:
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies,
it remains by itself alone. But if it dies,
it bears much fruit.”
John 12:24
Key points:
1. Read John 12:24 and explain the setting: Passion Week, when some Greeks came asking to see the Lord.
2. The Lord answered, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” putting glory and death in the same breath.
3. Introduce the three-level framework: living in it, dying in it, passing it on.
4. A reminder: doing God’s will is not something done once; it is three stages of a whole life.

brief21.title: Point 3b: Living in God’s Will
notes: Slide text:
Begin to obey; do what God says
Obedience happens not in the head, but in the feet
“Not my will, but yours, be done”
Luke 22:42
Key points:
1. Define “living in it”: beginning to obey, being willing to do what God says.
2. Mention the cost: the moment Abraham set out, his tents, livestock, standing and sense of security all had to move with him.
3. Optional: Moses said “but” five times before the burning bush — when the call comes, excuses often arrive first.
4. Key line: obedience is never completed in the head; it is completed with the feet.
5. Example: Luke 22:42, the Lord in Gethsemane.

brief21.title: Point 3c: Dying in God’s Will
notes: Slide text:
Hold on to the end; don’t give up because of circumstances
“Becoming obedient to the point of death,
yes, the death of the cross.”
Philippians 2:8
Key points:
1. Define “dying in it”: holding on to the end, not giving up because of circumstances.
2. Notice the words “to the point of death” in Philippians 2:8; the bottom line of our obedience is our real master.
3. Name our “so long as” clauses: so long as it doesn’t affect my income, doesn’t hurt my reputation, my family doesn’t object.
4. Data: Angela Duckworth’s 2007 research on grit, following new cadets through West Point training.
5. Bonhoeffer: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Martyred in 1945, at only thirty-nine.

brief21.title: Point 3d: Passing On God’s Will
notes: Slide text:
Moses raised up Joshua
Jesus raised up the Twelve
Paul raised up Timothy
True revival is life multiplying life
Key points:
1. Moses and Joshua (Numbers 27:18): passing on is not handing over a post; it is handing over a life.
2. Jesus and the disciples (Mark 3:14): first “that they might be with him”, then sending them out to preach — relationship first, ministry after.
3. Paul and Timothy (2 Timothy 2:2): four generations in a single verse.
4. Data: a single ear of wheat can usually yield thirty to fifty grains; the original grain can no longer be found.
5. 321 insight: only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Slide text:
Am I doing a task, or building a relationship?
One minute each evening to review three things
Obey with the heart, don’t analyse with the brain
Choose one verse each day and live it out
Key points:
1. Exercise 1: every evening, one minute to review three things, checking whether they made the relationship better.
2. Introduce the five areas to examine: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.
3. Exercise 2: each day choose one verse to live out that day, e.g. “be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19).
4. A reminder: don’t first analyse whether it is reasonable; first respond, “Lord, I am willing.”

brief21.title: Practice 3
notes: Slide text:
Deliberately build a relationship
A phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear
The aim is not to solve the problem,
but to let the other person feel loved
Key points:
1. Exercise 3: a phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear; phoning is better than messaging — a voice carries warmth.
2. The aim is not to solve the problem but to let the other person feel loved.
3. The eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
4. A gentle reminder: don’t lose people for the sake of tasks; don’t lose connection for the sake of getting things done.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard,
the Holy Spirit is my guide
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model (he lived in, died in and passed on the Father’s will), the Bible is my standard (Romans 12:2), the Holy Spirit is my guide.
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
3. The order: life first, then relationships, then ministry; first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.
4. The 920 practice and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); the 235 relationships are passing it on put into practice.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Not “how much I do”, but “how deeply I love”
Not “what I complete”, but “whom I connect with”
“This is eternal life, that they should know you”
Let Jesus be King; all glory to Jesus
Key points:
1. Return to the brother in the introduction: what he needed was not to stop serving, but to put the order back in place.
2. Eighteen years of offering will not be in vain; they will turn from “performance” into “fruit”.
3. Quote John 17:3: the definition of eternal life is “knowing” — it is relationship.
4. Three invitations: let Jesus be King over your obedience, your perseverance and your passing it on.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I will no longer be just someone who gets things done
I will be someone who builds relationships
Make me that grain of wheat that willingly falls into the ground
Living out Christ, becoming a Victor
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in declaring these together; slow down, and let them repeat line by line.
2. Pray for three groups: those who are busy yet distant, those whose obedience is stuck, and those who have not yet begun passing it on.
3. Invite each person to name one “2” in their heart and go and care for them today.
4. Blessing: may the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ; may we live out Christ and become Victors.

script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 147, entitled “The Centre of God’s Will Is Building Relationships”. Our theme verse is 1 John 2:17: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” Today we will take three steps: living in his will, dying in his will, and passing on his will.
Brothers and sisters, let me start with a question. What do you think “doing God’s will” means? Is it finishing a job, hitting a target, running a ministry well?

There was a brother who had served for eighteen years, and the church held an appreciation evening for him. When it was over, he sat in the emptied sanctuary and said, “I’ve done so many things, but I’m not sure whether God and I still really know each other.”
Brothers and sisters, the answer the Bible gives us is this: God’s will is not just about doing things; God’s will is about building relationships. God did not make us for work, but to walk with him.
On the way to the Garden of Gethsemane, the Lord Jesus said, “You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.” And in the next verse he says, “I have called you friends.”

Please see this key point: the Lord ties “doing” and “friends” together. The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much each one does, but whether he understands his master’s heart. A servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions. Obedience is the door into the relationship.
In Matthew 12:50 the Lord says, “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

Brothers and sisters, what a staggering statement. In the kingdom of God, the closest relationships rest not on blood, but on doing the Father’s will together. Obedience turns a crowd of strangers into one family.
From Genesis to the New Testament, God keeps repeating one thing: he wants people to listen to his word.
Adam failed because he did not listen. Abraham was blessed because he listened. Israel was chosen in order to listen. Saul was rejected because he did not listen.
Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that Saul did nothing. He fought battles; he offered sacrifices. What he failed at was not ministry but relationship.
So, to listen is to trust; to obey is to connect. It’s like a child listening to his father — not because of the rules, but because of love and trust.

Here is the 321 insight: obey God with the heart and you build the relationship; analyse God with the brain and you lose the relationship. Many people know a great deal yet are far from God, because relying on the brain is not the same as relying on the heart.
First John 2:17 tells us that everything in the world will pass away; only one thing remains forever — the one who does God’s will.
Please notice: John speaks of the “person”, not the “deeds”. Eternity is not stuck onto your results; eternity is stuck onto you as a person.
Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.” He didn’t call it a job, and he didn’t call it a responsibility; he called it food.
Brothers and sisters, doing God’s will is not a burden; it is life’s supply. If a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.
The Lord said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

Doing God’s will has three levels. First, living in God’s will: beginning to obey, being willing to do what God says. Brothers and sisters, obedience is not completed in the head; it is completed with the feet. At this stage we often meet difficulty, struggle, and the challenge of circumstances.

Second, dying in God’s will: holding on to the end, not giving up because of circumstances. Paul says the Lord became “obedient to the point of death”. If our obedience has a bottom line, that bottom line is our real master.

Third, passing on God’s will: not only living it out yourself but also helping others to live it out. Moses raised up Joshua; Jesus raised up disciples. This is life influencing life, life multiplying life.
True revival means life multiplying life — not one person on fire, but a whole company of people raised up. Only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.
Brothers and sisters, how do we put this lesson into practice?
First, ask yourself every day: right now, am I doing a task, or building a relationship? Every evening, take one minute to look back over three things.
Second, practise obeying with the heart rather than analysing with the brain. Each day choose one verse and deliberately live it out that day.
Third, deliberately build a relationship: a phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear. The aim is not to solve the problem, but to let the other person feel loved.
Don’t lose people for the sake of tasks; don’t lose connection for the sake of getting things done.
Dear brothers and sisters, God’s will is not a task list; it is a road of relationship.
When you truly grasp this, the focus is no longer “how much I do”, but “how deeply I love”; no longer “what I complete”, but “whom I connect with”.
May we live in his will, die in his will, and pass on his will. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let us pray together.

Dear Heavenly Father, please forgive us — we have so often substituted busyness for closeness, and ministry for relationship. Lord, I will no longer be just someone who gets things done; I will be someone who builds relationships. Make me that grain of wheat that willingly falls into the ground, living out Christ and becoming a Victor. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 147, entitled “The Centre of God’s Will Is Building Relationships”. Our theme verse is 1 John 2:17: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” In this lesson we will take three steps: living in his will, dying in his will, and passing on his will.

Let me begin with a true scene. There was a brother who had served in his church for eighteen years. Worship team, small group, conference organiser — wherever someone was missing, there he was. One year, at year’s end, the church held an appreciation evening for him, and from the platform the pastor counted off, one by one, all the things he had done.
When it was over, he sat alone in the emptied sanctuary. Later he said, “In these eighteen years I’ve done so many things. But I’m not so sure whether God and I still really know each other.”
Brothers and sisters, that sentence is like a needle. It is very easy for us to understand “doing God’s will” as a task list.
But the Bible shows us a deeper truth: God’s will is not just about doing things; God’s will is about building relationships.

Look at Genesis. When God made man, he did not first hand Adam a work schedule; he breathed his own breath into him, and walked with him in the garden. The first thing God called “not good” was this: “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

After man fell, the first thing God did was not to pronounce a sentence, but to call out, “Where are you?” This is the first question God asks man in the whole Bible, and it is a question about relationship.
Revival is the same: not lively meetings, but relationships restored — our relationship with God, with ourselves, and with one another.
Let’s look first at the background. John 15 belongs to the Lord’s Farewell Discourse; the setting is after the Last Supper, on the way to the Garden of Gethsemane.

The Lord knew the hour for him to leave the world had come. He did not lay down a constitution for an organisation, nor did he hand out job assignments. He spoke of a vine: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” And right here the Lord says, “You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.”

In the next verse the Lord says, “I have called you friends.” Brothers and sisters, the Lord ties “doing” and “friends” together. The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much each one does, but whether he understands his master’s heart. A servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions.

In Matthew 12, someone tells the Lord that his mother and brothers are waiting outside. But the Lord points to his disciples and says, “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” In the kingdom of God, the closest relationships rest not on blood, but on doing the Father’s will together.
From Genesis to the New Testament, God keeps repeating one thing: he wants people to listen to his word.

Adam failed because he did not listen to God. Abraham was blessed because he listened to God — at seventy-five he left his country, his relatives and his father’s house. Israel was chosen in order to listen to God. Saul was rejected because he did not listen to God; Samuel said, “To obey is better than sacrifice.”
Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that Saul did nothing. He fought battles, he offered sacrifices, and his ministry report looked splendid. What he failed at was not ministry but relationship.
So at the heart of all this history is not “right and wrong” but “relationship”. To listen is to trust; to obey is to connect.

You don’t hand the steering wheel to someone you don’t trust. It’s like a child listening to his father: a five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say, “Don’t move,” and he stops. He stops not because he has understood the traffic laws, but because he knows that voice, and he knows that voice loves him.

Turn it the other way round: the root of disobedience is not a lack of information; it is a broken relationship. When the serpent said to Eve, “Has God really said …?”, he was first shaking her trust. Once trust collapses, obedience collapses with it.

Psychology offers us some corroborating evidence. The British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and his colleague Mary Ainsworth tested it with her “Strange Situation” experiment: children with a secure attachment to their caregiver are actually more willing to explore, and also more willing to respond when the mother calls. The capacity to obey grows out of a secure relationship.
This is exactly the order of the gospel: it is not that we obey first and then God loves us; it is that God first loved us, and so we are able to obey.

Here is the 321 insight: obey God with the heart and you build the relationship; analyse God with the brain and you lose the relationship. Many people know a great deal yet are far from God. For “out of it is the wellspring of life”.
Our second point. First John 2:17 tells us that everything in the world will pass away; only one thing remains forever — doing God’s will.
Why? Because doing God’s will is not merely behaving correctly; it is being connected in God.
Please notice: John says it is “the one who does God’s will” who remains forever — the person, not the deeds. Eternity is not stuck onto your results; eternity is stuck onto you as a person.
It is like a tree. A branch joined to the root has life and bears fruit; a branch cut off from the root withers and dies.
Brothers and sisters, when a branch has just been cut, it looks exactly like the branches still on the tree — just as green, just as leafy. The difference only shows after a few days.
Our spiritual condition is like that too. A life cut off from God doesn’t wither at once; for a while it “seems fine”. That is exactly where the danger lies.

That day the Lord had walked a long road; he was tired and thirsty, and he sat by the well of Sychar. The disciples came back with food and urged him to eat, yet he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.”
He didn’t call it a job, and he didn’t call it a responsibility; he called it food. Doing God’s will is not a burden; it is life’s supply.

It’s just like eating — no one wakes up in the morning sighing, “Oh dear, three meals again today.” If obeying God has always felt like a chore in your heart, that usually means we haven’t yet tasted that it is food.
So please remember: if a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.

In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad’s team at Brigham Young University in the United States published a large meta-analysis bringing together 148 studies and more than 300,000 participants. They found that people with strong social connections had roughly a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival.
Even these perishable bodies of ours were made according to the principle of relationship. How much more our relationship with the everlasting God?
The 321 vision speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.
Our third point. The Lord said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
The Lord spoke these words in Passion Week. Some Greeks had come asking to see him, and the Lord said, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he spoke of this grain of wheat.
Brothers and sisters, the Lord put “being glorified” and “dying” in the same breath. Doing God’s will has three levels: living in it, dying in it, and passing it on.
The first level: living in God’s will means beginning to obey, being willing to do what God says.

This is the starting point, but at this stage we often meet difficulty, struggle, and the challenge of circumstances. Because the moment obedience touches the ground, it runs into a cost. If Abraham had merely agreed in his heart, nothing would have happened; the moment he set out, his tents, his livestock, his standing, his sense of security — all of it had to move with him.
Obedience has never been completed in the head; obedience is completed with the feet. In Gethsemane the Lord said, “Not my will, but yours, be done.”
The second level: dying in God’s will means holding on to the end, not giving up because of circumstances.

Jesus on the cross is the most complete example: “becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” Notice the words “to the point of death”. If our obedience has a bottom line, that bottom line is our real master.

In 2007 Angela Duckworth of the University of Pennsylvania published her research on “grit”. Following new cadets at West Point through gruelling training, she found that what predicted who would make it through was not fitness, not grades, but grit. How much more the road of the kingdom of heaven?
The martyred pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer said, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” In 1945 he was executed in a concentration camp, at only thirty-nine.
The third level: passing on God’s will means not only living it out yourself but also helping others to live it out.

Moses raised up Joshua. Joshua was not parachuted in; he was the one who had followed Moses all through the forty years in the wilderness. Passing on is not handing over a post; passing on is handing over a life.

Jesus raised up disciples: “that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” Relationship first, ministry after. Paul raised up Timothy, and charged him to entrust what he had heard to faithful men who would be able to teach others.

Let’s come back to that grain of wheat. A single ear can usually yield thirty to fifty grains. And the original grain? You can no longer find it. If you want to keep that one grain, you will only ever have that one grain; if you are willing to be buried, God will grow a whole field.
