script12.title: The Priority of Relationships
script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we read together “The Priority of Relationships”, with the subtitle: connect with God first, then face everyone and everything else. Our theme verse is John 17:3: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” To know God is eternal life. Let us grow quiet together and first give our hearts to God.

script12.title: Not Lacking Relationships — the Order Is Wrong
script: There was a sister whom everyone in her church praised as a wonderful co-worker. One day, after a time of service, she wept and said, “I’ve done so much for God, but it’s been a very long time since I last talked with him.” Brothers and sisters, did she lack relationships? No. What she lacked was order. God’s will is to build relationships; but today we go a step further: not every relationship is God’s will — the key lies in order. When the order is wrong, good things can turn wrong, and even spiritual actions can offend God. Graphite and diamond are both made of carbon; the only difference is the order of arrangement. The same material, in a different order, and the value is worlds apart.

script12.title: Theme Verse and Background
script: When were these words spoken? The Lord Jesus spoke them after the Last Supper, before he went to the cross. John 13 to 17 is the Upper Room Discourse, and chapter 17 is called the High Priestly Prayer. That night the Lord interceded for his disciples, and for all in every age who would believe in him. Brothers and sisters, you were in that prayer, and so was I. At just such a moment, the Lord gave a definition of “eternal life”. Listen carefully: eternal life is not a length of time; it is a depth of relationship.

script12.title: 1. The First Priority Is Our Relationship with God
script: Many people think eternal life simply means going to heaven when we die, or never dying. But the Lord says eternal life is knowing God. This word “know”, in the Greek, does not mean storing information in your head; it means coming to know a person through experience. So knowing God has never meant studying God; it means walking with him. Jeremiah 9:23–24 says: don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, don’t let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; let him who glories glory in knowing Yahweh. The Lord also said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness.” That one word, “first”, sets the order of a whole life.

script12.title: The Source of Love Is God
script: “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Brothers and sisters, we have no stored supply of love within us, only a flow of love. God is the source, and we are the pipe. If the pipe is cut off from the source, however hard you squeeze, no water will come out. When you fly, the cabin crew always say: when the oxygen masks drop, put on your own first, before helping others. Someone who has already run out of oxygen can save no one. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and running for more than eighty years, concludes that good relationships keep us happier and healthier. The Bible told us long before that we are made first of all for a relationship with God. Focus on Jesus, and the order is right; focus on yourself, and the order falls apart.

script12.title: 2. When the Order Is Wrong, Good Turns Wrong
script: Saul waited at Gilgal for Samuel — seven days. The people were scattering, the Philistines were pressing in, he could no longer stand firm, so he offered the burnt offering himself. Was offering sacrifice wrong? No. His wrong was that he did not wait for God. Samuel said, “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). The original word for “obey” means to hear and to act on what you hear. Sacrifice is giving something to God; obedience is giving ourselves to God. We would often rather sacrifice than obey, because sacrifice is something I can control, while obedience requires me to hand over my sovereignty.

script12.title: Self-Centred: Tasks; Selfless: God
script: Saul himself later said, “I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” Now the truth comes out — he had put people ahead of God. And the result? Yahweh rejected him from being king. In the New Testament, Martha was anxious and troubled about many things, and the Lord said: one thing is needed. The church in Ephesus was good on every count, yet the Lord said: you left your first love. Researchers who studied football goalkeepers found that they almost always dive left or right and rarely stay where they are; this is called “action bias”. Brothers and sisters, the mistake we most easily make under pressure is not laziness; it is reaching out to act ahead of God. The 321 vision says: the self-centred person will sacrifice relationships to reach the goal; the selfless person will lay down the task to keep the relationship.

script12.title: 3. God Values Relationship More Than Service
script: Lift your eyes to eternity. In Revelation 4, heaven has no reports and no performance targets — only worship. Revelation 21 says, “I will be his God, and he will be my son.” The Bible begins in Eden, with God present among people; the Bible ends in the New Jerusalem, with God dwelling among people. From beginning to end the whole Bible is about one thing: relationship. Paul says love never fails. Prophecy will stop, languages will cease, knowledge will be done away with; only relationship lasts for ever.

script12.title: God Doesn’t Want Workers; God Wants Sons
script: The prodigal son’s elder brother said to his father: these many years I have served you. He was in the house, but his heart was outside. The father said, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” What the father wanted was not his labour but his presence. Paul counted his pedigree, his education and his zeal as refuse, that he might gain Christ. Edward Tronick carried out the “Still Face Experiment”: when the mother suddenly goes expressionless and stops responding to her baby, within a few dozen seconds the baby breaks down in tears. The mother is still there, the care is still there — only the relationship has stopped. We need not only to be fed, but to be responded to. That is why 321 says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry.

script12.title: Practice: Reordering
script: Three practices — start them today. First, each day build your relationship with God first, then step into the day’s tasks. Don’t reach for your phone first; pray first, draw near to God first, for a regular five to fifteen minutes. Second, before each thing you do, ask first: will this affect my relationship with God? Stop and ask at least three times a day. Third, when tasks and people clash and pressure rises, first pray one sentence: “Lord, I choose to align myself with you first.” Don’t lose obedience because of the hurry; don’t lose closeness because of the busyness. Let’s also deepen these with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Once doesn’t count as practice; repetition does — and take it to your “2” as well.

script12.title: Closing and Call
script: Brothers and sisters, you can be very busy serving and yet be far from God; you can do many right things and yet live in the wrong order. The key to life is not how much you do, but whom you connect with first. When the order is right, everything is right; when the order is wrong, everything is in disarray. Today the Lord is not asking you to lay down your service; he is asking you to put your service back in its proper place. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

script12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
script: Let us pray together. Lord! I want to reorder my life and make you first in my life. I will no longer put tasks ahead of you; I will no longer let busyness replace relationship. I will connect with you first, and then face all people and all tasks. All my life, let me not just do many things for you, but walk with you and live out Christ. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May you connect with God first today, then face everyone and everything else, live out the life that belongs to God, and become a Victor.

script21.title: The Priority of Relationships
script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we come together to read “The Priority of Relationships”, with the subtitle: connect with God first, then face everyone and everything else. Our theme verse is John 17:3: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” To know God is eternal life. Let us first be still for a moment, and ask the Holy Spirit to speak to us himself this morning.

script21.title: Not Lacking Relationships — the Order Is Wrong
script: Let me begin with a scene. There was a sister whom everyone in her church praised as a wonderful co-worker. She led a small group, ran the choir, looked after the kitchen and drove the sick to hospital; her calendar was packed solid. One day, after a time of service, she broke down and wept, and said, “I’ve done so much for God, but it’s been a very long time since I last talked with him.” Brothers and sisters, did she lack relationships? She had relationships with people, with tasks, with the church. What she lacked was not relationship but order. In our last lesson we saw that God’s will is to build relationships; today we go a step further: not every relationship is God’s will — the key lies in order.

script21.title: Order Determines Value
script: How important is order? Take the same seven digits: in the right order, the call goes through; in the wrong order, you ring a stranger. Take the same notes: in a different order, they can make a requiem or a lullaby. Chemists tell us further that graphite and diamond are made of exactly the same element — carbon; the only difference is the order in which the atoms are arranged. One is black and soft; the other is crystal-clear and hard. Brothers and sisters, the same twenty-four hours, in the right order, become a diamond that glorifies God; in the wrong order, they become black coal that wears us down. Today we will see three truths: relationships have an order; order determines right and wrong; and order determines whether we are living within God’s will.

script21.title: Theme Verse and Background
script: When were these words spoken? The author of John’s Gospel is John, the disciple whom the Lord loved; it is generally thought to have been written between AD 85 and 95, in his old age in Ephesus. Chapters 13 to 17 are known as the Upper Room Discourse, the farewell words the Lord spoke after the Last Supper and before going to the Garden of Gethsemane. By chapter 17 he no longer speaks to the disciples; he lifts up his eyes and speaks to the Father, and so this chapter is called the High Priestly Prayer. Brothers and sisters, that night he prayed not only for his disciples but for all in every age who would believe in him — you were in that prayer, and so was I. What someone leaves as a parting charge always lies heaviest on their heart. He did not say, “Do a bit more for me”; he said, “Know me — this is eternal life.”

script21.title: 1. The First Priority Is Our Relationship with God
script: Many people think eternal life simply means going to heaven when we die, or never dying. That isn’t entirely wrong, but it falls far short. By the Lord’s own definition, eternal life equals knowing God — that is, entering into a relationship with God. John 3:36 says, “One who believes in the Son has eternal life” — in the present tense. It is not something we have only after death; we have it now. Brothers and sisters, this distinction matters enormously. If eternal life is only a length of time, then believing in the Lord is like buying insurance, and the point is the future; if eternal life is a depth of relationship, then believing in the Lord is entering a relationship of love, and the point is now.

script21.title: Knowing Is the Most Intimate Fellowship
script: The word “know” here is the Greek γινώσκω. It does not mean how much data is stored in your head, but coming to know a person through experience. It corresponds to the Hebrew yada’. In Genesis 4:1, “The man knew Eve his wife”, the original uses exactly that word, yada’ — the most intimate kind of knowing. So when the Bible speaks of knowing God, it never means studying God; it means walking closely with him. Brothers and sisters, ask yourself honestly: do I “know about God”, or do I “know God”?

script21.title: What Matters Most Is Not Success
script: Jeremiah puts it with a razor’s edge: don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, don’t let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh (Jeremiah 9:23–24). Learning, status and money are the three summits people strive for, and God says none of them is anything to boast about; the only thing worth boasting in is knowing him. That is why the Lord said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment.” The commandments are not a jumbled list; they have an order. The Lord also said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness.” That one word, “first”, sets the order of a whole life.

script21.title: The Source of Love Is God
script: “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Brothers and sisters, we have no stored supply of love within us, only a flow of love. God is the source, and we are the pipe; if the pipe is cut off from the source, however hard you squeeze, no water will come out. The cabin crew always say: when the oxygen masks drop, put on your own first, before helping others. Someone who has already run out of oxygen can save no one. Without this foundation, our relationship with others becomes twisted, our relationship with ourselves falls into confusion, and our relationship with things falls out of balance. Augustine said: our heart is restless until it rests in you. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, following people since 1938 for more than eighty years, tells us too: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.

script21.title: 2. When the Order Is Wrong, Good Turns Wrong
script: Saul was the first king of Israel, and neither of his two falls came from doing anything obviously evil; both came from doing the right thing in the wrong order. The first was at Gilgal. The Philistines were pressing in and the people were scattering; he waited seven days, the time Samuel had set, and still Samuel had not come, so he offered the burnt offering himself. The very moment he finished, Samuel arrived and said, “You have done foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of Yahweh your God, which he commanded you.” Brothers and sisters, offering sacrifice was a good thing, a spiritual thing. So where was the wrong? The wrong was that he did not wait for God. He put sacrifice ahead of obedience, and the task ahead of God.

script21.title: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
script: The second fall came after the battle against the Amalekites. God commanded that everything be destroyed, but Saul spared King Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, and even said they were to be sacrificed to Yahweh. Samuel’s reply is our theme verse today: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). The Hebrew for “obey” is shama’, meaning to hear and to act on what you hear; to hear without doing is the same as not hearing at all. The Shema, which Israel recites every day, opens with “Hear, Israel.” Sacrifice is giving something to God; obedience is giving ourselves to God. We would rather sacrifice than obey, because sacrifice is something I can control, while obedience requires me to hand over my sovereignty.

script21.title: Three New Testament Warnings
script: The New Testament gives three warnings. The first is gentle: the Lord said to Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Busyness is not sin; the danger comes when busyness replaces closeness. The second is a rebuke: the Lord said to the church in Ephesus, you left your first love; they were good on every count, but they had lost love and were left only with doing. The third is the most sobering: in Matthew 7, some say, Lord, didn’t we prophesy, cast out demons and do mighty works in your name? And the Lord says: I never knew you. They had ministry, gifts and results; the only thing they lacked was knowing. In 2007 Michael Bar-Eli and his colleagues studied football goalkeepers and found that, facing penalty kicks, they almost always dive left or right and rarely stay where they are; this is called “action bias”. Brothers and sisters, the mistake we most easily make under pressure is not laziness; it is reaching out to act ahead of God.

script21.title: Self-Centred: Tasks; Selfless: God
script: Saul’s confession exposes the truth: “I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” He feared people more than he feared God. The result: because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king. 321 tells us that the root of the fall is the self-centred life, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The self-centred person will sacrifice relationships to reach the goal; the selfless person will lay down the task to keep the relationship. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

script21.title: 3. God Values Relationship More Than Service
script: Please lift your eyes to the farthest horizon of all — eternity. Before the throne in heaven in Revelation 4 there are no meetings, no reports, no performance targets. The four living creatures say day and night without rest: Holy, holy, holy! The elders lay their crowns before the throne. The whole picture of heaven is about one thing only: relationship with God. Revelation 21 says God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them; then comes that most tender promise: “I will be his God, and he will be my son.” The Bible begins with God’s presence in Eden and ends with God dwelling among people in the New Jerusalem. The beginning and the end are both relationship. Paul says: love never fails.

script21.title: Walk with God, Gain Christ
script: Genesis 5 records a long litany of “and he died”, and only one man is different: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.” The Bible does not record what he built or what he achieved; it records only this: he walked with God. Micah 6:8 also distils God’s requirement into one sentence: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. Paul says, I count all things to be a loss, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ. The Greek for “refuse” is σκύβαλον — dregs thrown out. He threw away his pedigree, his education and his zeal, not to gain a ministry but to gain Christ. Brothers and sisters, this is the watershed: are you pursuing gaining something, or gaining him?

script21.title: God Doesn’t Want Workers; God Wants Sons
script: If a child only helps his father with the work but has no relationship with him, the father will not be satisfied. The prodigal son’s elder brother is an example. He said, “Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours.” He was in the house, but his heart was outside; the word he used was “served”, not “with you”. The father said, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” What the father wanted was not his labour but his presence. The developmental psychologist Edward Tronick’s “Still Face Experiment” shows us that when a mother suddenly goes expressionless, within a few dozen seconds the baby breaks down in tears. The mother is still right there, and the care hasn’t stopped — she has only stopped the relationship. Deep down in how we are made, we need not only to be fed, but to be responded to, to be seen and to be loved.

script21.title: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
script: So 321 says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; the order of service is life first, then relationships, then ministry. These three stages cannot be reversed. Relationship without life is mere socialising; ministry without relationship is mere engineering. Many rifts in churches arise because we do things backwards — charging into ministry first, patching up relationships afterwards, and only at the end discovering that life has long since run dry. 321 also gives us the order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. The first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism says: man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. Not “to do lots of things for God for ever”, but “to enjoy him”.

script21.title: Practice (1)
script: Our lesson gives us three practices. First, each day build your relationship with God first, then step into the day’s tasks. Don’t reach for your phone first; pray first, draw near to God first, for a regular five to fifteen minutes. In 1927 the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik showed that unfinished tasks stay especially vivid in our memory — the Zeigarnik effect; so the moment we open our eyes, unfinished business automatically queues up. If the first thing we do on waking is scroll our phone, then before the day has even begun, our hearts are already filled with other people’s agendas. Same place, same time, phone in another room; don’t aim for long, aim only for real. Second, before each thing you do, ask first: will this affect my relationship with God? At least three times a day — before you go out, before lunch, before bed — ask, and then write one line.

script21.title: Practice (2)
script: Third, when tasks and people clash, choose to guard your relationship with God. Don’t lose obedience because of the hurry; don’t lose closeness because of the busyness. The practice is simple: first pray one sentence, “Lord, I choose to align myself with you first.” Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the sentence Saul most needed that day at Gilgal. When pressure comes, the heart races and our thinking narrows; a short prayer is like grabbing hold of the handrail before stepping into the rapids. Let’s deepen this with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information — write the truth down; Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to show where my order has gone wrong; Conviction — accept from the heart that relationship matters more than doing; Implementation — tomorrow morning, the first thing is not your phone but prayer; Evaluation — two minutes each evening to look back; Correction — adjust at once when you drift; Repetition — thirty days makes a practice; Multiplication — walk it together with your “2”.

script21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
script: Let’s place what we have seen today into the blueprint of 321. Jesus is my role model — Mark 1:35 says that early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus rose and went out to a deserted place to pray; the evening before, the whole town had crowded at the door, yet he went first to be alone with the Father. The Bible is my standard — our feelings say, get the job done first; the Bible says, to obey is better than sacrifice. The Holy Spirit is my guide — he will remind you: you haven’t been still for three days now. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; in the end, the question of order is a question of the throne. The Goal: establish God’s system — and a system must have order. The fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — is itself an order. 920 reminds us that only when our relationship with God is right can we bear the fruit of the Spirit before our “2”. Fruit is borne, not made.

script21.title: Closing and Call
script: Dear brothers and sisters, the key to life is not how much you do, but whom you connect with first. When the order is right, everything is right; when the order is wrong, everything is in disarray. You can be very busy serving and yet be far from God; you can do many right things and yet live in the wrong order. This morning the Lord is calling us. He is not asking you to lay down your service; he is asking you to put your service back in its proper place. He doesn’t complain that you do too much; his heart simply aches that you do it so alone. To let Jesus be King means to let him sit in first place — not second place, not near the front, but first place. To let Jesus receive all the glory means we no longer steal a little glory for ourselves from our ministry.

script21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
script: Let us pray together. Lord! I want to reorder my life and make you first in my life. I will no longer put tasks ahead of you; I will no longer let busyness replace relationship. I will connect with you first, and then face all people and all tasks. Forgive me for the many times I reached out to act ahead of you, for the times I pushed you aside because I feared people. Place a fresh longing for you within me, so that each morning you are the first one I think of, and under pressure you are the first one I call on. All my life, let me not just do many things for you, but walk with you and live out Christ. Let Jesus reign as King; let Jesus receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May you connect with God first today, then face everyone and everything else, live out the life that belongs to God, and become a Victor.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Hardest Person to Live With Lives Inside You
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

A sister once said to me: “Pastor, I get on quite well with the people at church, and I’m on reasonably good terms with my colleagues. With my family there’s the occasional friction, but it’s manageable. But there’s one person I fight with every day, from morning till night, and it hasn’t stopped for thirty years.” I asked her, “Who is that person?” She lowered her head, and after a long, long pause she said quietly: “It’s me.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever known that? Late at night, when all is still, the lights are off and the door is locked, and you’re lying in bed alone. At that moment, the voice that is quickest to condemn you, quickest to rake over your past, quickest to remind you that “you’re not good enough”, does not come from your enemy; it comes from your own heart. By day you can forgive others; by night you refuse to forgive yourself.

We often think the pain in our lives comes from difficult circumstances, from clashes with people, from things not working out. We pour enormous effort into changing our circumstances, changing other people, changing things. Yet for all the changing, the pain is still there. Why? Because the root of the problem is not outside; it is inside. If someone has no good relationship with themselves, even if they moved to a deserted island, they would still have to live with someone very hard to live with — themselves.

In our last lesson we saw together that the first priority in relationships is “our relationship with God”. God is the source; cut off from the source, every relationship runs dry. Today we take one step further, to see the second key in the order of relationships: our relationship with ourselves.

Here are two sentences, brothers and sisters; please hold them in your hearts:

Without a relationship with God, there can be no relationship with ourselves.

Without a relationship with ourselves, there can be no relationship with others.

This is not a slogan from psychology; it is the order of Scripture. When God created humankind, first came the relationship between God and man — God breathed the breath of life into man’s nostrils; then came man’s relationship with himself — “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25); and only last came the relationships between people, and between people and all creation. When people sinned and their relationship with God was broken, the very first thing that happened next was that their relationship with themselves broke — they realised they were naked, sewed fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves, and then hid. Brothers and sisters, covering up and hiding are the oldest symptoms of a person’s broken relationship with themselves.

The Reformer John Calvin, at the opening of Book One, Chapter One of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, wrote a sentence that has been quoted for nearly five hundred years: nearly all our wisdom consists of two parts — the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. He goes on to say that the two are bound together, and that no one ever truly knows himself unless he has first looked upon the face of God. That is the heart of today’s lesson.

So today we are not here to learn a set of psychological techniques for “loving yourself”. We are here to see afresh, in God’s light, one truth: our relationship with ourselves grows out of our relationship with God; and a life in which the inside and the outside agree is lived out by the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Settings
sections.html:
Today’s message rests on three passages. Let’s first get to know their background briefly, so that we don’t read them out of context.

The first is Matthew 22:37–40. These words were spoken during Passion Week. The Lord Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey on Sunday and cleansed the Temple on Monday; in the days that followed, the chief priests, scribes, Pharisees and Sadducees took turns testing him with one question after another. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar? In the resurrection, whose wife will that woman be? Finally a lawyer came forward and asked him: “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?”

The Jewish rabbis of the time divided the Law of Moses into six hundred and thirteen commandments and argued endlessly over which weighed most. This was an academic trap and a spiritual trap — because whichever commandment Jesus chose, he would offend one faction or another.

Yet Jesus’ answer gathered up the whole mountain range of the law in one stroke. He quoted Deuteronomy 6:5, the Shema that every devout Jew recited morning and evening; and he quoted Leviticus 19:18: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He put one first and the other second, and then said: “The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” The Greek word behind “depend” means “to hang” — the whole Old Testament is like a door hung on these two hinges. Brothers and sisters, for a door to open smoothly, both hinges must be aligned; lose one, and the door hangs crooked.

The second is James 1:22. James was the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and the leader of the church in Jerusalem. His letter may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament, written to Jewish Christians scattered abroad and suffering persecution. James is practical, direct and doesn’t beat about the bush: in its one hundred and eight verses there are nearly sixty commands. What concerned him most was this: faith without works is dead. So he says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

The third is Romans 7:15 and 8:2. Romans is Paul’s letter to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited, written around AD 56–57, probably from Corinth. Chapter 7 is the most naked confession in the whole Bible: “For I don’t know what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15) Paul is not describing here how bad an unbeliever is; he is describing how utterly powerless a person becomes when relying only on the law and on their own willpower. He writes all the way to Romans 7:24, where he cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” Then his pen turns, and chapter 8 opens with the light of dawn: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus… For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order of these three passages: Matthew tells us “the relationship we should have”, James points out “the symptoms of the break”, and Romans gives us “the way out to victory”. That is also the order of today’s three key points.

sections.heading: 1. The Precondition for Loving Your Neighbour as Yourself: A Healthy Relationship with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the first key point.

“A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matthew 22:39)

When we read this verse, we usually see only the first part: “love your neighbour”. We put the whole weight of the verse on “love your neighbour”, and then reproach ourselves: why can’t I manage to love? But in this sentence the Lord Jesus has placed a key, and that key is in the last word — “yourself”.

“Love your neighbour as yourself” — in the original, “love your neighbour as you love yourself”. The little Greek word for “as” is both a scale and a measuring cup. What the Lord Jesus means is this: the way you treat yourself is the mould for the way you treat others.

Life confirms it everywhere. Someone who is extremely harsh on themselves finds it hard to be lenient with others; someone who judges themselves in their heart every day will judge others the moment they open their mouth; someone who will never forgive themselves finds it hard to truly forgive others. Conversely, someone who lives in God’s grace every day has a gentle gaze and gracious words. For no one can give what they do not have.

Many people cannot love others, not because others are bad, but because there is no love inside themselves. If you draw water from a dry well, however many times you lower the bucket, it comes up empty.

So here is the question: on what basis can I accept myself?

If the basis is “I perform well”, then on the day I fail I cannot accept myself. If the basis is “other people praise me”, then on the day they turn away, I collapse. If the basis is “I’m better than so-and-so”, then I must live my whole life in comparison and never find rest.

The Bible gives us an entirely different basis:

“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.” (Hebrews 4:15–16)

Brothers and sisters, look at the logic of these two verses. We can come “with boldness”, not because we are good enough, but because the throne is “the throne of grace”; not because we have no weaknesses, but because that High Priest can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities”. When we come, we are not holding a report card; we come with empty hands. And what we receive is not wages, but mercy and grace.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, let’s look at four more passages:

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) God loves us not after we have become better, but while we were yet sinners.

“to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). Our standing as accepted is “in the Beloved”, not in ourselves.

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The authority to condemn is in God’s hands; since God does not condemn, what right do I have to condemn myself every day?

“We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) All love — including that healthy way of regarding yourself, neither inflated nor belittling — flows from this source: God first loved us.

Brothers and sisters, we must make a particular distinction here. The self-acceptance the Bible speaks of is not at all the “feeling good about yourself” that is so fashionable today. In a major literature review published in 2003 in the journal Psychological Science in the Public Interest, the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues found that high self-esteem in itself does not make people do better at school, get on better with others or behave less badly, and that educational programmes designed to boost self-esteem have limited effect. In other words, trying to build your worth by constantly telling yourself “I’m amazing” is a house built on sand.

What truly makes us secure is not “my assessment of myself” but “God’s declaration over me”. The difference between the two is the difference between sand and rock.

I often use this illustration. Take a hundred-dollar note, screw it up into a ball, trample it underfoot and smear it with mud — what is it worth? Still a hundred dollars. Because its value lies not in its appearance but in the central bank that issued it. Brothers and sisters, your worth does not lie in the state you’re in today, but in the one who issued you — God created you in his own image and bought you back with the blood of his beloved only Son. The psalmist says: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.” (Psalm 139:14)

In the light of 321, this becomes even clearer.

The self-centred person is either insecure or proud.

Notice that insecurity and pride look like opposite poles, but they actually share the same root — both put the focus on the self. The proud person says, “I’m better than you.” The insecure person says, “I’m worse than you.” The subject of both sentences is “I”, and the yardstick of both is “other people”. So the proud person, once they fall, becomes insecure; the insecure person, once they succeed, becomes proud. They ride up and down on the same seesaw and never know peace all their lives.

The selfless person, however, has a third way. Selflessness is not having no self, not destroying the self, still less despising the self God made. Selflessness is “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) Selflessness is not entering emptiness but entering into the fullness of Jesus; not being erased but being filled.

So the selfless person can honestly say: I have weaknesses, but I am not defined by my weaknesses; I have gifts, but I don’t boast in my gifts. That is exactly what Paul says: “But by the grace of God I am what I am… yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) What a free thing to say! No need to put yourself down, no need to puff yourself up; simply return to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, please store this key truth in your heart: our relationship with ourselves comes from our relationship with God.

You don’t first learn to love yourself and then become worthy to come before God; you are first loved by God, and then you learn how to see yourself. Reverse that order, and your whole life goes out of shape. This is exactly the order of relationships 321 speaks of: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. This order can’t be skipped, and it can’t be swapped.

sections.heading: 2. A Good Relationship with Yourself: A Life Where Inside and Outside Agree
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the second key point. Since our relationship with ourselves matters so much, is there a mark by which we can test whether that relationship is healthy? There is.

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

“Deluding your own selves” — the Greek verb carries the sense of “miscalculating”, like someone who has done their sums wrong yet is convinced they’re right. James says that a person who hears the word but doesn’t do it is keeping false accounts on themselves. The income column in their heart is full of teachings heard, tears shed and amens said, but none of it has ever truly been entered into the books.

James then gives a very vivid picture: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, what does it mean not to have a good relationship with yourself? It means hearing one thing, thinking another, saying another and doing another. What you believe in your heart isn’t lived out; what you say with your mouth, you can’t do yourself. What happens to such a person? Conflict within, a painful life, no peace, no joy.

A little earlier in the same chapter, James has already given his diagnosis of such a person: “He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.” (James 1:8) “Double-minded” in the original is literally “two-souled”. When a person has two voices, two directions and two sets of standards inside, how can they have peace?

On the other hand, when what a person believes in their heart, thinks in their mind, says with their mouth and does in their actions all agree, they become joyful, free and light.

The Lord Jesus said: “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” (Matthew 5:37) The psalmist prays: “Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (Psalm 51:6) What God values has never been the surface: “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

There’s a spiritual illustration here that fits very well.

Think of a car: the steering wheel turns left, but the tyres point right — what happens? It pulls, it judders, it loses control. Anyone who drives knows that when the wheel alignment is out, you have to keep fighting the steering wheel and the car still drifts; the tyres wear unevenly, fuel consumption goes up, and by the end of the journey you’re especially tired. But when everything points the same way, the car runs smoothly; you only need to rest your hands lightly on the wheel, and it goes straight and true by itself.

The same is true of us: when inside and outside don’t agree, life goes out of control; when inside and outside agree, life is lived in peace.

Here’s one more illustration. Before an orchestra plays, the oboe sounds a standard A, and the whole orchestra tunes to it. The International Organization for Standardization has set this note at four hundred and forty vibrations per second — that is, 440 hertz. Notice: it isn’t the violins tuning to the cellos; the whole orchestra tunes together to the same standard note. If everyone tuned to their own pitch, it wouldn’t be music; it would be noise. Our lives are the same: it isn’t me tuning to you, but each of us first tuning to God, and then harmony between us comes naturally.

Psychology offers supporting evidence here too. In his 1961 book On Becoming a Person, the humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers put forward the idea of “congruence”. He held that when a person’s inner experience, their conscious sense of self and their outward expression match one another, that person is on the road to health and maturity; but when inside and outside are split, they become anxious, defensive and exhausted. Another social psychologist, Leon Festinger, proposed his famous “theory of cognitive dissonance” in 1957: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t agree, a marked discomfort arises within them, and they instinctively look for a way to remove it — either by changing their behaviour or by bending their beliefs.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where the danger lies. When what we believe and what we do don’t agree, if we refuse to change our behaviour, we will slowly lower the standard, revise the truth and find excuses for ourselves. This is the most frightening process in “deluding your own selves” — not a single lie, but a shift, inch by inch.

Let me give you another scene from life. A brother shared in his small group that God had moved him to forgive his father, and everyone was moved to tears. After the meeting, in the car park, his father rang. He glanced at the phone and rejected the call. What did he feel inside at that moment? It wasn’t peace; it was being torn apart. Brothers and sisters, our pain often comes not from being insufficiently spiritual, but from our inside and our outside being out of alignment.

In medicine there is a class of illnesses called autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. The principle is simple but very sad: the immune system, meant to protect the body, mistakes the body’s own tissue for an enemy and attacks it. The body isn’t brought down by an outside enemy; it is wounded by itself. Brothers and sisters, a life in which inside and outside don’t agree is a spiritual autoimmune disease — your greatest drain comes not from attacks outside, but from self-attack within.

So we must hold on to this key truth: the mark of a good relationship with yourself is that the inside and the outside agree.

In the light of 321: rely on the heart, and you’ll be whole; rely on the brain, and you’ll be divided.

The person who relies on the brain is calculating how others see them, while also calculating how to look spiritual, while also calculating what’s most to their own advantage. Three lines pull against each other — how could they not be tired? The person who relies on the heart looks only to Jesus, listens to the voice of the Holy Spirit, speaks the truth and walks in the truth; inside there is only one line. That is why 321 says: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Solomon wrote this principle down long ago: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 3. From Inner Struggle to Victory: Building Your Relationship with Yourself by the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the third key point.

The first two points may already have pierced our hearts. We admit it: I often don’t accept myself, and I’m often not the same inside as outside. So where is the way out?

The Bible does not leave us in self-reproach. First it lets one of the greatest apostles put into words what is in our hearts:

“For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: it is Paul who says this. Not a new believer, but Paul — who made three missionary journeys and was thrown into prison for the Lord. He says: I want to do good, but I can’t; I know what’s right, but I can’t live it out.

He describes the dilemma in even finer detail: “For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18)

Notice this line: “desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.”

Brothers and sisters, this sentence hits the nail on the head. We never lack resolutions. We make resolutions every New Year’s Day, at every special conference, after every Sunday sermon. What we lack is not resolve; what we lack is power.

This is where we struggle too: we know we shouldn’t get angry, yet we can’t control it; we know we should love others, yet we can’t do it; we know we should obey God, yet we keep failing.

Why?

Paul gives the answer, but not at the start of chapter 7 — only after chapter 7 has reached a dead end. He goes all the way to the bottom and cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24) Brothers and sisters, notice that he asks “who”, not “what”. He doesn’t ask, “What method is there?” He asks, “Who is there?” No method could save him; only one person could. So the next sentence is: “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)

And then the door of chapter 8 swings open:

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

The word “law” here carries the sense of “a law of nature, a principle”. There are two laws here: the law of sin and of death, and the law of the Spirit of life. Brothers and sisters, a law can’t be abolished by effort; it can only be overcome by a higher law.

We all know about gravity. Let go of a pen and it falls; however hard you grit your teeth, you can’t change that. Yet an aircraft weighing hundreds of tonnes can climb thirty thousand feet into the sky. Has gravity disappeared? No. A higher law — aerodynamics — has overcome it. Once the plane’s engines cut out, gravity takes effect immediately.

Brothers and sisters, the Christian life is exactly like this. The law of sin has not been abolished, but there is a higher law — the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus — that has set us free. So the secret of our victory is not gritting our teeth against gravity; it is keeping the engines running and letting the wind of the Holy Spirit hold us up.

There is another illustration hidden in the original languages of the Bible. The word for “Spirit” is ruach in Hebrew and pneuma in Greek, and both words mean “wind” and “breath” at the same time. The Lord Jesus said: “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8) For a sailing ship to cross an ocean, no sailor is strong enough to row across the Pacific; the sailor’s skill lies not in making wind, but in setting the sails and holding the rudder true. Brothers and sisters, yet we so often furl our sails and then row with all our might. That is “relying on the brain and ourselves”.

So the answer is clear: not by effort, but by the Holy Spirit.

In Galatians Paul puts this secret very practically: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) And again: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25) The Lord Jesus himself said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice the Lord’s words: not “you can do a little less”, but “you can do nothing”. A branch doesn’t need to worry about bearing fruit; a branch needs only one thing — to stay joined to the vine.

When we return to our relationship with God and rely on the Holy Spirit, something wonderful happens: our faith and our actions begin to agree. Not that we grit our teeth and haul our behaviour up to match our faith, but that life grows from within and naturally bears fruit. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice: fruit is “borne”, not “manufactured”.

Here I want to give a special reminder to brothers and sisters who are in a weak place: when you can’t do it, don’t reproach yourself, don’t give up — turn.

Self-reproach puts the focus on yourself; turning puts the focus on Jesus. Self-reproach pulls you deeper and deeper; turning gives you strength at once.

Psychological research also confirms this direction. Since 2003, Kristin Neff, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, has developed research on “self-compassion”, and the results consistently show that people who beat themselves up harshly after failing are actually more likely to avoid, procrastinate and fail again; while those who can acknowledge their weakness and keep going are more willing to take responsibility and get back on their feet more quickly. Of course, our foundation goes deeper than psychology — we rely not on being kind to ourselves, but on the High Priest who can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities”.

The Church Father Augustine, in the first chapter of his Confessions, wrote the summary of his whole life: Lord, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Brothers and sisters, that sentence says everything about the human condition. The restlessness inside us is not because we haven’t tried hard enough, but because we have not yet come to rest in him.

So hold on firmly to this key truth: rely on yourself, and you struggle; rely on the Holy Spirit, and you overcome.

In the light of 321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you can live it out; rely on the brain and yourself, and you can’t.

When a person is connected with God and lives by the Holy Spirit, they will be the same inside and out, have peace in their heart and live with joy.

That is what it means to have a good relationship with yourself.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Order of Relationships Cannot Be Reversed
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set today’s message within the whole picture of 321, it becomes clearer still.

First, the Three Foundations.

Jesus is my role model. The Lord Jesus is the only person in history whose inside and outside agreed completely. What he thought in his heart, said with his mouth and did with his hands were one and the same. He said he was gentle and humble in heart, and he really did wash his disciples’ feet; he said he would lay down his life, and he really did go to the cross. He did not merely speak the truth; he is the truth.

The Bible is my standard. My view of myself cannot take other people’s comments as its standard, nor my own feelings; it can take only God’s word as its standard. Feelings deceive, but God’s word stands firm in heaven for ever.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. As we said in the third point: agreement between inside and outside is not something we achieve by self-cultivation; it is the fruit the Holy Spirit bears within us.

Second, the Two Core Values.

Let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, that chaotic kingdom inside you needs a King. When you sit on the throne yourself, you are at once the defendant, the prosecutor and the judge, and you will judge yourself to exhaustion. When Jesus takes the throne and the authority to judge is handed back to him, you are set free.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. A truly selfless person need not take the credit when they succeed, and need not fall apart when they fail, because the glory was never theirs in the first place. This is the deepest secret of being at peace with yourself — no longer needing achievement to prove yourself.

The Goal: establish God’s system. What God wants is not a group of people who are harmonious on the surface and torn apart inside, but a people who are the same inside and out and love one another, to be his system on earth.

Third, the self-centred life and selflessness.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Today we have seen that in our relationship with ourselves, the self-centred life bears two kinds of fruit: the pride of self-exaltation, and the pride of self-rejection. Yes, self-rejection is also a form of pride, because it is still saying: “God’s view doesn’t count; mine is the one that counts.”

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This principle applies not only between people, but also between a person and themselves. The more harshly you treat yourself, the stronger the resistance inside you; the more you return to God in grace, the faster you are healed within.

Fourth, the fivefold change.

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice the order: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today’s lesson begins precisely with the mindset — exchanging the mindset “I must be good enough to deserve love” for the mindset “I am already loved, so I can become good”. Once the mindset changes, life loosens up.

Fifth, the shift in perspective.

From the human to God’s — not asking “How do others see me?” but “How does God see me?” From the earthly to the heavenly — my worth lies not in an earthly report card but in heaven’s book of life. From the temporary to the eternal — today’s failure is not the end of the story. From the worldly to the godly — the world says “love yourself” and puts the self at the centre; the Bible says true freedom is putting Jesus at the centre.

Sixth, the 920 practice.

Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Brothers and sisters, there’s a lesson here that is often overlooked: the “2” you have known the longest is in fact yourself. If you can’t be patient and gentle with yourself, how will you be patient and gentle with others? Start today practising the fruit of the Spirit on yourself — be patient with yourself, because God is patient with you.

Seventh, 235 relationships.

Become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with selfless people; establish “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, someone whose inside and outside don’t agree cannot have a true spiritual companion, because they don’t dare let anyone see their real self. Only when you are at peace with yourself can you open up to others; and only when you open up can you have real companions. So our relationship with ourselves is not a private matter; it directly decides whether we can establish God’s system.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living: Building a Right Relationship with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word without doing it is deluding ourselves. So we must turn today’s message into three actions we can practise.

Practice 1: Each day, declare and receive God’s love, and learn to accept yourself

Don’t define yourself by your past, your failures or your performance; see yourself through God’s love.

Every morning, declare your identity with one sentence of truth: “I am loved by God.” “I am accepted.”

Brothers and sisters, declaring is not self-hypnosis; it is putting back into your heart what God has already said. God says: “you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). This isn’t boasting; it’s agreeing with God’s word.

How to practise: each morning, declare your identity with one sentence of truth. You can use today’s verses: I am accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6); in Christ Jesus I am not condemned (Romans 8:1).

Practice 2: Practise “doing what you say”, building a life where inside and outside agree

Don’t just hear the word and be moved; choose to live it out. The truth you hear today, go and do today.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t make ten resolutions at once; ten resolutions made together are as good as none. Choose just one today — the smallest, simplest one you can actually do today.

How to practise: each day, choose the simplest act of obedience and carry it out. For example: the phone call you need to make today — make it now; the name that came to mind today — pray for that person now; the thing you promised your child today — do it this evening.

Practice 3: When you are weak, don’t rely on yourself — turn to the Holy Spirit

When you find you can’t do it, don’t reproach yourself and don’t give up; turn to God.

Just say one sentence in your heart: “Lord, I rely on you. I can’t do it; please help me.”

Brothers and sisters, this one short prayer is worth more than an hour of self-condemnation. Self-reproach is going round and round inside yourself; prayer is plugging straight into the power supply.

How to practise: whenever you struggle, pray one sentence at once and turn to the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 6. Taking the Practices Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
321 teaches us that there are eight stages in changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to carry the three practices above all the way through.

Stage 1, Information. Today you have received this: our relationship with ourselves comes from our relationship with God; agreement between inside and outside is the mark of health; only by the Holy Spirit can we overcome. Please copy today’s three passages onto a card — Matthew 22:39, James 1:22 and Romans 8:2 — and put it where you’ll see it every day.

Stage 2, Revelation. Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: Lord, in what area have I kept refusing to accept myself? In what area do I hear one thing and do another? Pray: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Stage 3, Conviction. Once you’ve seen it, agree with God’s view and stop arguing. If God says you are forgiven, don’t rake over the past again. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) To keep condemning yourself after confessing is to disbelieve God’s faithfulness.

Stage 4, Implementation. Do that smallest thing today. Don’t wait until you feel right; don’t wait until circumstances improve. Faith has never been seeing first and then walking; it is walking first and then seeing.

Stage 5, Evaluation. Each evening, take three minutes: did what I said and what I did line up today? Was there anything I said but didn’t do? David said something very honest: “When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.” (Psalm 32:3) Without evaluation, things pile up inside; with evaluation, there is release.

Stage 6, Correction. When you find a mismatch, adjust at once. It might mean going to apologise, going to make good on something you promised, or deleting an exaggerated remark. Correction is not humiliation; correction is freedom.

Stage 7, Repetition. Obedience once is an event; repeated obedience is a life. Wheel alignment isn’t something you set once and never have go out again; after a long time on the road the car still has to go back to the garage for a check. Our hearts, too, need to come back to the Lord every day to be recalibrated.

Stage 8, Multiplication. When you yourself have experienced freedom, go and take someone with you. Tell them today’s three sentences: our relationship with God decides our relationship with ourselves; only when inside and outside agree is there true peace; only by the Holy Spirit can we overcome. Then walk alongside them for a while. This is 235 — once you have your “2”, you begin to have your “3”, and in the end it grows into a “5”.

Brothers and sisters, these eight stages are not a course; they are a road.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Align with God First, Then Be at One with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, I want to remind you of one thing: your greatest enemy is not other people, but that “self that is out of agreement within”.

Stop deceiving yourself. Stop living divided.

What God wants to give you is a life that is real, free and joyful. The Lord Jesus said: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:32) Notice: not “you will know doctrine”, but “you will know the truth”; and not that the truth gives you knowledge, but that the truth makes you free.

True joy is not outward smooth sailing, but inward agreement.

Aligned with God, at one with yourself. Such a person, whatever their circumstances, can stand firm and live with joy.

A compass is a fine picture of this. The needle of a compass doesn’t look at the needles beside it; it points to one place only. And every navigator knows that there is an angle of difference between true north and magnetic north, which must be corrected for, or on a long voyage you will drift away from your destination. Brothers and sisters, our hearts have an angle of difference too — our old mindsets, old wounds, old condemnation. We need to come back every day to God’s word to correct it.

This is the order of our whole lives: first connect with God, then align with ourselves, then love others, and only last get on with tasks. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Don’t reverse it; don’t skip over it.

This morning I want to invite you to do three things.

First, hand over to the Lord that self you have never been willing to forgive. Since God does not condemn you, stop condemning yourself.

Second, that thing you “said but never did” — go and do it today. Even if it is only a phone call, an apology or a hug.

Third, put down the oar you’ve rowed with until you’re exhausted, and set your sails. Stop relying on the brain and yourself; start relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit.

Let Jesus be King — King of your thoughts, King of your tongue, King of your actions, King of every hidden corner within you. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when you live out a life that is real, whole and free, what people see is not how strong you are, but how real Jesus is.

May we, all our lives, first connect with God, then align with ourselves, live out a real life, build healthy relationships, and step by step become overcomers.

prayer: Lord! I want to build a right relationship with myself.
No more rejecting myself; no more deceiving myself.

I confess that I often define myself by my performance, and often condemn myself in my heart. Lord, please forgive me, for you have already accepted me in Christ, yet I still refuse to accept the one you have accepted.
I will accept myself in your love, and live out the truth in the Holy Spirit.
Let my heart, my thoughts, my words and my actions all be at one in you.

Whatever I believe in my heart, give me strength to live it out; whatever I say with my mouth, keep me to doing every bit of it. When I am weak and cannot do it, remind me not to reproach myself, not to give up, but simply to turn to you.
Make me live a life of peace, joy and freedom, live out Christ, and become an overcomer.
May my home, my small group and my workplace all see your glory through one real life.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!

Harshly, neglectfully, or in grace? Is that the very same way you treat a particular person close to you? Please share one specific example.

James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” Is there something you “know but haven’t done” lately that has left you without peace inside? This week, what is the smallest, most concrete act of obedience you plan to take? Say it out loud, so the group can pray for you and ask how it went at the next meeting.

blog.title: The Hardest Person to Live With

blocks.x: Lives inside you

A sister once said to me: “I get on reasonably well with my colleagues, and with my family there’s the occasional friction, but it’s manageable. But there’s one person I fight with every day, and it hasn’t stopped for thirty years.”
I asked her, “Who is that person?”
She lowered her head, and after a long pause she said quietly: “It’s me.”

Have you ever known that? Late at night, when all is still, the voice that is quickest to condemn you, quickest to rake over your past, does not come from your enemy; it comes from your own heart. By day you can forgive others; by night you refuse to forgive yourself.

We often think our pain comes from difficult circumstances and clashes with people, so we pour enormous effort into changing our circumstances and changing other people. Yet for all the changing, the pain is still there. Because the root is not outside; it is inside.
1. The key to “love your neighbour as yourself” is “yourself”
The Lord Jesus said: “A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matthew 22:39)

We usually put the whole weight on “love your neighbour”, and then reproach ourselves: why can’t I manage to love? But the key is in the last word — “yourself”. In the original it reads “love your neighbour as you love yourself”, and that little word “as” is a scale: the way you treat yourself is the mould for the way you treat others.

Someone who is extremely harsh on themselves finds it hard to be lenient with others; someone who judges themselves every day will judge others the moment they open their mouth. No one can give what they do not have; if you draw water from a dry well, the bucket always comes up empty.

So on what basis can I accept myself? If the basis is “I perform well”, then on the day I fail I collapse; if the basis is “other people praise me”, then on the day they turn away I fall apart. The Bible gives us another basis: “Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.” (Hebrews 4:16) We can come with boldness, not because we are good enough, but because the throne is the throne of grace. Take a hundred-dollar note, screw it up into a ball and trample it underfoot — what is it worth? Still a hundred dollars. Its value lies not in its appearance but in the one who issued it.
2. The mark of a good relationship with yourself: inside and outside agree
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

“Deluding your own selves” carries the sense in the original of “miscalculating”: the income column in the heart is full of teachings heard and tears shed, but none of it has ever truly been entered into the books. Hearing one thing, thinking another, saying another and doing another — that brings conflict within.

It’s like a car: the steering wheel turns left, but the tyres point right, and the car pulls and loses control. Once the wheel alignment is out, you have to keep fighting the steering, and by the end of the journey you’re especially tired. When everything points the same way, the car runs smoothly.

Psychology offers supporting evidence too. In 1961 Carl Rogers put forward the idea of “congruence”: people whose inner and outer lives match are on the road to health, while those split inside and out become anxious and exhausted. Leon Festinger’s 1957 “theory of cognitive dissonance” goes further: when beliefs and behaviour don’t agree, if people refuse to change their behaviour, they slowly revise the truth and lower the standard. Self-deception is not a single lie, but a shift, inch by inch.
3. The way out is not more effort, but the Holy Spirit

Paul says: “For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15) He was no new believer; he was an apostle who had been thrown into prison for the Lord. He puts it even more plainly: desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. We never lack resolutions; what we lack is power.

Paul reaches a dead end and cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” Notice that he asks “who”, not “what”. And then the door of chapter 8 swings open: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

Let go of a pen and it falls — that’s gravity; yet an aircraft weighing hundreds of tonnes can climb thirty thousand feet. Gravity hasn’t disappeared; a higher law has overcome it. For a sailing ship to cross an ocean, the sailor’s skill lies not in making wind but in setting the sails. Yet we so often furl our sails and then row with all our might.

In the light of 321: the self-centred person is either insecure or proud, and the subject of both is “I”. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you can live it out; rely on the brain and yourself, and you can’t.
Three practices to start today
1. Every morning, declare your identity with one sentence of truth: I am loved by God; I am accepted.
2. The truth you hear today, go and do today — choose just one smallest action.
3. When you’re weak, don’t reproach yourself or give up; pray one sentence at once: “Lord, I rely on you. I can’t do it; please help me.”
True joy is not outward smooth sailing, but inward agreement. First connect with God, then align with yourself, and then love others.
Reflection
This week, is there something you “know but haven’t done” that is robbing you of peace inside? Today, what is the smallest act of obedience you are willing to take first?
