2. Ask: could the one who walks across first be you?
3. Quotation: Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said we cannot do great things, only small things with great love.
4. Call: let Jesus be King in every one of your relationships; let him receive the glory from them.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I will take the initiative to love
I will forgive; I will bless
Use me to pass life on
All glory to Jesus. Amen
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in praying aloud together; gentle tone, a pause after each line.
2. Invite each person to hold one name in their heart, and choose to forgive and to bless.
3. Ask God to use our lives to influence lives, bring forth life and pass life on.
4. Blessing and sending: may we live in God’s love, love one another, build one another up and become overcomers.

brief21.title: Let God’s Love Flow
notes: Slide text:
The Priority of Relationships (Part 3): Our Relationship with Others
“Let’s love one another,
for love is of God.”
(1 John 4:7)
Key points:
1. Greet everyone; announce the lesson title and read the key verse, 1 John 4:7, in full.
2. State the main thread: let God’s love flow — through me, out to others, on to the next generation, into God’s kingdom.
3. Preview four points: proof, loving enemies, passing on, revival across generations.
4. Warm tone suited to the morning; invite everyone to be still and turn their hearts to God.

brief21.title: Introduction 1: The Third Level
notes: Slide text:
The order of relationships can’t be reversed
First with God, then with ourselves
then with others, last with things
Today, the third level: others
Key points:
1. Review the order of relationships: first God, then ourselves, then others, last things.
2. The last two lessons covered God and ourselves; today we enter the third level.
3. Stress that the order can’t be reversed: if the source is blocked, the outlet will be blocked.
4. Opening question: is there a relationship in your life that has been stuck for a long time?

brief21.title: Introduction 2: Not Technique, but Life
notes: Slide text:
Our relationships with others are not a problem of technique
but a problem of life
Without love that comes from God,
however hard we try, we cannot truly love
Key points:
1. Example: two sisters in the same choir for seven years, three people apart, not one complete sentence in seven years.
2. Ask: is worship like that pleasing to God?
3. Illustration: an unplugged fan turns once per push; plugged in, it turns all day by itself.
4. Data: the Harvard Study of Adult Development since 1938; Professor Waldinger’s conclusion — the quality of relationships determines lifelong health and happiness.
5. Data: Holt-Lunstad’s team, 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies and over 300,000 people — strong social connections, about 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival.

brief21.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
“He who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen,
how can he love God whom he has not seen?”
The aged apostle John’s touchstone for the churches
Key points:
1. Author: the apostle John, the disciple whom the Lord loved, shepherding the churches around Ephesus in old age.
2. Date and readers: around AD 85–95, to believers he calls “little children”.
3. Setting: early Gnostic ideas seeping in; some claimed to know God and be in the light, yet hated their brothers.
4. Style: “If a man says … he is a liar” is the touchstone pattern, for examining ourselves.
5. Add: the Sermon on the Mount is the King’s constitution; “hate your enemy” was a rabbinic addition, never commanded in the Old Testament.

brief21.title: 1.1 Love Is of God
notes: Slide text:
“Everyone who loves has been born of God”
“He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God,
for God is love.”
Key points:
1. Read 1 John 4:7–8 in full.
2. Original language: the New Testament describes God’s love with ἀγάπη, a love of the will that gives itself — unlike family affection, friendship or desire.
3. “God is love” — love is not one of God’s attributes; it is his very being.
4. Romans 5:5: the Holy Spirit “poured” God’s love into our hearts — tipped out, brimming over.
5. Illustration: when the tap runs dry, the problem often isn’t at the outlet; go and check the water tank.

brief21.title: 1.2 Whoever Loves God Will Love People
notes: Slide text:
“We love him, because he first loved us.”
If you can’t love the brother you see,
how can you love the God you can’t see?
Key points:
1. Read 1 John 4:19–21.
2. The word “first” fixes the order: we don’t squeeze out love; God loves first.
3. Illustration: someone saying, “I’m an excellent swimmer — I just never get into the water.”
4. Scripture interprets Scripture: Matthew 22:37–39, “A second likewise” — the two commandments are two sides of one coin.

brief21.title: 1.3 Love Is the Mark of a Disciple
notes: Slide text:
“By this everyone will know
that you are my disciples,
if you have love for one another.”
Key points:
1. Read John 13:34–35.
2. What is “new” is the standard: not “as yourself” but “as the Lord” — just as I have loved you.
3. Stress: not gifts, not eloquence, not numbers, but love for one another.
4. Church history: Tertullian’s Apology records the pagans saying, “See how they love one another.”
5. 321 light: get it right with God and you’ll get it right with people; get it wrong with God and things will go wrong with people.

brief21.title: 2.1 Love Your Enemies
notes: Slide text:
“Love your enemies…
pray for those who persecute you.”
(Matthew 5:44)
Loving the unlovable, loving those who hurt you
Key points:
1. Read Matthew 5:43–45.
2. Add verses 46–48: even tax collectors love those who love them; be perfect as your Father in heaven is perfect.
3. Explain the Father’s standard: sun on the evil and the good, rain on the just and the unjust.
4. Name the difficulty: loving the one whose name alone makes your stomach knot.

brief21.title: 2.2 The Root of the Difficulty: Self
notes: Slide text:
We keep score because I feel short-changed
We get even because my dignity was touched
We judge because I must prove I’m right
Underneath lies one word: self
Key points:
1. The heart of 321: the self-centred life is the root of the fall; pride is the root of the problem.
2. Unpack: keeping score is feeling short-changed, getting even is wounded dignity, judging is needing to be right.
3. Scripture: Romans 12:19, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay”; refusing to forgive is sitting in God’s seat.
4. Definition: forgiveness doesn’t say “it doesn’t matter”; it hands the account book to the righteous Judge.
5. 321 light: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

brief21.title: 2.3 Forgiveness Is an Act of the Will
notes: Slide text:
Holding a grudge, blood pressure and heart rate rise;
turning to forgiveness, they come down
(Witvliet, 2001)
Corrie ten Boom: the hand first, then the feeling
Key points:
1. Data: Witvliet, Psychological Science, 2001 — holding a grudge raises blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension; turning to forgiveness lowers them.
2. A reminder: refusing to forgive doesn’t make the other person ill; it only makes you ill.
3. Testimony: in Munich in 1947, after speaking on forgiveness, Corrie ten Boom met a guard from Ravensbrück.
4. The key: she first prayed, “Lord, I can’t; give me your forgiveness,” then woodenly held out her hand.
5. Conclusion: not feeling first then the hand, but the hand first then the feeling; forgiveness is an act of the will.

brief21.title: 2.4 Only Selflessness Can Love Enemies
notes: Slide text:
“Father, forgive them.”
Only selflessness can love its enemies
The self-centred love only their own
Key points:
1. Scripture: Luke 23:34, the Lord on the cross praying for those who crucified him.
2. Scripture: Acts 7:60, Stephen under the stones praying for those killing him.
3. Galatians 2:20: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
4. Romans 12:14, 21: bless, and don’t curse; overcome evil with good.
5. Quotation: Dr Martin Luther King, Jr., Strength to Love (1963) — hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.

brief21.title: 3.1 Make Disciples of All Nations
notes: Slide text:
“Go and make disciples
of all nations.”
(Matthew 28:19)
Tutors pass on information; fathers pass on life
Key points:
1. Read Matthew 28:19–20.
2. Original language: the main verb is “make disciples of all nations”; go, baptising and teaching are participles around it.
3. 1 Corinthians 4:15: though you have ten thousand tutors, you don’t have many fathers.
4. Contrast: tutors pass on information, fathers pass on life; disciples can’t be produced by broadcast.

brief21.title: 3.2 Generation to Generation
notes: Slide text:
Moses to Joshua: into the Promised Land
David to Solomon: building the temple
Elijah to Elisha: picking up the cloak
Paul to Timothy: entrusting faithful men
Key points:
1. Moses to Joshua: Deuteronomy 31:7; the one who led them out of Egypt was not the one who led them into Canaan.
2. David to Solomon: 1 Kings 2:2–3; the one who prepared and the one who built belonged to two generations.
3. Elijah to Elisha: 2 Kings 2:9, asking for a double portion of his spirit.
4. Paul to Timothy: 2 Timothy 2:2, four generations of handing on in one verse.
5. A scientific picture: Professor Simard’s forest research — large trees send carbon, nitrogen and water through mycorrhizal networks to seedlings in the shade.

brief21.title: 3.3 For Such a Time as This
notes: Slide text:
“Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom
for such a time as this?”
(Esther 4:14)
Your position is a trust, not a comfort
Key points:
1. Read Esther 4:14 in full, including the warning in the first half.
2. Application: the position God gives you is not for comfort but for such a time as this.
3. Reminder: workplace, family, profession and network are no accident; all are a trust.
4. Scientific support: Rizzolatti’s team discovered mirror neurons in the 1990s — people learn by watching how you live, not by hearing how you talk.
5. 321: 235 relationships — first a 2, then a 3, then become part of a 5.

brief21.title: 4.1 Unity So the World May Believe
notes: Slide text:
“That they may all be one…
that the world may believe that you sent me.”
Competing brings loss; connecting brings growth
Key points:
1. Read John 17:21: unity exists so that the world may believe.
2. Ephesians 4:3: “being eager” to keep unity — unity doesn’t happen automatically.
3. Psalm 133:1, 3: where brothers live in unity, Yahweh commands the blessing.
4. Application: when churches compete, God’s kingdom suffers loss; when they connect, it expands.

brief21.title: 4.2 Generations in Partnership Bring Revival
notes: Slide text:
Old men dream dreams; young men see visions
(Joel 2:28)
Herrnhut first covenanted to unity;
three months later the Spirit was poured out
Key points:
1. Malachi 4:6: turning the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the children to their fathers.
2. Joel 2:28: old men dream dreams, young men see visions.
3. History: Herrnhut founded in 1722, the brethren arguing endlessly; covenant of unity on 12 May 1727.
4. History: on 13 August the same year the Spirit was poured out; a 24-hour prayer watch followed for a century, with missionaries sent to every continent.
5. Illustration: the young have fire but no stove; the old have a stove but no fire; put the fire in the stove and it warms the whole winter.

brief21.title: Practices, Part 1
notes: Slide text:
Take the initiative to love one person daily
A word of encouragement, concern, time together
Pray three days for someone hard to love
Bless him, change me, intercede for him
Key points:
1. Practice 1: each day deliberately bless one person, in word or deed; don’t wait to be loved.
2. Information and implementation: remember 1 John 4:19; send one specific blessing today.
3. Practice 2: pray for three days for someone you find hard to love.
4. The three days: day one, ask God to bless him; day two, ask God to change me; day three, intercede for his family, work and health.
5. Correction: if your heart is still hard, learn Corrie ten Boom’s prayer.

brief21.title: Practices, Part 2
notes: Slide text:
Deliberately build relationships that pass life on
Regularly care for one spiritual companion
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
1. Practice 3: begin regularly caring for one spiritual companion or new believer, thirty minutes once a week.
2. Content: read a passage of the Bible together, pray together, listen to him.
3. Evaluation: after a month ask him, “Over this past month, what has God done in you?”
4. Multiplication: after a year, ask him to take someone under his wing too — the four generations of 2 Timothy 2:2.
5. Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard,
the Holy Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King
920: live out the 0 before every 2
235: companions, parents and children, comrades
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
2. The Two Core Values and the Goal: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory, establish God’s system.
3. Fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; perspective shifts from the human to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal.
4. 920 practice: everyone I relate to is my “2”; live out the selfless “0”; bear the ninefold fruit of Galatians 5:22–23.
5. 235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Let God’s love flow
Let life be passed on
Individuals renewed, church built, kingdom extended
Will you be the first to walk across?
Key points:
1. Back to the beginning: can the two sisters’ seven-year wall come down? Yes, but someone must walk across first.
2. Ask the congregation: could the one who walks across first be you?
3. Quotation: Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said we cannot do great things, only small things with great love.
4. Concrete call: make a phone call, say “I’m sorry”, pray for one name for three minutes.
5. Point to the core: let Jesus be King in every one of your relationships, and receive all the glory from them.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I will take the initiative to love
I will forgive; I will bless
Use me to pass life on
All glory to Jesus. Amen
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in praying aloud together; slow the pace, a pause after each line.
2. Invite each person to hold one name in their heart, and choose to forgive and to bless.
3. Ask God to use our lives to influence lives, bring forth life and pass life on.
4. Intercede for church unity, partnership between generations and revival in the kingdom.
5. Blessing and sending: may we live in God’s love, love one another, build one another up, accomplish God’s will together and become overcomers.

script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to the third lesson on “the priority of relationships” — our relationship with others. Relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today we reach the third level. Our key verse says: “Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God.” (1 John 4:7) Please remember this: love has a source.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with a scene. Two sisters had stood in the same choir for seven years, with only three people between them, and in seven years they never exchanged a single complete sentence. Every Lord’s Day they sang together and said “Amen” together; when the service ended, one went east and the other went west. I have to ask: is worship like that pleasing to God? Today books on communication and interpersonal skills are piled high. But the Bible shows us a deeper root: our relationships with others are not a problem of technique; they are a problem of life. Let me give you a picture. Take an electric fan that isn’t plugged in. Push it with your hand and it will turn; but one push gives one turn, and the moment your hand stops, it stops. Once it’s plugged in, though, it turns by itself, all day long. Brothers and sisters, without love that comes from God, however hard we try, we cannot truly love people.

The author of this letter is the apostle John. In old age he lived in Ephesus; by then almost all the other apostles had been martyred, and he alone remained. At the time a way of thinking was seeping into the church: some people kept saying, “I know God,” yet were cold and scornful towards the brothers around them. So old John wrote the most direct of sentences: “he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20) Brothers and sisters, this sentence isn’t for inspecting other people; it is for inspecting ourselves.

The first key point: our relationships with others are the proof of our relationship with God. Scripture says: “everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God. He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.” (1 John 4:7–8) The Bible doesn’t say God has love; it says God is love. And it says: “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) God loved first, and so we have love to pour out. The Lord also said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35) Not gifts, not ability, not knowledge, but love. So 321 tells us: get it right with God, and you’ll get it right with people; get it wrong with God, and things will certainly go wrong with people.

The second key point: the highest level of loving people is loving our enemies. The Lord said: “love your enemies… and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you.” (Matthew 5:44) Why is this so hard? Brothers and sisters, because it isn’t human ability; it is God’s life. When we are still keeping score, still getting even, still passing judgement, underneath it all lies the very same word — self. In 2001 the psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet found that when people dwell on grudge-holding imagery, their blood pressure and heart rate rise; when they turn towards forgiveness, these come down. Refusing to forgive doesn’t make the other person ill; it only makes you ill. Corrie ten Boom met a concentration camp guard in Munich. She couldn’t hold out her hand, so she prayed silently: “Lord, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness.” Then she held out her hand, and love flowed through. Brothers and sisters, only selflessness can love its enemies; the self-centred life will only ever love its own.

The third key point: our relationships with others exist to pass on and complete God’s plan. The Lord said: “Go and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19) When we build relationships with people, we often stop at two things: getting along nicely and supporting one another. Both are very good, but neither is the finishing line. Paul says: “though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers.” (1 Corinthians 4:15) Tutors pass on information; fathers pass on life.

Brothers and sisters, God’s work has never been finished by one person alone. Moses led the people out of Egypt; Joshua led them into Canaan. David prepared the materials for the temple; Solomon built it. Elijah was taken up to heaven; Elisha picked up the cloak. Mordecai said to Esther: “Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14) The natural world gives us a picture too. Professor Suzanne Simard, studying forests, found that trees don’t stand each on its own but are connected through underground mycorrhizal networks, and large trees send nutrients to the seedlings in the shade beneath them. Brothers and sisters, the church is not a row of roadside trees; the church is a forest whose roots are all joined.

The fourth key point: relationships across generations and communities bring revival to the kingdom. The Lord Jesus prayed: “that they may all be one… that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Unity exists so that the world may believe. When churches compete with one another, God’s kingdom suffers loss; when they connect with one another, God’s kingdom expands. In 1727 the brethren at Herrnhut had been arguing endlessly; on 12 May they covenanted to live in unity, and on 13 August the Holy Spirit was mightily poured out, followed by more than a hundred years of unbroken prayer watch. Please remember this order: first unity, then outpouring. The young have fire but no stove; the old have a stove but no fire; put the fire into the stove, and it can keep the house warm all winter long.

Brothers and sisters, let’s gather today’s message together. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The 920 practice: everyone I have a relationship with is my “2”, and before them I want to live out the selfless “0” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. The 235 relationships: find your spiritual companion, establish your spiritual parents and children, and enter a fivefold-ministry team of comrades. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Today there are three practices. First, take the initiative to love one person every day; don’t wait to be loved — a word of encouragement, a gesture of concern, some time spent alongside them. Second, pray for three days for one person you find hard to love: on the first day ask God to bless him, on the second ask God to change me, on the third intercede for him specifically. Third, deliberately build relationships that pass life on, regularly caring for one spiritual companion or new believer. Brothers and sisters, don’t just do networking; make disciples.

Let’s go back to the two sisters at the beginning. Can a wall that has stood for seven years come down? Yes, it can. But not by time — by one person walking across first. Brothers and sisters, could the one who walks across first be you? Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love. This morning you don’t need to do anything great; you only need to do one small thing: make a phone call, say “I’m sorry”, pray for one name for three minutes. Let Jesus reign as King in every one of your relationships; let Jesus receive the glory from every one of your relationships.

Let us pray together. Lord, I want to build relationships after your own heart — not only to be loved, but to take the initiative to love. Lord, there is a name in my heart right now; I choose to forgive, I choose to bless. Use my life to influence lives, to bring forth life and to pass life on. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May we spend our whole lives in God’s love, loving one another, building one another up, accomplishing God’s will together, and becoming overcomers.

Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to the third lesson on “the priority of relationships” — let God’s love flow. Our key verse says: “Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God.” (1 John 4:7) Please remember this: love has a source. Today we will look at four things: our relationships with others are the proof of our relationship with God; the highest level of love is loving our enemies; relationships exist to pass life on; and connection across generations brings revival.

Let’s first review an order. 321 tells us that the order of relationships must never be turned upside down: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. In the first lesson we looked at God — the source. In the second we looked at ourselves — the outlet. Today we reach the third level — others. Brothers and sisters, let me ask you a question: is there a relationship in your life that has been stuck where it is for a long time? Stuck for a year? Five years? Ten years? Please hold that name in your heart.

Let me describe a scene. Two sisters had stood in the same choir for seven years, with only three people between them. Every Lord’s Day they sang together and said “Amen” together; when the service ended, one went out by the east door and the other by the west door, and in seven years they never exchanged a single complete sentence. Nobody remembers any more what started it. The matter was small, but the wall was high. Brothers and sisters, is worship like that pleasing to God? Today books on communication skills are piled high, but the Bible shows us a deeper root: our relationships with others are not a problem of technique; they are a problem of life. Take an electric fan that isn’t plugged in. Push it with your hand and it will turn; one push, one turn, and the moment your hand stops, it stops. Plug it in, and it turns by itself all day. Without love that comes from God, however hard we try, we cannot truly love people. Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, followed more than seven hundred men across their whole lives, and its director, Professor Robert Waldinger, concluded: what keeps people healthy and happy across a lifetime is not wealth, and not fame, but good relationships.

The author of this letter is the apostle John, the disciple who leaned against Jesus’ breast. It is generally dated between AD 85 and 95, and was very likely written from Ephesus. By then he was a white-haired old man, and almost all the other apostles had been martyred. He calls the believers “little children”, like a father speaking to his sons and daughters. At the time a way of thinking was seeping into the church: some people kept saying, “I know God,” yet were cold and scornful towards the brothers around them. So old John wrote the most direct of sentences: “he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20) Brothers and sisters, this sentence isn’t for inspecting other people; it is for inspecting ourselves.

The first key point: our relationships with others are the proof of our relationship with God. Scripture says: “He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.” (1 John 4:8) Please notice: the Bible doesn’t say God “has” love; it says God “is” love. When the New Testament describes God’s love, the word it uses is ἀγάπη. Family affection, friendship and passionate desire all assume that the other person deserves it or that I feel something; only this love springs from the will and gives itself away. The first three are in us by nature; the fourth is received from God. Paul says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.” (Romans 5:5) Poured — filled until it overflows.

Then John says: “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) The word “first” fixes the order: it isn’t that we squeeze out some love and then God loves us; it is that God loved us first, and so we have love to pour out. So he says that if a man says he loves God but hates his brother, he is a liar. If you can’t bring yourself to love the brother you can see, how could you possibly love the God you cannot see? It’s like someone saying, “I’m an excellent swimmer — I just never get into the water.” The Lord bound the two commandments together: loving God is the first, and “A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matthew 22:39) “Likewise” means of equal weight — these are not two things, but two sides of one thing.

On the night he was betrayed, the Lord said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35) Brothers and sisters, the Lord didn’t say by your gifts; he didn’t say by your eloquence; he didn’t say by your learning or your numbers. The Lord said: by your love for one another. The church father Tertullian recorded what the pagans of his day said: “See how they love one another.” So 321 says: get it right with God, and you’ll get it right with people; get it wrong with God, and things will certainly go wrong with people. When you find that whatever you do you simply can’t love a certain person, don’t rush to fix that person; go back before God and ask: “Lord, is something blocked between you and me?”

The second key point: the highest level of loving people is loving our enemies. The Lord said: “love your enemies… and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:44–45) Loving lovable people isn’t hard; loving people who love you isn’t hard. What’s hard is loving the person who has hurt you, loving the one whose name alone makes your stomach knot the moment it crosses your mind. The Lord himself explained: “For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?” (Matthew 5:46) Loving your own people needs no new birth and no Holy Spirit.

Why is it so hard? Brothers and sisters, because there is still a “self” inside us. We keep score because “I” have been short-changed; we get even because “my” dignity has been touched; we pass judgement because “I” need to prove I’m more right than he is. Underneath all three lies the very same word. 321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When I refuse to forgive, I climb into the judge’s seat, but the Bible says: “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.” (Romans 12:19) Forgiveness doesn’t say, “This doesn’t matter.” Forgiveness hands the account book over to the righteous Judge. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Whoever humbles himself first is the first to go free.

Psychology offers supporting evidence. In 2001 the psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and her colleagues published an experiment in the journal Psychological Science: while participants dwelt on grudge-holding imagery, their blood pressure, heart rate and muscle tension all rose; when they turned towards forgiveness, these indicators promptly came down. Brothers and sisters, refusing to forgive doesn’t make the other person ill; it only makes you ill. Corrie ten Boom of the Netherlands lost her sister in a concentration camp. In 1947, after speaking on forgiveness in Munich, a man held out his hand to thank her, and she recognised him at once as a guard from the camp. Her hand stayed frozen at her side and simply would not reach out. She prayed silently: “Lord Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness.” Then she woodenly thrust out her hand, and a warmth flowed through her. Please notice the order — not the feeling first and then the hand, but the hand first, and then the feeling came.

On the cross our Lord prayed: “Father, forgive them.” (Luke 23:34) Under the stones Stephen prayed: “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” (Acts 7:60) Brothers and sisters, both are selfless prayers. 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite; no longer I, but Christ living in me. Paul says: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Only selflessness can love its enemies; the self-centred life will only ever love its own. Dr Martin Luther King, Jr. said: hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.

The third key point: our relationships with others exist to pass on and complete God’s plan. The Lord said: “Go and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19) When we build relationships with people, we often stop at getting along nicely and supporting one another. Both are very good, but neither is the finishing line. In the original of the Great Commission there is only one main verb — make disciples; “go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” are all participles revolving around it. And disciples cannot be produced by broadcast; disciples are brought up by life. Paul says: “though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers.” (1 Corinthians 4:15) Tutors pass on information; fathers pass on life.

Brothers and sisters, God’s work has never been finished by one person alone. Moses led the people out of Egypt but never entered Canaan; he said to Joshua: “Be strong and courageous!” (Deuteronomy 31:7) David prepared the materials for the temple but did not build it; he charged Solomon: “You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man.” (1 Kings 2:2) Before Elijah was taken up, Elisha asked: “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” (2 Kings 2:9) Before his martyrdom Paul charged: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Four generations in one verse.

There is one more pair: Mordecai and Esther. At the moment when their people’s survival hung in the balance, Mordecai said: “Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14) Brothers and sisters, the position God has given you isn’t there to make you comfortable; it is there for such a time as this. Your workplace, your family, your profession, your network — none of them is an accident; all of them are a trust. The natural world gives us a picture too. The forest ecologist Professor Suzanne Simard found that trees don’t stand each on its own but are connected through underground mycorrhizal networks, and large trees send nutrients to the seedlings in the shade beneath them. The church is not a row of roadside trees; the church is a forest whose roots are all joined. Life influences life; life multiplies life.

The fourth key point: relationships across generations and communities bring revival to the kingdom. The Lord Jesus prayed: “that they may all be one… that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Notice the second half — unity exists so that the world may believe. Paul says: “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) The word “eager” tells us that unity doesn’t happen automatically; it costs something. When churches compete with one another, God’s kingdom suffers loss; when they connect with one another, God’s kingdom expands. The psalm says: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1)

Now look between the generations. The last verse of the Old Testament says: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers.” (Malachi 4:6) On the day of Pentecost Peter quoted Joel: “Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.” (Joel 2:28) The passion of the young plus the wisdom of the old equals the power of God’s kingdom. The young have fire but no stove; the old have a stove but no fire; put the fire into the stove, and it can keep the house warm all winter long. Church history gives us a witness: a band of Moravian brethren fled to Germany and built Herrnhut; at first they argued endlessly and were on the verge of splitting apart. On 12 May 1727 they made a covenant to be of one heart, and three months later, on 13 August, the Holy Spirit was mightily poured out at Communion, followed by more than a hundred years of unbroken prayer watch. Please remember this order: first unity, then outpouring.

Today there are three practices. First, take the initiative to love one person every day, rather than waiting to be loved — a word of encouragement, a gesture of concern, some time spent alongside them. Please do it today: choose one person and send a sincere, specific blessing, not a pleasantry. Second, practise forgiveness and blessing, especially towards difficult people: don’t avoid them, don’t judge them, choose to bless them. The way to practise is to pray for three days for one person you find hard to love: on the first day ask God to bless him, on the second ask God to change me, on the third intercede for his family, his work and his health.

Third, deliberately build relationships that pass life on. Don’t stop at friendship; take one person under your wing and help him know God better. Arrange to meet him once a week for thirty minutes; read the Bible together, pray together, listen to him. After a month, ask him: over this past month, what has God done in you? After a year, ask him to go and take someone under his wing too. Brothers and sisters, there are eight stages in changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Many people stop at the first stage — they hear a great deal but never put it into practice; others do it once and then stop. Real change means walking all eight stages.

Let’s gather the message together. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The 920 practice: everyone I have a relationship with is my “2”, and before them I want to live out the selfless “0”, so as to bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Brothers and sisters, not one of these nine fruits can be produced shut away in your room — patience needs someone to be patient with, kindness needs someone to be kind to, gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. The 235 relationships: find your “2”, establish your “3”, enter your “5”. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, we are coming to the end. A true relationship is not just a connection; it is — letting God’s love flow, and letting life be passed on. It flows because there is a source; it is passed on because there is a direction. When we live out relationships like this, individuals will be renewed, the church will be built up, and the kingdom will be extended. Let’s go back to the two sisters at the beginning. Can a wall that has stood for seven years come down? Yes, it can. But not by time — by one person walking across first. Could the one who walks across first be you? Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love. This morning you only need to do one small thing: make a phone call, say “I’m sorry”, pray for one name for three minutes.

Let us pray together. Lord, I want to build relationships after your own heart — not only to be loved, but to take the initiative to love. I confess that I am so often waiting — waiting for others to love me first, to apologise first; please forgive me. I want to love my brothers and sisters, and to love the unlovable too, living out your life. Lord, there is a name in my heart right now; I choose to forgive, I choose to bless. Use my life to influence lives, to bring forth life and to pass life on. Make our church one, and let the generations work in partnership. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May we spend our whole lives in God’s love, loving one another, building one another up, accomplishing God’s will together, and becoming overcomers.

sections.heading: Introduction: Busy All Our Lives, Yet Forgetting Whom We Were Busy For
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

I’d like to start by asking you to picture a very familiar scene.

It’s ten o’clock on a Sunday night. A brother who has served for many years switches off the church lights and is the last to leave. Today he has taught two classes, carried chairs back and forth three times, and dealt with two phone calls full of complaints. He drives to the exit of the car park, then suddenly stops and sits in the driver’s seat, not wanting to pull away. He isn’t crying; he isn’t angry. He is simply tired. So tired that he says something to himself that startles even him: “I’ve done so much — but who on earth is it all for?”

Brothers and sisters, that question isn’t asked by unbelievers. It is asked by the most faithful.

Over these four lessons we have come to see that relationships have an order: first our relationship with God, second our relationship with ourselves, third our relationship with others. Today we come to the last level, and the one most easily put in the wrong place — our relationship with things.

Many people make “getting things done” the centre of gravity of their lives. We carry a ruler in our hearts, and it measures three things: how much we did, how well we did it, and whether it produced results. As children we were measured by exam scores; as adults at work we’re measured by performance; when we come into the church we measure attendance. We are so used to being measured that eventually we assume God carries the same ruler.

But, brothers and sisters, God sees things completely differently.

What God values is not things; what God values is people within relationships.

When relationships are right, things will come right of their own accord; when relationships are wrong, even the best of things will go sour. A perfect gathering can, in the course of being organised, break the hearts of the co-workers. A successful pastoral visit can, on the drive home, leave a spouse’s heart cold. The task gets done, but the people are left in pieces — and success like that is a loss on God’s books.

So today we need to understand two things. First, our relationship with things is the last in the order, not the first. Second, precisely because it is the last, it is the one most easily moved to the front.

The sociologist William Bruce Cameron, in his 1963 book Informal Sociology, wrote a much-quoted line: “Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.” That sentence isn’t Scripture, but it is like a mirror that shows up our blind spot: we very easily treat “what can be counted” as “what matters”, and so we push to the back the very thing God values most yet is hardest to quantify — relationships.

This lesson today is meant to help us put the order back the right way round. It isn’t telling us not to do things; it is telling us to do things in the right order. Because when people are right, things will be right.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Stewards, Faithfulness, and That Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias
sections.html:
To understand today’s message, we first need to step into the setting of three passages.

The first is 1 Corinthians chapter 4. The apostle Paul wrote this letter to the church in Corinth around AD 54 to 55, while he was living in Ephesus on his third missionary journey. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia — a port city, a commercial city, and a city that prized achievement and eloquence above all. When that culture made its way into the church, it turned into factions: one said, “I follow Paul,” another, “I follow Apollos,” another, “I follow Cephas” (1 Corinthians 1:12). They were measuring God’s servants with the world’s ruler.

How does Paul respond? He doesn’t argue about who is stronger; he changes how they define their identity. “So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2)

The Greek word for “steward” is οἰκονόμος (oikonomos), made up of “house” (oikos) and “to manage, to distribute” (nemō). It refers to a servant who manages the household’s affairs on his master’s behalf and hands out the food rations at the proper time. In Roman society the steward was often a capable slave, holding the keys, the account books and the granary, with a great deal of authority — but always under one unshakeable condition: the house was not his. Everything in his hands belonged to someone else.

So Paul says that what a steward is measured by is not performance but “faithfulness”. The Greek word for “faithful” is πιστός (pistos), from the same root as “faith” (pistis), meaning “trustworthy, reliable, fit to be entrusted with something”. Faithfulness isn’t an adjective about ability; it is an adjective about relationship. Whether a person is reliable is always said in relation to another person.

The second passage is the parable of the talents in Matthew 25. It is the second parable the Lord Jesus told his disciples on the Mount of Olives during Passion Week, as he spoke of the end of the age. It follows straight after the parable of the ten virgins, and is followed by the scene of the judgement of the nations. The master gave, according to each one’s ability, five talents, two talents and one. Notice the master’s praise: the one who received five gained five more, and the master said, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” The one who received two gained two more, and the master said exactly the same words (Matthew 25:23). Different results, the same praise. Because what God measures is not quantity but faithfulness.

The third passage is John chapter 21. This is the third time the risen Lord appeared to his disciples, by the Sea of Tiberias. Peter said, “I’m going fishing,” and went back to the place where he had been called three years before, back to the trade he knew best. Before the cock crowed he had denied the Lord three times, and now his heart was broken. Jesus didn’t begin by rebuking him, nor by handing out assignments. Jesus first lit a charcoal fire, grilled the fish, and invited him to breakfast. Only when breakfast was over did the Lord speak.

The Lord’s first question was not, “Are you still going to work?” but, “Do you love me more than these?” The verb in the original is ἀγαπᾷς (agapas). “These” could mean these fish, these boats, or these companions. Whatever it refers to, the Lord’s meaning is clear: before entrusting the flock, first settle the relationship of love for me.

Brothers and sisters, three passages, three scenes, all pointing to the same truth: the foundation of serving is not ability but relationship; the measure of serving is not results but faithfulness.

sections.heading: 1. Our Relationship with Things: God Values Faithfulness, Not Results
sections.html:
“It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2)

“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ ” (Matthew 25:21)

God’s standard for looking at things is not success or failure, not big or small, not much or little, but this: faithfulness.

The weight of one word: faithful

We often take “faithful” to mean “hanging on for a long time”. Hanging on for a long time is certainly not easy, but faithfulness in the Bible goes deeper than that. As we said, πιστός (pistos) means “trustworthy”. Whether a steward is faithful isn’t judged by how much is left in the storehouse, but by whether he has followed his master’s wishes and used his master’s goods where his master wanted them used.

The Lord Jesus stated the principle very plainly: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10) Faithfulness isn’t a performance in one big matter; it is consistency across countless small ones.

So whether the matter is great or small, what God looks at is whether you are faithful, whether you are acting according to his heart.

“To everyone who has will be given”

“For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.” (Matthew 25:29)

At first hearing this sounds very harsh, as if God favoured the strong. But we have to look at the context. The one who had everything taken away wasn’t the one who gained a little; he was the one who never put his talent to use at all. He buried his one talent in the ground, and his reason was, “Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man” (Matthew 25:24). His problem wasn’t ability; it was that he had his master wrong. His relationship with his master was fear, not trust; and since the relationship was cold, all he could do with the task was “play it safe and keep the capital”.

So what this verse means is this: to the faithful, God entrusts more; the unfaithful lose even what they had. God’s increase flows along the lines of relationship.

The key truth: God values “people being right”, not “getting lots done”

This is the first sentence today to engrave on your heart: God values people being right, not getting lots done.

Psychology offers some very sobering supporting evidence. In 1981 the psychologists Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley, and Susan Jackson set out three dimensions of “burnout”: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. Pay special attention to the second — depersonalisation. It means that a worn-out person begins to treat the people around him as “cases”, as “workload”, and no longer as people. The World Health Organization (WHO), in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) adopted in 2019, also listed burnout as a syndrome connected with occupational phenomena, defined as “resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where things end up when self-centred people do the work: first they rate the task above the person, then they turn people into tasks, and in the end they lose themselves as well.

A 321 Insight: working from the heart, or calculating with the brain

321 says it very clearly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll fret. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Work from the heart, and the result is faithfulness; calculate with the brain, and the result is comparison and pressure.

Self-centred people care about results, about comparison, about performance, because their sense of worth has to be supplied by what they achieve. Selfless people care about only one thing: am I being faithful to God? When a self-centred person finishes a job, he asks, “What do people think of me?” When a selfless person finishes a job, he asks, “Lord, are you pleased?”

A small example from daily life. A sister in one church was responsible for scrubbing the kitchen. For twenty years nobody applauded her for it. Once someone asked her whether she found it tiring. She said, “I’m not scrubbing floors. I’m getting a place ready for the Lord’s meal.” Brothers and sisters, the same cleaning cloth is drudgery in the hands of the self-centred and service in the hands of the selfless. The difference isn’t in the task; it’s in her relationship with the Lord.

Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said: “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.” That saying fits the Lord’s heart: God has no shortage of great things to be done; what he wants is people who love and are faithful.

sections.heading: 2. True Faithfulness: Acting According to God’s Heart
sections.html:
“I will raise up a faithful priest for myself who will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind.” (1 Samuel 2:35)

Faithfulness isn’t only seeing a thing through and never giving up; more important still, it is doing it according to God’s heart.

What faithfulness means, seen from the house of Eli

The setting of this verse is very grave. The era of the judges was drawing to a close, and the priest Eli was old. His two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were desecrating the sacrifices in the tabernacle at Shiloh and treating Yahweh’s offerings with contempt. God sent a man of God to speak to Eli, announcing that he would raise up a faithful priest.

Notice how God defines “faithful”: “who will do according to that which is in my heart.” The Hebrew word for “faithful” is נֶאֱמָן (ne’eman), from the same root as the “Amen” (aman) with which we close our prayers. Its basic meaning is “firm, reliable, able to stand”. The faithfulness God wants is to stand firm on God’s heart like a pillar, not to spin busily inside our own plans like a windmill.

Eli’s sons were not idle. They were at work in the tabernacle every day. Their service was full, but their hearts were empty; their hands were on the altar, but their hearts were on the sacrificial meat. This reminds us that a person can do the most unfaithful things in the holiest of places.

Wrong direction: the harder you try, the further off you go

Many people work very hard, but in the wrong direction: zealous yet out of step with God’s heart, diligent yet outside God’s will.

Why does this happen? Because they have not first built a relationship with God. Without relationship you don’t know God’s heart; without knowing God’s heart you cannot truly be faithful.

Here is an example you can actually work out. If your heading is off by one degree, it looks negligible. But by trigonometry, after a hundred kilometres you’re off by about 1.7 kilometres; after a thousand kilometres you’re off by more than seventeen. One degree at the start decides which city you end up in. Brothers and sisters, our relationship with God is the first degree of our life.

The Bible spelled out this principle long ago: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul kept back the best of the cattle and sheep, saying they were to be sacrificed to Yahweh. It sounded very spiritual, but it was disobedience. God wasn’t complaining that his offerings were poor; God wanted his heart.

The Lord Jesus himself is the most perfect role model: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19) Jesus is my role model — his service wasn’t self-initiated; it flowed from his relationship with the Father.

The key truth: the foundation of faithfulness is our relationship with God

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Paul says this in the middle of the dispute over eating food sacrificed to idols. Those strong in faith said, “I can eat it”; those weak in faith didn’t dare; and each side judged the other. Paul moves the focus from “May this be done?” to “For whom is this being done?”

So: what you do isn’t what matters; whom you do it for is what matters.

Psychological research also catches a glimpse of this dividing line. The American psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan put forward Self-Determination Theory in 1985, distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic motivation. And Deci’s experiments in 1971 found that when an external reward is brought into something people already enjoy, their intrinsic motivation may actually be weakened. In other words, once the reason for doing something shifts from “I love it” to “what will I get for it?”, joy begins to drain away.

Brothers and sisters, serving is just the same. When the reason we serve shifts from “I love the Lord” to “I want to be seen”, joy disappears and only weariness is left.

A 321 Insight: with your focus on Jesus, you’ll do the right things

321 reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances.

With your focus on Jesus, you’ll do the right things; with your focus on yourself, you’ll only do your own things.

Here is a very practical test: when something has been done well but nobody knows you did it, does your heart go cold? If it does, your focus is still on yourself. This isn’t condemnation; it’s a health check. Once the check has shown it up, hand it to the Lord and let him bring us, little by little, out of the self-centred life and into selflessness.

sections.heading: 3. Relationship First, Then Ministry: When People Are Right, Things Are Right
sections.html:
“So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ ” (John 21:15)

Jesus’ order with Peter is crystal clear: first he asks, “Do you love me?” — that is relationship; then he says, “Feed my lambs” — that is ministry. Relationship first, then ministry.

The Lord’s three questions and three charges to Peter

The Lord asked three times, and gave his charge three times. The first: “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) The second: “Tend my sheep.” (John 21:16) The third: “Feed my sheep.” (John 21:17)

The three questions answer to Peter’s three denials; the three charges are the Lord with his own hands putting a broken man back at his post.

Notice two things the Lord did not do. First, the Lord did not say, “Go and prove yourself to me first, and then I’ll hand the sheep over to you.” Second, the Lord did not say, “Since you have fallen, the ministry had better go to someone else.” The Lord restored the relationship first, and then restored the charge. Because in God’s kingdom, relationship is the root of ministry, not its reward.

This is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Life turned upside down: the more you do, the more tired you get

Many people do the opposite: they get things done first, and talk about relationships later. The result can be put in a few words — more work, more weariness, broken relationships and an empty heart.

This isn’t scaremongering. The story of Martha is a mirror: “Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’ ” (Luke 10:41–42)

What Martha was doing wasn’t wrong; she was serving Jesus. But the Lord said she was “anxious and troubled about many things”. The word for “anxious” in the original carries the sense of being distracted, pulled in different directions. If the things we do for the Lord do not flow out of time spent with the Lord, they will pull us away from his presence — and that is the deepest paradox of serving.

Paul puts it even more severely: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3) Feeding the poor is a good deed; giving up one’s body is a great deed; but without love — that is, without right relationship — on God’s books it still comes to nothing.

The Lord Jesus also warned us in advance: “Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’ ” (Matthew 7:22–23) He doesn’t deny that they did things. What he denies is this: “I never knew you” — there was no relationship.

The key truth: first the right people, then the right things

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people since 1938, for more than eighty years. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has pointed out publicly many times that what best predicts whether someone will be healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships. This is the longest study of human lives ever carried out, and the direction it points in is astonishingly consistent with the order of the Bible: relationships can carry a person’s whole life better than achievements can.

The conclusions of scientific research simply confirm, from a long way off, what the Creator said long ago.

Life flowing out into ministry: the lame man stands up

“But Peter said, ‘I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!’ ” (Acts 3:6)

“He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength. Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.” (Acts 3:7–8)

Why could Peter heal this man who had been lame from birth? Not because he had learnt a method, but because the Lord was in him. He wasn’t “carrying out a ministry”; he was letting the life within him flow out. He said, “I have no silver or gold” — he had no resources in his hands. He said, “what I have, that I give you” — he had Christ within.

Later the council arrested them for questioning, and the Bible says: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) Notice this: what people perceived was not their learning, but that they “had been with Jesus”.

So when the council forbade them to preach, “Peter and John answered them, ‘Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.’ ” (Acts 4:19–20)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the tone of that sentence. It isn’t “I have to do this job”, but “we can’t help telling”. They weren’t speaking for the sake of a task; their relationship with the Lord had filled them to the point where nothing could hold it back.

A 321 Insight: life flows out into ministry; ministry does not produce life

The Lord himself said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce fruit; a branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Fruit is “borne”, not “squeezed out”.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fivefold change follows the same order: when the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry naturally changes. Today many people want to skip the first four steps and change the ministry directly — and they work very hard, yet bear no fruit.

sections.heading: 4. The Faithful Steward: Doing Things Within Relationships, Building Relationships
sections.html:
“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

God’s heart is not only that things get finished, but that life is passed on and relationships are built.

“Commit” is a relational act

When Paul wrote 2 Timothy he was a prisoner in Rome, and he knew the time of his departure had come (2 Timothy 4:6–8). These are his last words. What matters most to a man about to die? Not how many projects he leaves behind, but how many people.

The Greek word for “commit” is παρατίθημι (paratithēmi). In the commercial and legal language of the day it meant “depositing” something valuable in the hands of a trustworthy person for safekeeping. That act can only happen within a relationship; you wouldn’t hand the family fortune to a stranger.

Look at the four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, the faithful men who will be able to teach others, and the others they will teach. What links those four generations together is not an institution but relationships. Spiritual life has never been passed on by copying; it is passed on by walking alongside.

This is the “235 relationships” of 321: becoming the “2”, spiritual companions, with a selfless person; establishing the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then becoming the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team. The expansion of God’s kingdom is the expansion of relationships.

The faithful steward: not damaging relationships while working, but building them

The faithful steward has two marks: while doing the work, he doesn’t damage relationships; while doing the work, he builds relationships.

This is hard, because work always comes with pressure, deadlines and demands for quality. When the pressure comes, the first thing we’re inclined to sacrifice is people — we speak a little faster, our faces grow a little darker, and a single “I’ll just do it myself” pushes someone away. The task gets finished, and the relationship goes cold.

Here there is some powerful supporting evidence. Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, in a study published in Administrative Science Quarterly in 1999, put forward the concept of “psychological safety”: in a team whose members believe they can admit mistakes and raise questions without being humiliated, learning and performance are actually better. The findings of Google’s “Project Aristotle”, published in 2016, likewise named psychological safety as the most critical factor in high-performing teams.

In other words, even the world’s research on organisations has found that when you take care of people, the work actually goes better; when you sacrifice people, the work ends up worse.

God said it long ago: “he who is greatest among you will be your servant.” (Matthew 23:11)

Spiritual summary: when people are right, things are right

So we can boil today’s message down to two sentences: when people are right, things are right; when people are wrong, things go wrong.

“People being right” here means all three relationships are right: right with God, right with ourselves, right with others.

Right with God — I know whose I am and whose work I’m doing. Right with myself — I don’t rely on what I do to prove myself; in Christ I am already accepted. Right with others — I don’t treat people as tools; I treat them as brothers.

When these three relationships are right, the things we do will come right of their own accord.

An old preacher who served for many years up in the mountains once said something I have never forgotten: “We’re not getting the work done; we’re bringing people up.” Brothers and sisters, the work will pass away, but people last for ever.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Achievement to Selfless Faithfulness
sections.html:
When we set today’s message within the framework of 321, the thread becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model — he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) The source of all he did was his relationship with the Father.

The Bible is my standard — it isn’t results that have the final say, nor other people’s opinions; it’s God’s word. It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who shows us God’s heart, so that we are not merely busy but sent.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — my diary is under his management, my priorities are his to arrange; let Jesus receive all the glory — when the work succeeds, the applause goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not a machine that uses people up; it is a family that brings people before God.

The self-centred life and selflessness: the deepest watershed in how we work

When self-centred people work, the task is their mirror: they want to see their own worth in the result. When selfless people work, the task is their altar: they offer everything up to the Lord.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In the way we work, pride often looks very devout: “I’ll just do it myself,” “only I can,” “it has to be me.” Humility, on the other hand, is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nine times out of ten, conflict between co-workers isn’t about truth; it’s about whose method gets adopted.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. When a person no longer needs his work to prove himself, Satan loses his most useful lever.

The shift of perspective: four moves “from … to …”

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: people look at results; God looks at motives.

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: earth hands out certificates; heaven hands out crowns. “Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (Revelation 2:10)

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the worldly way is “get the job done first and worry about the people later”; God’s way is “bring the people right first, and the job will get done”.

The 920 practice: living out selflessness in every task

The 920 practice reminds us that every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. Today we carry that into the realm of “things”: when you and a co-worker are working on something together, that co-worker is your “2”; when you’re rushing a project at the office, that colleague is your “2”. In that task, practise living out the selfless (0) life, and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Pay special attention to “patience” and “gentleness” — these two fruits only grow when “the job is urgent but the people are slow”. Tasks, it turns out, are the soil in which God grows fruit in us.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

321 draws the order of serving as a path: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

Look: “Service” comes fourth, not first. Much of the weariness in the church today comes from people starting to run at step four. Without Spirit, without Understanding, without Life, going straight to Service, we end up doing spiritual work in the strength of the flesh.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Doing Things in the Right Order
sections.html:
Practice 1: Check every day — am I just doing things, or am I working together with God?

Don’t just be busy; make sure: am I working within God’s heart?

How to practise: each day, before you do anything, first pray one sentence: “Lord, is this what you want me to do?”

That one-sentence prayer takes only five seconds, yet it can set the direction of the whole day right. “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1) Those who work together with God are building; those who don’t are labouring in vain.

Practice 2: Practise faithfulness in small things rather than chasing big things

Don’t despise small things: be faithful in small things and God gives increase; neglect small things and your spiritual life drains away.

How to practise: each day, do one “seemingly insignificant small thing” really well.

Wash a bowl, return a phone call, set out the chairs neatly, read a message properly to the end before replying. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10) Small things are God’s practice ground for us, and God’s examination hall too.

Practice 3: Deliberately build relationships while doing things, rather than sacrificing them

In serving and at work, don’t hurt people for the sake of efficiency; don’t damage relationships for the sake of results.

How to practise: today, in one particular task, deliberately “put people first”.

For example: before a meeting starts, greet people first; before handing out an assignment, first listen to the other person’s difficulties; when you’re desperate for results, first say, “Thank you — I know these last few days have been hard work.” “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Using the eight stages of changing our mindset to take the practice deeper

First, Information: copy today’s key sentence somewhere you’ll see it — God values people being right, not getting lots done.

Second, Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, so that this sentence moves from the paper into your heart. You might pray: “Lord, let me see whether I am really loving you, or proving myself.”

Third, Conviction: admit to God, and to yourself, that in the past you put things before people and put people before God, and that this was the wrong order.

Fourth, Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, before you do anything, first ask: “Lord, is this what you want me to do?”

Fifth, Evaluation: in the evening, take three minutes to look back — today, did I hurt anyone in order to get a job done?

Sixth, Correction: if you did, go and mend it tomorrow. One apology is worth more than ten successes.

Seventh, Repetition: don’t do it for just three days. God’s work takes shape through repetition; as habits take shape, life takes shape.

Eighth, Multiplication: bring this practice to your “2”. Find a spiritual companion, and each week ask one another: “This week, did you sacrifice a relationship in order to get something done?”

A Gentle Reminder: it isn’t a lack of effort; it’s the wrong order

Many people fail not because they don’t try hard, but because they put things above relationships: to get things done, they lose God; to finish the job, they lose people.

A family falls apart in quarrels over renovating the house; a team wounds one another putting on a big conference; a father, wanting to give his children a better life, misses their entire childhood. All of these are good things, but the price is far too high.

God’s heart is this: relationships first, then things.

Paul says: “each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.” (1 Corinthians 3:13) On that day, what the fire burns up will be the wood, hay and stubble; what remains will be everything we have faithfully offered within our relationships.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Be a Good and Faithful Servant
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, at the end of life, what counts is not how many things you did, but this: were you faithful to God, and did you build relationships?

Relationships are eternal; things are temporary.

One day we will all stand before the Lord. On that day nobody will ask you how many conferences you ran, how many contracts you signed, how many people you led. The Lord will say only one thing — the one thing we all long to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” (Matthew 25:21)

So may we live our whole lives in the right order: God first, then ourselves, then others, and only last of all things.

Then our lives will not only bear fruit but have true worth, and before God we will be good and faithful servants.

When you go home today, please do one thing: open your diary and look over this week. In all those boxes, where is God? Where are you? Where are the people closest to you? If the order is wrong, put it right now. Let Jesus reign as King — beginning with your diary. Let Jesus receive all the glory — beginning with the most insignificant little task you have.

keyVerses: 1 Corinthians 4:1–2
“So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.”
Matthew 25:21
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ ”
John 21:15

“So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ ”
declarations: Lord, I will adjust my relationship with things: no longer centred on things, but centred on you.
I will be a faithful steward, acting according to your heart in everything.
Let me first build my relationship with you, then build relationships with people, and then do my work within those relationships.
May all that I do glorify you, build relationships and live out Christ, so that I become an overcomer.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: Practise faithfulness in small things rather than chasing big things
Deliberately build relationships while doing things, rather than sacrificing them
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for speaking to us this morning.

Lord, we confess that we so often put things before you, and results before people. We are busy, but not always working together with you; we work hard, but not always within your heart. Please forgive us.

Put “faithfulness” within us, so that we are faithful even in the smallest things. Put “order” within us, so that we draw near to you first, then build relationships with people, and then do our work within those relationships.
Lord, let our serving flow out of life, not be squeezed out by pressure. May every small thing we do become a sign of our love for you.
Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our work, reign as King in our serving. May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Corinthians 4:2: “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” Please share: this week, what “insignificant little thing” is God asking you to do faithfully? How do you plan to do it?

John 21:15: “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” Think about it honestly: recently, has some task become a barrier between you and the Lord, or between you and your family? How are you willing to adjust the order?
