2. Deming, Out of the Crisis: the most important figures needed for management are unknown or unknowable.
3. What truly decides whether an organisation lives or dies is very often exactly what cannot be measured.
4. The result: we spend even more time repairing relationships, and pay an even greater price.

brief21.title: Point 3d: Slow Is Truly Fast
notes: Slide text:
Martha, distracted with much serving
Mary has chosen the good part
Fast isn’t always right; right is truly fast
Key points:
1. Martha loved the Lord and was diligent; the problem was not that her work was bad, but that the order was wrong.
2. What Mary chose was not a more important task but a more important place — sitting at the Lord’s feet.
3. Greek chronos is clock time; kairos is the time God has appointed.
4. Mischel’s marshmallow test: whether a child would wait depended on trusting the one who made the promise; the root of delayed gratification is trust.
5. Isaiah 28:16: “He who believes shall not act hastily.” Proverbs 21:5: everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty.

brief21.title: Point 4a: God Wants to Build People
notes: Slide text:
God’s heart is not to build structures
but to build people, to build disciples
The Lord left no constitution;
he left twelve men
Key points:
1. Structures exist to protect and serve people; once the structure becomes the goal, people become tools.
2. In three and a half years the Lord put up no building, wrote no book, drew up no system; he simply gave himself to twelve men.
3. It looks wildly inefficient, yet two thousand years on it has filled the whole earth.
4. Psalm 127:1: unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labour in vain.

brief21.title: Point 4b: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
notes: Slide text:
Get the order right: life flows
relationships connect
ministry bears fruit of its own accord
Love one another: the mark of disciples
Key points:
1. Get the order wrong, and ministry swells, relationships drain away, and life withers.
2. Illustration: Pando, the quaking aspen stand in Fishlake National Forest, Utah — more than forty thousand trees above ground, one root system and one life below.
3. The 235 relationships: 2 is spiritual companions, 3 is spiritual parents and children, 5 is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
4. John 13:35: if you love one another, everyone will know that you are my disciples.

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Slide text:
Today, put people before tasks
Care for the person, then the task
Ask about the relationship before the solution
In conflict, stop and ask yourself first
Key points:
1. How to practise 1: today, in one matter, first take time to understand how the other person feels.
2. One sentence is enough: “Are you all right?” “What are you really thinking about it?”
3. Matthew 5:23–24: first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift — even worship comes after reconciliation.
4. How to practise 2: when conflict comes, first stop and ask yourself, “How is my relationship with this person?”
5. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

brief21.title: Practice 3 and a Gentle Reminder
notes: Slide text:
A little slower, but a little more right
Slow down; put the relationship first
Efficient is not the same as fruitful
Without relationship, there is no life
Key points:
1. How to practise 3: in one matter, deliberately slow down and give priority to building the relationship.
2. James 1:19: swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
3. Galatians 6:9: let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season.
4. Gentle reminder: don’t let “solving problems” take the place of “building relationships”.
5. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Slide text:
Three Foundations, Two Core Values,
the Goal: God’s system
Self-centred values tasks; selfless values people
Mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
3. The self-centred person will always put tasks ahead of people, because tasks prove me; only the selfless person can put people ahead of tasks.
4. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — ministry comes last.
5. The 920 practice: everyone we relate to is our “2”; before them, live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Life’s greatest investment is relationships
Tasks pass away; relationships remain
From solving problems to building relationships
Let Jesus be King and receive the glory
Key points:
1. Nobody will remember your busiest project in five years, but the one sentence you said will be remembered for a lifetime.
2. 1 Corinthians 13:8: love never fails; verse 13: the greatest of these is love.
3. When you begin to turn from solving problems to building relationships, you begin to walk in God’s will.
4. Call: let Jesus be King, and you no longer need to prove yourself by results; let Jesus receive the glory, and you no longer need to rush for people to see you.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, rectify the priority of my life
Let me value people above tasks
Make me one who passes on life
Making disciples, welcoming revival
Key points:
1. Confession: we put tasks ahead of people, efficiency ahead of relationships, results ahead of life.
2. Thanksgiving: while we were still sinners, the Lord first laid down his life for us and restored the relationship.
3. Petition: Holy Spirit, remind us to look at the people first, not to take shortcuts, and first to restore our relationship with God.
4. Blessing: may our families, small groups and church, because the order is right, overflow with life and be joined together into God’s system.
5. Close with “Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.”

script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 153. The title is “Rectify the Priority”, and the subtitle is “From Solving Problems to Building Relationships”. Our theme verse is Matthew 28:19: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” Brothers and sisters, today we are going to face a very crucial question together: is our life, in the end, about solving problems, or about building relationships?

Let me begin with a scene. There was a brother who was the best in his church at getting things done. One year he was put in charge of a conference for more than a thousand people: four months of preparation, and everything arranged beyond reproach. On the night the conference ended, the lights went out one by one, the co-workers drifted off one after another, and he sat alone in the empty hall. In that moment he realised: in those four months, every word he had spoken had been about “things”; not a single word had been about “people”.
The job got done, but the people scattered.

There’s a saying commonly attributed to Goethe: if you fasten the first button of your life wrongly, you will never fasten the last one rightly. Brothers and sisters, doing up buttons doesn’t take strength; it takes order. Get the first one wrong, and the harder you push, the more crooked the shirt becomes.
Let’s look at the background of our theme passage. Matthew 28 is the summit of the whole book. The place is a mountain in Galilee; the time is after the Lord’s resurrection.

In the Greek original this passage has only one main command, and that is “make disciples of all nations”; “go”, “baptising” and “teaching” are all participles. So the heart of the Great Commission isn’t pulling off some big event; it is making disciples.

And how did the Lord himself do it? Mark 3:14: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” Look at the order — first being with him, then being sent; relationship first, ministry after.
Our first point: when relationships are right, things will come right.

There’s a well-turned saying: “With connection, there’s no problem; without connection, there’s a problem.” Its spiritual meaning is this: when the relationship is right, problems are easily solved; when the relationship is wrong, problems keep multiplying.

The very same sentence, from someone you trust, is care; from someone you don’t trust, it’s an attack. Brothers and sisters, we often think we are stuck on things, when really we are stuck on relationships.
321 tells us that relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last with things.

When our relationship with God is good, we become willing. When our relationship with ourselves is good, we become joyful — because rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. When our relationships with others are good, we become of one heart.
People like this work with motivation, with joy and with unity. Conversely, when relationships are poor, people are unwilling, joyless and divided, and however simple the task, it becomes hard.
So here is a key truth: God’s work is not driven by pressure; it is carried by relationship.
Our second point: solving problems alone loses people’s hearts.

Many people are in the habit of “dealing with the issue, not the person”. It sounds fair, but it so often overlooks the person. And the result is this: the problem is solved, but the person is hurt; the task is finished, but the relationship is broken.

That isn’t how God does it. Romans 3 says that all have sinned — “being justified freely by his grace”. In dealing with us, God doesn’t put judgement first; he puts relationship first. Jesus did not solve the problem first; he restored the relationship first.

The lesson gives us a comparison that cuts to the heart: a doctor who treats only the disease and not the person may cure the illness yet wound the heart. In 1984 Beckman and Frankel published a study in the Annals of Internal Medicine and found that, on average, doctors interrupted their patients eighteen seconds after they began to speak. Eighteen seconds is enough to deal with a symptom, but not enough to get to know a person.
Our third point: why do we turn the order upside down?

The first reason is that we are unwilling to pay the price. Building relationships takes time, companionship, prayer and patience; but solving problems is fast, efficient, and you can see the result. So people very easily choose the quick way rather than the right way.
But brothers and sisters, quick doesn’t mean right. Proverbs 19:2 speaks of “being hasty with one’s feet and missing the way.”

The second reason is that we prize time and results. Modern people talk about efficiency, performance and results. But relationships are hard to quantify, and hard to see straight away. So we give up on relationships and chase results.
And the result? We end up spending even more time repairing relationships, and paying an even greater price.
The Lord said to Martha, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.” What Martha was doing wasn’t bad; the order was wrong.
So please remember: what is fast is not necessarily right; what is right is what is truly fast.
Our fourth point: rectifying the priority, returning to God’s heart.

God’s heart is not to build things, not to build structures, but to build people, to build disciples, to build relationships. The Lord Jesus didn’t leave behind a constitution; he left behind twelve men.
When we turn our focus from “things” back to “people”, lives are changed, the church is renewed, and revival comes.
This is the core 321 insight: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Get the order right, and life flows, relationships connect, and ministry bears fruit of its own accord.
Brothers and sisters, there are three practices for today.

First, today deliberately put people before tasks: in one matter, first take time to understand how the other person feels. Second, when a problem comes, first ask, “How is the relationship?” and only then, “How do I solve it?” Third, choose to go a little slower, but a little more right.
A gentle reminder: you can be very efficient and yet bear no fruit. Because without relationship, there is no life.
Dear brothers and sisters, life’s greatest investment is not in tasks but in relationships.
Tasks pass away; relationships remain.

When you begin to turn from “solving problems” to “building relationships”, you begin to walk in God’s will. May we, all our lives long, rectify the priority and return to God’s heart; building lives, building relationships, building disciples, and welcoming God’s revival. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let’s pray together.

Dear Heavenly Father, we confess that we so often put tasks ahead of people, and results ahead of life. Please forgive us. Lord Jesus, thank you that while we were still sinners, you restored the relationship first. Holy Spirit, please remind us: look at the people first, then the task; a little slower, but a little more right.
Make us people who pass on life, people who make disciples. We pray in the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 153. The title is “Rectify the Priority”, and the subtitle is “From Solving Problems to Building Relationships”.

Our theme verses are Matthew 28:19: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” and Romans 3:23–24: “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;”
There’s a saying commonly attributed to Goethe: if you fasten the first button of your life wrongly, you will never fasten the last one rightly.

Brothers and sisters, doing up buttons doesn’t take strength; it takes order. Get the first one wrong, and the harder you push, the more crooked the shirt becomes; the more conscientious you are, the more neatly you get it wrong.

So many people spend their lives busy, worn out and discouraged — not because they don’t try hard enough, but because the order is wrong. When the order is wrong, life falls into disorder; when the order is right, everything comes right.

Let me begin with a scene. There was a brother who was the best in his church at getting things done. One year he was put in charge of a conference for more than a thousand people: four months of preparation, and everything from registration to the car-park traffic flow arranged beyond reproach.

On the night the conference ended, the lights went out one by one, the co-workers drifted off one after another, and he sat alone in the empty hall. In that moment he realised: in those four months, every word he had spoken had been about “things”; not a single word had been about “people”.
The job got done, but the people scattered.

Brothers and sisters, stories like this also happen in the office, at the dinner table, between husbands and wives, between parents and children. So today, please answer honestly: is our life about solving problems, or about building relationships?

First, the background. The author of Matthew is Matthew the tax collector, writing to Jewish believers who knew the Old Testament well. Chapter 28 is the summit of the whole book; the place is a mountain in Galilee, and the time is after the Lord’s resurrection.
There’s an important detail here: in the Greek original this passage has only one main command, and that is “make disciples of all nations”; “go”, “baptising” and “teaching” are all participles.

So the heart of the Great Commission is not running events, not setting up structures, but making disciples. The word “disciple” means a learner, a follower — in the rabbinic tradition, someone who walked behind his teacher, eating and living with him. Disciples were never formed by a curriculum, but by a relationship.
Our first point: when relationships are right, things will come right.

There’s a well-turned saying: “With connection, there’s no problem; without connection, there’s a problem.” Its spiritual meaning is this — when the relationship is right, problems are easily solved; when the relationship is wrong, problems keep multiplying.

The very same sentence, from someone you trust, is care; from someone you don’t trust, it’s an attack. When the relationship is good, one phone call settles it; when the relationship is bad, ten meetings won’t bring agreement.
Brothers and sisters, we often think we are stuck on things, when really we are stuck on relationships.
321 tells us that relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last with things.

When our relationship with God is good, we become willing. Psalm 110:3 says, “Your people offer themselves willingly.” Someone who has grown distant from God will still serve, but his hands are still moving while his heart has already left.

When our relationship with ourselves is good, we become joyful. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.
When our relationships with others are good, we become of one heart. Psalm 133:1 says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!”
So here is a key truth: God’s work is not driven by pressure; it is carried by relationship.

In Exodus 33, God said he would send an angel to lead the way, only he himself would not go with them. But Moses said, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” What Moses wanted was not Canaan; it was God himself.
The Lord also said, “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” Fruit isn’t squeezed out; fruit grows out of connection.

North America’s coast redwoods can grow to more than a hundred metres, yet their roots are only two or three metres deep. Why don’t they fall? Because their roots spread out sideways in every direction and intertwine with the trees beside them. When the gale comes, the whole forest bears it together.

Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed people for more than eighty years. Its director, Professor Robert Waldinger, sums up the conclusion in a single sentence: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.
Our second point: solving problems alone loses people’s hearts.
Many people are in the habit of “dealing with the issue, not the person”, handling everything through systems, rules and efficiency. It sounds professional, but it overlooks the “person”.

And the result is this: the problem is solved, but the person is hurt; the task is finished, but the relationship is broken. A task can be done over again; a relationship cannot easily be started over again.
The Lord said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” Systems are made for people, not people for systems.

Let’s look at how God does it. Romans 3 says that all have sinned — “being justified freely by his grace”. Our problem is a fact, and God doesn’t play it down; but God doesn’t put judgement first; he puts relationship first.
Romans 5:8 says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” God didn’t wait until we had sorted our problems out before he loved us.

Three pictures: when Adam sinned and hid, God asked, “Where are you?” When the prodigal son came home, his father “ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him”. After Peter had denied the Lord, the Lord asked, “Do you love me more than these?” Relationship first, problem after.
The lesson gives us a comparison that cuts to the heart: a doctor who treats only the disease and not the person may cure the illness yet wound the heart.

In 1984 Beckman and Frankel published a study in the Annals of Internal Medicine and found that, on average, doctors interrupted their patients eighteen seconds after they began to speak. Eighteen seconds is enough to deal with a symptom, but not enough to get to know a person.

Brothers and sisters, don’t we also often interrupt at eighteen seconds? Our child has said half a sentence and we’re already giving answers; a brother has only just mentioned his struggle and we’re already giving correction. We think we’re helping; in fact we’re shutting a door.
So 321 says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than results.
Our third point: why do we turn the order upside down? There are two reasons.

First, we are unwilling to pay the price. Building relationships takes time, companionship, prayer and patience. Time cannot be compressed — you cannot grow three years of trust in thirty minutes. Companionship cannot be outsourced — you cannot hire someone else to be your child’s father for you.
And solving problems? It’s fast, it’s efficient, and you can see the result. So people very easily choose the quick way rather than the right way.
But Paul chose the slowest way of all. He said, “we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls.” He gave two things: the gospel, and his own life.
Brothers and sisters, quick doesn’t mean right; only what is right will last.

Proverbs 19:2 speaks of “being hasty with one’s feet and missing the way.” So many of our careless words, misunderstandings and decisions we bitterly regret come not because there is no love in our hearts, but because our feet move too fast.

Seen from 321, the root of being unwilling to pay the price is the self-centred life. Self-centred people are in a hurry for results, because results prove me; selfless people are not in a hurry, because what they want is the name of Jesus.
Pride always wants to take the shortcut; humility is willing to take the long way round. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.
Second, we prize time and results. Modern people talk about efficiency, performance and results. But relationships are hard to quantify, and hard to see straight away.
You spend two hours over coffee with a young person, and it can’t be written into a report; you pray for a sister for a whole year, and on the annual report it’s a blank.

The management guru W. Edwards Deming said in Out of the Crisis that the most important figures needed for management are unknown or unknowable. What truly decides life or death is very often exactly what cannot be measured.
And the result? We end up spending even more time repairing relationships, and paying an even greater price.

The best-known example is in the home of the Lord Jesus’ own friends. Martha welcomed the Lord into her house. She loved the Lord and was extremely diligent, yet the Bible says she “was distracted with much serving”.

The Lord said, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part.” The Lord didn’t say that what she was doing was bad; what the Lord said was this — the order was wrong.
Greek has two words for “time”: chronos is clock time, kairos is the time God has appointed. Modern people manage chronos frantically, yet often miss kairos.

Walter Mischel’s marshmallow test at Stanford found that children who could delay gratification later did better; and later researchers pointed out that whether a child is willing to wait depends on whether he trusts the person who made the promise. So the root of delayed gratification is not willpower but trust.
Isaiah 28:16 says, “He who believes shall not act hastily.” What is fast is not necessarily right; what is right is what is truly fast.
Our fourth point: rectifying the priority, returning to God’s heart.
God’s heart is not to build things, not to build structures, but to build people, to build disciples, to build relationships.
Structures exist to serve people. But when the structure becomes the goal, people become tools; when the numbers become master, lives become costs.

The Lord Jesus didn’t leave behind a constitution; he left behind twelve men. For three and a half years he put up no building, wrote no book, drew up no system; he gave himself to twelve men. It looks wildly inefficient, yet two thousand years on it has filled the whole earth.
Psalm 127:1 says, “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.”
This is the core 321 insight: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Get the order right, and life flows, relationships connect, and ministry bears fruit of its own accord.

In Fishlake National Forest in Utah there is a stand of quaking aspen called “Pando”. Above ground it is more than forty thousand separate trees, yet below ground it is one root system, one single life, and it is reckoned to be one of the largest known organisms on earth.

Above ground it looks like forty thousand trees; below ground it is one life. This is God’s system. These are the 235 relationships: “2” is spiritual companions, “3” is spiritual parents and children, “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
The Lord said, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
Brothers and sisters, there are three practices for today.

First, today deliberately put people before tasks. How to practise: today, in one matter, first take time to understand how the other person feels. One sentence is enough: “Are you all right?” The Lord said, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Even worship comes after reconciliation.

Second, when a problem comes, first ask, “How is the relationship?” and only then, “How do I solve it?” How to practise: when conflict comes, first stop and ask yourself. Because the moment conflict comes, the flesh’s first reaction is always “I must win”. But pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
Third, choose to go a little slower, but a little more right. How to practise: in one matter, deliberately slow down and give priority to building the relationship.
James 1:19 says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” Scripture settled long ago what should be fast and what should be slow.
A gentle reminder: you can be very efficient and yet bear no fruit. Because without relationship, there is no life. Don’t let “solving problems” take the place of “building relationships”.

For these three practices to become life in us, we need to walk through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Let’s put today’s truth back into the picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person will always put tasks ahead of people, because tasks can prove me; only the selfless person can put people ahead of tasks.
The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — please notice that ministry comes last.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before that person, live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Brothers and sisters, among the nine graces of the fruit, not one is efficiency, and not one is performance; every one of them can only grow within relationships.
Dear brothers and sisters, life’s greatest investment is not in tasks but in relationships. Tasks pass away; relationships remain.
The project that keeps you busiest this year — in five years nobody will remember it. But the one sentence you said to someone when you were at your busiest, they will remember all their life.
1 Corinthians 13 says, “Love never fails.” “The greatest of these is love.”

When you begin to turn from solving problems to building relationships, you begin to walk in God’s will. May we, all our lives long, rectify the priority and return to God’s heart; building lives, building relationships, building disciples, and welcoming God’s revival.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father, we confess: we so often put tasks ahead of people, efficiency ahead of relationships, results ahead of life. Please forgive us.
Lord Jesus, thank you. While we were still sinners, you did not first condemn us; you first laid down your life for us. You did not first solve the problem; you first restored the relationship.

Holy Spirit, please remind us: look at the people first, then the task; a little slower, but a little more right. Write this order on the tablets of our hearts — life first, then relationships, then ministry.

May our families, our small groups and our church, because the order is right, overflow with life and be joined together into God’s system. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. We pray in the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!

sections.heading: Introduction: The First Button Done Up Wrong
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin with a very small but very important question: have you ever done up the first button of a shirt in the wrong hole? Get the first one wrong, and every button after it goes wrong too. You look down: the collar is crooked, the hem hangs uneven, and however much you tug, it won’t sit straight. At that point the easiest fix is not to shift the lower buttons across one by one, but to go back to the first one, undo it, and fasten it again.

Spiritual life is the same. We often spend a great deal of effort adjusting the lower buttons — adjusting our emotions, our circumstances, our relationships, our plans, our schedules — yet we rarely stop to ask: is my first button done up right?

In the spiritual life there is a question that is absolutely crucial and yet so often overlooked: is our “order” right?

Very often we think the point of faith is “solving problems”. The prayer most often heard in church is “Lord, please take this thing away”; the expectation most often in our hearts is “Once this problem has passed, then I’ll have peace.” But brothers and sisters, Jesus keeps bringing us back to a deeper core — “building relationship”.

When the order is wrong, we go round and round inside our problems; when the order is right, we overcome within the relationship.

This is the second lesson on the theme “rectify the priority”. This morning God wants to show us something very concrete: the real key is not whether the problem has been solved, but whether we are connected with God.

Let me tell you about an experience many people have had. A sister once said with great honesty, “The most on-fire six months of my life were the six months my husband was ill. In those six months I prayed every day, wept every day, read the Bible every day, clung to God every day. Then his test results came back normal, and I … disappeared.” She said it very honestly, and it cuts deep. The problem pushed her into God’s presence; when the problem left, so did she. Her faith was built not on “God”, but on “need”.

Faith like this produces a very strange result: we actually need problems in order to stay devout. Once the wind drops and the sea is calm, we lose our reason for drawing near to God. So someone once half-jokingly prayed, “God, if I go too long without any trouble, please give me a little reminder.” Brothers and sisters, that is not faith; that is treating God as a tool.

There is an even more hidden version of this, and it’s found in ministry. Some people are at church all year round — leading worship, leading small groups, visiting, running the sound desk — so busy that not a single weekend is their own; yet when things go quiet, their hearts feel empty. Because they have given all their time to “God’s work”, but no time to “God”. The buttons of ministry are all neatly fastened, but the first button, the relationship, hangs loose.

In today’s lesson God wants to rectify our priority. He wants us to fasten that first button properly again — not solving the problem first, but building the relationship first; not dealing with things first, but coming back first into the Father’s presence.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, One Line
sections.html: The main passages for this lesson come from three scenes set more than a thousand years apart, yet they join into one very clear line. Once we get the background clear, the power of the text comes through.

sections.heading: 1. Matthew 6: Prayer in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum, who was sitting at the tax office when the Lord called him (Matthew 9:9). The book is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jews and Jewish Christians, which is why it quotes the Old Testament so extensively — to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament.

The theme passage comes from the “Sermon on the Mount” (Matthew 5–7). Before Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray, he first corrects two wrong kinds of prayer. The first is the Pharisees’ performance prayer, standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. The second is the Gentiles’ transactional prayer: “In praying, don’t use vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.” (Matthew 6:7) The Gentile mindset was that God is hard to please and has to be persuaded, so you must keep repeating, keep raising the stakes, keep going on longer, in order to get an answer in exchange.

Then Jesus says something that cuts the ground from under all of that: “Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) Feel the weight of this: since the Father already knows, prayer cannot be “informing God”, nor can it be “persuading God”. So what is prayer? Jesus answers with his very next words — “Our Father in heaven”. Prayer is a child coming back into the presence of the Father.

sections.heading: 2. Exodus 15: The Bitter Water of Marah
sections.html:
The author of Exodus is Moses. Scholars hold two views on the date of Israel’s exodus from Egypt, the fifteenth century BC or the thirteenth century BC; this passage is set shortly after the crossing of the Red Sea.

“Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water. When they came to Marah, they couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter. Therefore its name was called Marah.” (Exodus 15:22–23) “Marah” in Hebrew is מָרָה (marah), and it simply means “bitter”. The victory song by the Red Sea had only just been sung (Exodus 15:1–21); the tambourine in Miriam’s hand was still warm — and three days later they could no longer sing.

sections.heading: 3. Numbers 14: Unbelief at Kadesh
sections.html: Numbers 14 is that night at Kadesh Barnea when the Israelites, having heard the bad report of the ten spies, the whole congregation wept aloud and wanted to choose another leader and go back to Egypt. Barely more than a year out of Egypt, they had seen it all — the ten plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, water from the rock — not one thing missing; and yet they fell at the very gate of the promised land. God’s verdict goes straight to the heart: they had seen the miracles, yet still they did not believe.

sections.heading: 4. Romans 8: A Declaration in the Shadow of the Sword
sections.html:
Romans was written by the apostle Paul around AD 56–57, at the end of his third missionary journey, in Corinth, to the church in Rome, which he had not yet met. The believers in the city of Rome were already living in the shadow of persecution; not long afterwards, in AD 64, came the great fire of Rome, Nero laid the blame on the Christians, and persecution broke out in full force. Tradition holds that Paul himself was martyred under Nero.

Romans 8 is the summit of the whole letter. It was not in easy times that Paul wrote that nothing “will be able to separate us from God’s love”. He first lists in a single breath seven of the most savage things — oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword (Romans 8:35) — and only then does he say: none of these can cut us off.

Brothers and sisters, look at this line: on one side, the bitter water of Marah; on the other, the swords of Rome. Before the bitter water, people complained; before the sword, people overcame. Where does the difference lie? Not in the size of the problem, but in the depth of the relationship. This is the order this lesson sets out to rectify.

sections.heading: 1. The Nature of Prayer: Not Solving Problems, but Building Relationship
sections.html:
“Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9)

When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, the first words were not “Lord, help me”, nor “Lord, please take this hardship away”, but “Our Father in heaven”.

This is a profound revelation: the starting point of prayer is not a problem; the starting point of prayer is a relationship.

Light from the original: not “the Most High”, but “Abba”

“Father” here in Greek is Πάτερ (pater). When Jesus prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane, he used the Aramaic Ἀββά (abba), the most natural and intimate word a child at home uses for his father. Paul twice preserves this word exactly as it is: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15)

Notice the difference between a slave and a son. A slave comes into his master’s presence always to report, to collect his wages, to ask for a reward; a son can come into his father’s presence with nothing at all on his mind — he has simply come home. The slave is concerned with “Is the job done?”; the son is concerned with “Is Dad there?” The very first words of the Lord’s Prayer settle our identity the moment we open our mouths: we are children, not employees.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: To Know God Is Eternal Life

In the same passage Jesus first says, “Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) Since the Father already knows our needs, prayer clearly isn’t for passing information on to God.

Then, in the same chapter, Jesus spells out the whole order: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) The word “first” is about order. When the order is right, things will be added to you; when the order is wrong, you can grab at things your whole life long and never gain God.

In John’s Gospel, Jesus gives a definition of eternal life: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) Brothers and sisters, the definition of eternal life is not “all my problems solved” but “knowing”. Knowing is the language of relationship, not the language of a transaction.

The Old Testament prophets speak with the same voice: “Let’s acknowledge Yahweh. Let’s press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.” (Hosea 6:3) “Let’s press on to know Yahweh” — not pressing on for answers, but pressing on for him.

An Illustration from Life: The Child Who Only Calls When He Needs Money

Imagine a child who has left home to study. He phones home once a month, and every call opens the same way: “Dad, this month’s money …” Of course the father sends it, because he is the father. But after he puts the phone down, how does that father feel? What he wants isn’t to send the money off; what he wants is to hear his child’s voice.

Then one day the child rings and says, “Dad, nothing’s wrong — I just wanted to talk to you.” You can imagine the look on that father’s face. Brothers and sisters, our Heavenly Father is waiting for a call like that, too.

In recent years we’ve all learned the phrase “left on read”. But there is something that hurts even more: “only replying when you need something”. With God, we so often only reply when we need something. God has never turned our requests away; he is simply waiting, all the time, for a call where “nothing’s wrong”.

Confirmation from Psychology: The Secure Base

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby (1907–1990) put forward attachment theory, and his colleague Mary Ainsworth (1913–1999) tested it in the 1970s with her “Strange Situation” experiment. The research found that infants who had formed a secure attachment to their caregiver were actually the most willing to leave their mother and explore the toys in the room — because they knew she was there and they could go back to her at any moment. Psychology calls this a “secure base”.

This is exactly a picture of the spiritual life. Someone with a secure relationship with God does not get out of facing the world; rather, he has more courage to face it, because he knows he can return to the Father at any time. By contrast, someone whose relationship is unsteady panics at the first stir of trouble, because he isn’t sure whether God is there, whether God likes him, whether God will pay him any attention this time.

In church history, Augustine opens his Confessions with words that have been repeated for well over a thousand years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The restlessness of the human heart comes not from having too many problems, but from not yet having come home to the Father who made us.

A 321 Insight

Jesus is the focal point, not our problems; Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The 321 order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Prayer is the most direct training ground of relationship. When we return to the relationship, problems no longer rule us — not because the problems have shrunk, but because God has grown bigger.

sections.heading: 2. Faith That Seeks Only Miracles Cannot Last
sections.html:
“The people murmured against Moses, saying, ‘What shall we drink?’” (Exodus 15:24)

The Israelites had only just witnessed the enormous miracle of the Red Sea parting. With their own eyes they had seen the walls of water stand up; with their own feet they had walked across the dry seabed; with their own ears they had heard the whole Egyptian army go under behind them. Miriam took up her tambourine and danced, and the whole nation sang with one voice. Yet their faith lasted only three days. The moment they met the problem of “bitter water”, they complained at once.

This exposes something very serious: if faith is built on “miracles”, it cannot last; only when faith is built on “relationship” does it stand firm.

Miracles Cannot Manufacture Faith

“because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.” (Numbers 14:22–23)

They saw the miracles, yet still did not believe — this is Scripture’s most grievous diagnosis of that generation. The problem was never whether God was at work, but whether people knew God.

In the New Testament, Jesus said the same thing: “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” (John 6:26) After the five loaves and two fish, the crowds following him were enormous; but when Jesus began to speak of the cross, people drifted away. What they wanted was bread, not the Lord who gives the bread.

John’s Gospel also records a very sobering passage: “Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did. But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone, and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.” (John 2:23–25) They “believed”, yet Jesus did not entrust himself to them — because that kind of believing stopped at the miracles and never entered into relationship.

A Cycle: Problem-Driven Faith

When people want God only to solve their problems, they fall into a cycle: when there’s a problem, they ask God; when the problem is solved, they forget God; when the next problem comes, they ask God again.

321 has a name for this cycle: the self-centred life — putting ourselves at the centre, placing God beneath our own needs, using God to solve our difficulties. This is the very same old road of the ancient serpent in the Garden of Eden: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Satan never urges people to do without God; he only urges them to put themselves at the centre and make God revolve around them. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place.

Confirmation from Psychology: Hedonic Adaptation

Psychology has a well-known finding called “hedonic adaptation”, also known as the “hedonic treadmill”, first put forward by Brickman and Campbell (Brickman & Campbell, 1971). In 1978 Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman (Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman) published a classic study comparing the happiness of lottery winners with that of ordinary people, and found that after a while the big winners were not noticeably happier than the control group.

In other words, when you get the very thing you thought would make you happy for the rest of your life, the happiness drifts back to where it started. Brothers and sisters, isn’t this the bankruptcy of the assumption “once the problem is solved I’ll have peace”? The water turned sweet, but ahead lay the wilderness of Sin; the manna came down, yet they still longed for the meat pots of Egypt. The empty place in the human heart was not made by problems, so it cannot be filled by solving problems either. Pascal says in his Pensées, in essence, that there is an infinite abyss in the human heart that can be filled only by an infinite and unchanging object — that is, by God himself.

At Marah the Point Was Not the Water, but God

Look at how the story goes on: “Then he cried to Yahweh. Yahweh showed him a tree, and he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet. There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them.” (Exodus 15:25) Of course God healed the water. But in that same place God did something more important: he laid down a statute and an ordinance, he tested them, and then he revealed his own name — “for I am Yahweh who heals you.” (Exodus 15:26)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: God did not say “I give you water”; God said “I am the one who heals you.” The water was the gift; God was the answer. The Israelites saw only the bitter water turn sweet, and missed the God who had come right up to them and revealed himself. We are often just the same — we take the gift and miss the One who gave it.

Here is a very simple comparison. A husband comes home from a business trip with a present for his wife. If she unwraps the present and then turns and walks away, how will he feel inside? He brought the present home because he wanted to see her, not because she needed that present.

A 321 Insight

Relying on the brain and ourselves, we pursue results; relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we pursue relationship.

Only through selflessness, letting Jesus reign as King, will our faith be steady and unshaken by circumstances. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into and living out the fullness and victory of Jesus — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The Israelites changed their route, but not their mindset; the people came out of Egypt, but Egypt did not come out of their hearts. So those forty years in the wilderness were spent going round and round — not around a road, but around a mindset.

sections.heading: 3. Those Who Build Relationship Overcome in All Things
sections.html:
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35)

“No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” (Romans 8:37)

“For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38–39)

Paul Was Not a Man Without Problems

The Paul who wrote these words was the man who had been flogged, beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked three times, and had spent a night and a day in the open sea (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). The seven things he lists are not rhetoric; they are his CV. He wasn’t standing on a calm shore saying the storm is nothing to fear; he was standing in the middle of the storm saying: this storm cannot cut me off from my relationship with the Lord.

So he did not overcome by means of his circumstances; he overcame by means of the relationship.

Light from the Original: More Than Conquerors

“More than conquerors” in Romans 8:37 is, in Greek, ὑπερνικῶμεν (hypernikōmen). νικάω (nikaō) means “to overcome”; put ὑπέρ (hyper, “beyond”) in front of it, and together it means “to super-overcome”, “to win by far”. Not a narrow win, not a costly win, but a win with plenty to spare.

The word for “separate” is χωρίζω (chōrizō), meaning “to divide, to part”. The word Paul uses is not “attack” but “separate”. The enemy’s real aim has never been to make you miserable; it is to separate you from God. So what we really need to guard is not our comfort, but our connection.

Two Pictures: The Anchor and the Root

The first picture is the anchor. “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil;” (Hebrews 6:19) A ship that has dropped anchor still rocks in the wind and waves, but it does not drift away. Overcoming doesn’t mean not rocking; overcoming means not drifting away.

The second picture is the root. California’s coast redwoods can grow to nearly a hundred metres tall, the tallest trees on earth; yet their roots are not deep, usually only a few metres. The reason they can stand for a thousand years is that root and root weave together underground into one great mat. Height in isolation is the most dangerous thing; life in connection is the most secure. Brothers and sisters, our security lies not in our own height, but in our connection.

Confirmation from Research: Relationships Shape a Whole Life

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has been following the same group of people since 1938, and is one of the longest-running studies of adult development in existence; its current director is Robert Waldinger of Harvard Medical School. More than eighty years of data point to a simple conclusion: what makes people healthier and happier across their whole lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Science’s conclusion stops at the relationships between people; Scripture extends that line upward, to the relationship between people and God. If human relationships can shape the health and happiness of a whole life, how much more our relationship with the ever-living God?

The Problem Remains, but the Heart Is at Rest

When people truly build a relationship with God, three very concrete things begin to show: the problem remains, but the heart is not stirred up; circumstances change, but faith is not shaken; outside there is upheaval, inside there is rest.

This isn’t numbness, nor is it escapism. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” (Psalm 46:1) The psalmist doesn’t say God makes trouble disappear; he says God is a very present help in trouble. And the same psalm ends: “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) We become still not because everything has been sorted out, but because we know that he is God.

This is the life of an overcomer. An overcomer is not someone with no battles to fight, but someone who, in the middle of the battle, never leaves his Commander’s side.

A 321 Insight

Selflessness unites us with Christ; union means victory. “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The 321 order is life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today’s lesson deals with the very furthest upstream layer — our relationship with God. Only when the upstream runs clear will the downstream run clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: When the Order Is Right, Everything Is Right
sections.html:
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the first thing Jesus did on earth was to go out into the wilderness to pray early in the morning, before it was light, drawing near to the Father first and then going out to serve people; the Bible is my standard — it is not my feelings, nor the size of my problems, that decide how closely I draw near to God, but God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide — rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the King is not someone I order about; the King is the one I obey; let Jesus receive all the glory — when the problem is solved, the glory goes to him; when the problem is still there, I still worship him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not piled up out of lots of people and lots of activity; it is a company of people who have a real relationship with God, being built together.

The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of our problems. Treating God as a tool for solving problems is the most refined form of the self-centred life — calling on God with our lips, while “self” sits enthroned in our hearts. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The Fivefold Change

321 says the fivefold change runs: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. What this lesson sets out to change is that very first button — our mindset. From “faith is about solving problems” to “faith is about building relationship”. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships naturally change; and when relationships change, only then will ministry bear real fruit. The order cannot be reversed.

To people whose ministry was overflowing, Jesus spoke the most terrifying words: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.” (Matthew 7:23) They had preached, cast out demons and done mighty works in the Lord’s name; every box under ministry was ticked, but the box under relationship was blank. Brothers and sisters, don’t turn ministry into a substitute for relationship.

The Shift in Perspective

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: people ask, “When will this be over?”; God asks, “How much have you come to know me in this?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: on earth we see bitter water; heaven sees the tree — a foreshadowing of the cross.

From the temporary to the eternal: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

From the worldly to the godly: worldly faith seeks “things going smoothly”; godly faith seeks “being right with God”.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice is this: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, practise living out the selfless (0) life, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice one thing: not one of the nine graces is “problems disappearing”. Fruit grows out of relationship; it isn’t handed out after a problem is solved. Someone whose relationship with God is right can grow patience, peace and joy even while the problem is still there.

The 235 relationships are these: with a selfless person become a “2”, spiritual companions; establish “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. When you start to have a spiritual companion with whom you don’t talk about problems but simply talk about God, your faith has moved from being problem-driven to being relationship-driven.

The Path of Serving

Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). This path begins with the Spirit, not with tasks; it ends with God being glorified, not with problems being solved. When the order is right, the path is right.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will drive each one deep using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Every day, set aside a “prayer with no agenda”

Focus of the practice: for the relationship alone, not for problems.

Each day, set aside a time to pray — not to ask for anything, but simply to draw near to God. You might begin like this: “Heavenly Father, I come before you not to ask for anything, but to draw near to you.” Let your heart grow still before God, and learn to enjoy being with him.

Information: first hold on to today’s truth — the Father already knows what I need (Matthew 6:8). Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see that you are a son, not a slave. Conviction: say to God in your heart, “I believe,” and admit that in the past you have treated him as a tool. Implementation: start with five minutes; set an alarm, and for five minutes ask for nothing at all, just say, “Lord, I love you; I’ve come simply to be with you.” Evaluation: in those five minutes, where did your heart wander off to? Did you sit down and immediately start planning your schedule? Correction: write your to-do list on a piece of paper first and put it to one side, so that your heart is free. Repetition: twenty-one days in a row, at the same time and in the same place every day. Multiplication: find a brother or sister to do this twenty-one-day practice with you, and remind each other.

David’s prayer can be our model: “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.” (Psalm 27:4) What he wanted was to dwell in the house, not to grab something and leave.

Practice 2: When a problem comes, first ask, “What is God’s heart in this?”

Focus of the practice: from solving problems to seeking God.

When you meet a problem, don’t rush to get it solved; first ask: Lord, what do you want me to learn in this? Which side of you do you want me to come to know better? Let the problem become a doorway to knowing God, not a source of anxiety.

Information: remember the lesson of Marah — what God revealed beside the bitter water was “I am Yahweh who heals you” (Exodus 15:26). Revelation: ask God to let you see some aspect of himself in the midst of your hardship. Conviction: believe that if this has come to me, God surely has a good purpose in it. Implementation: get a “problem notebook”; on the left write the problem, and on the right write only one sentence — “In this, I have come to know God’s ____.” Evaluation: look back after a week — is the right-hand column still empty? Correction: if it is, it means I am still asking God for a method, not for himself. Repetition: build the reflex of “ask for his heart first, then ask for a method”. Multiplication: tell your small group the testimonies in your right-hand column.

Moses’ example is the best contrast. He did not say, “Please take the hardship away”; he said, “please show me your way, now, that I may know you” (Exodus 33:13), and again, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” (Exodus 33:15) What Moses wanted was not an easy road, but God going with him.

Practice 3: Practise Holding On to the Relationship in Every Circumstance

Focus of the practice: circumstances do not decide the relationship.

In good times and bad, stay connected with God every day — prayer, Bible reading, worship. Remind yourself: I don’t draw near to God because of my circumstances; I draw near to him because I love him. A life like this will grow more and more secure.

Information: see clearly the difference between “drawing near to God because of circumstances” and “drawing near to God because I love him”. Revelation: let the Holy Spirit show you which seasons of your life you prayed in only because you were afraid. Conviction: resolve to let love be your motive — “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) Implementation: set an “immovable appointment” that doesn’t change in good times or bad. Evaluation: this week, was there a day you skipped it because “nothing was going on today”? Correction: shorten the time but don’t cancel it — better five minutes than zero. Repetition: three months without a break, and it becomes the skeleton of your life. Multiplication: bring one person in to keep this appointment with you.

Asaph’s testimony is worth learning by heart: “Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.” (Psalm 73:25) “But it is good for me to come close to God. I have made the Lord Yahweh my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.” (Psalm 73:28)

A Gentle Reminder: Where Peace Comes From

Many people think, “Once the problem is solved, I’ll have peace.” But the order God gives is exactly the opposite: it is not solving the problem that brings peace; it is building the relationship that brings peace.

Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.” (John 14:27) The peace the world gives is to take the problem away; the peace Jesus gives is that he himself comes.

Isaiah also says it very clearly: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.” (Isaiah 26:3) The condition of peace is not that nothing is happening around us, but that our hearts are steadfastly trusting in him.

So don’t fix your focus on the problem; fix your focus on Jesus. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll be joyful; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll be troubled.

When Peter was walking on the water, the wind and waves were there the whole time; while he looked at Jesus he kept walking, and when he looked at the waves he began to sink. Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t the waves that changed; it was his focus.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: When the Relationship Is Right, Everything Is Right
sections.html:
When prayer turns from “asking for our circumstances to change” to “longing to know God”, and when faith turns from “solving problems” to “building relationship”, your life will enter a whole new level.

Problems no longer rule you, circumstances no longer bind you, because you have taken hold of what matters most — your relationship with God.

Every sailor knows this principle: set off from harbour just one degree off course, and it looks trivial; but after a hundred kilometres you will be nearly 1.8 kilometres off target. A one-degree difference in our order becomes a world of difference by the end of a life. So this morning we are not here to do one more thing; we are here to correct our heading by one degree.

Let Jesus be King — the King is not a consultant I’ve called in to solve my problems; the King is the Lord I obey all my life. Let Jesus receive all the glory — not waiting until the problem is solved to give him the glory, but now, at this very moment, while the problem is still unsolved, giving him the glory.

At the start of his book The Knowledge of the Holy, A. W. Tozer says that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us. Brothers and sisters, when you think of God, what comes to mind — a “God who solves problems”, or a “Father who loves you”? That answer decides the order of your whole faith.

This morning, let us rectify the priority together. Not dealing with the problem first, but coming back first into the Father’s embrace. Because when the relationship is right, everything is right.

prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I will no longer make solving problems my centre; I will make building my relationship with you my priority.

Lord, forgive me for treating you as a tool in the past — calling on you when I needed something, and drifting away when I didn’t. Today I return to my place as a son, back into the Father’s presence.
Whatever my circumstances, I will draw near to you, know you and trust in you. In good times I will not leave you; in hard times I will not complain against you.
I believe that nothing can separate me from your love. Not oppression, not anguish, not persecution — not even the sword.
I want to live in your presence and become a steady, joyful overcomer. Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9) Think back honestly: over the past month, how much of your praying has been “asking for things”, and how much has been “drawing near to God”? What does that proportion tell you? How, specifically, will you adjust it?

“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution …?” (Romans 8:35) In the hardship you are facing that is still unresolved, at what moment have you felt “I’m about to be cut off”? blog.title: Is Your Faith About Solving Problems, or Building Relationship?

blocks.x: Have you ever done up the first button of a shirt in the wrong hole? Get the first one wrong, and every button after it goes wrong too. The easiest fix is not to shift the lower buttons across one by one, but to go back to the first one and fasten it again.
Spiritual life is the same. We spend a great deal of effort adjusting our emotions, our circumstances and our relationships, yet we rarely stop to ask: is my first button done up right?
Praying Only When There’s a Problem, Drifting Away When There Isn’t
A sister once said with great honesty, “The most on-fire six months of my life were the six months my husband was ill. Then his test results came back normal, and I … disappeared.”
The problem pushed her into God’s presence; when the problem left, so did she. Faith like this produces a very strange result: we actually need problems in order to stay devout.
But when Jesus taught his disciples to pray, the first words were not “Lord, help me”.
“Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9)

Just before this he had said, “your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) Since the Father already knows, prayer cannot be informing God, nor can it be persuading God. The starting point of prayer is not a problem; it is a relationship.
Faith That Seeks Only Miracles Lasts Just Three Days

The Israelites had seen the Red Sea part with their own eyes; Miriam took up her tambourine and danced, and the whole nation sang. And then? They went three days in the wilderness and found no water, and when they came to Marah — “Marah” simply means “bitter” — they complained at once. Three days after the victory song by the Red Sea, they could no longer sing it.

If faith is built on miracles, it cannot last; only when faith is built on relationship does it stand firm. Psychology has a finding called “hedonic adaptation”: a classic 1978 study showed that even lottery winners’ happiness drifts back to where it started after a while.

But Marah has a beautiful sequel: God healed the water, and in that same place he revealed his own name — “for I am Yahweh who heals you.” (Exodus 15:26) He did not say “I give you water”; he said “I am the one who heals you.” The water was the gift; God was the answer.
The Problem Remains, but the Heart Is at Rest

When Paul wrote that nothing “will be able to separate us from God’s love”, he was not standing on a calm shore. He had been flogged, stoned and shipwrecked three times. The oppression, anguish, persecution and sword he lists are not rhetoric; they are his CV. He did not overcome by means of his circumstances; he overcame by means of the relationship.
It is like a ship that has dropped anchor: it still rocks in the wind and waves, but it does not drift away. Overcoming doesn’t mean not rocking; overcoming means not drifting away.

Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, and its conclusion is simple: what makes people healthier and happier across their whole lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships. If that is true of relationships between people, how much more of our relationship with God?
Three Small Things You Can Do Today
1. Every day, set aside five minutes for a “prayer with no agenda”. Ask for nothing; just say, “Heavenly Father, I come before you not to ask for anything, but to draw near to you.”
2. When a problem comes, don’t rush to get it solved; first ask, “Lord, which side of you do you want me to come to know better in this?”
3. Set an immovable appointment that you don’t cancel in good times or bad. I don’t draw near to God because of my circumstances; I draw near to him because I love him.

It is not solving the problem that brings peace; it is building the relationship that brings peace. Don’t fix your focus on the problem; fix it on Jesus. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll be joyful; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll be troubled.
When faith turns from “solving problems” to “building relationship”, your life will enter a whole new level. Because when the relationship is right, everything is right.
Questions for Reflection
→ Looking back over the past month, how much of your praying has been “asking for things”, and how much has been “drawing near to God”? What does that proportion tell you?
