brief12.title: Discipline Is for Restoration
notes: Slide text:
Rectify the Priority (Part 3)
“For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines…
God deals with you as with children”
(Hebrews 12:6–7)
Key points:
1. Greet the congregation; announce the title and theme verses: Hebrews 12:6–7 and Genesis 3:9.
2. Explain that this is the third lesson in the “rectify the priority” series: the first two rectified the order of prayer; today rectifies the order of discipline.
3. State the lesson’s main thread in one sentence: truly godly discipline is not for solving problems; it is for restoring relationships.
4. Preview the three points: putting the task above the person loses hearts; love-centred discipline says “I’ll walk with you as you change”; God disciplines to restore people.

brief12.title: Introduction: Your First Words Give Your Heart Away
notes: Slide text:
The milk is spilled — what do you say first?
“How could you be so careless!”
or “Did you hurt yourself?”
Our first words reveal our inner order
Key points:
1. Describe the kitchen scene: milk spilled, glass shattered, the child frozen in the middle.
2. Contrast two kinds of first words: one aimed at the thing (cloth, floor), one aimed at the person (did you hurt yourself?).
3. Name the three things we most often ask when someone does wrong: how to correct it, how to solve it, how to get back to normal.
4. Turn: God cares not only about “what have you done wrong?” but even more about “where are you, the person, right now?”

brief12.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
“Yahweh God called to the man…
‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)
Discipline in the original: upbringing, not punishment
God cares not about the incident, but the relationship
Key points:
1. Hebrews background: author unknown — Origen said God alone knows; around AD 60–70, written to persecuted Jewish believers tempted to turn back.
2. Hebrews 12:8: discipline is not the breaking off of a relationship; it is the very proof of sonship.
3. From the original: Hebrew yasar, Greek paideia, whose root is “child” — the whole education by which a child is raised to maturity.
4. The setting of Deuteronomy 8:5: forty years in the wilderness were upbringing, not punishment — raising slaves into sons and daughters.

brief12.title: Point 1: Task Above Person Loses Hearts
notes: Slide text:
Controlling people with rules
Forcing change with pressure
Getting results with punishment
Things under control, hearts lost
Key points:
1. Quote Deuteronomy 8:5: “as a man disciplines his son” — not as a jailer manages a prisoner.
2. Three things happen in the heart: feeling rejected, feeling negated, feeling unable to get up again.
3. Paul warns twice: Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21, “so that they won’t be discouraged”.
4. Picture: a crooked fruit tree forced straight with an iron bar works at once but never bears fruit again; supported gently by a stake, it grows straight from the inside.

brief12.title: The Vicious Circle and God’s Charge
notes: Slide text:
Problem, punishment, backlash, harsher punishment
“You haven’t bound up that which was broken…
You haven’t sought that which was lost”
(Ezekiel 34:4)
Key points:
1. Describe the vicious circle: the problem brings punishment, punishment brings backlash, backlash brings harsher punishment, and in the end the relationship breaks and hearts are lost.
2. The structure of Ezekiel 34:4: five “things not done”, all about people; one “thing done” — ruling with force and with rigour.
3. Psychology: Diana Baumrind (1966–1971) and the contrast between authoritarian and authoritative parenting.
4. Data: Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor’s 2016 meta-analysis in the Journal of Family Psychology — seventy-five studies, over 160,000 children; physical punishment had no positive link with compliance.
5. 321 insight: put the task above the person and you lose hearts; when the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

brief12.title: Point 2: I’ll Walk with You as You Change
notes: Slide text:
“one who loves him is careful to discipline him”
(Proverbs 13:24)
Three cores: relationship, companionship, restoration
Love first, discipline after
Key points:
1. God’s discipline is not tossing out “Fix it yourself!” but saying “I’ll walk with you as you change.”
2. Emphasise Proverbs 13:24, “disciplines him at all times” (as the Chinese renders it): not showing up only when something goes wrong, but always there.
3. The order of Hebrews 12:6: first “whom the Lord loves”, then “he disciplines”.
4. Psalm 23:4: “Your rod and your staff, they comfort me” — tools of discipline become a comfort because of the relationship.

brief12.title: Restoring Is Mending Nets and Setting Bones
notes: Slide text:
“restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”
(Galatians 6:1)
The original: mending nets, setting a dislocation
Nets take time; bones take closeness
Key points:
1. From the original: katartizō — the same word as “mending their nets” in Matthew 4:21; in ancient medicine it also meant setting a dislocated bone.
2. Paul adds “looking to yourself”, a reminder that the restorer’s greatest danger is pride.
3. 2 Corinthians 2:7–8: lest he be swallowed up with excessive sorrow; confirm your love toward him.
4. Illustration: a father tells his son, “You have to take responsibility for this, but from tomorrow, every step you take, Dad will walk it with you.”
5. Psychology: Carl Rogers (1957), unconditional positive regard; John Gottman, positive to negative interactions of about five to one.

brief12.title: Point 3: God First Asks, “Where Are You?”
notes: Slide text:
God did not ask, “What have you done?”
God first asked, “Where are you?”
God cares not about the incident, but the relationship
It wasn’t God who hid; it was humanity
Key points:
1. Genesis 3:9 is God’s first word after humanity sinned — in Hebrew, ayyekkah.
2. The all-knowing God needed no information; he asked to restore the relationship.
3. Humanity covered itself with fig leaves and hid among the trees; God was still walking in the garden, still calling out.
4. Ask: this morning, is there a corner inside you where a leaf-clad version of yourself is hiding too?

brief12.title: God Disciplines to Win People Back
notes: Slide text:
He promised redemption (Genesis 3:15)
He made garments to cover shame (Genesis 3:21)
He drove them from Eden so sin would not last forever
Humbly accept discipline and receive grace
Key points:
1. Genesis 3:15 is the “first gospel”: while humanity was still shifting the blame, God spoke the promise of salvation first (see Romans 2:4).
2. Genesis 3:21: humanity used leaves, God used skins; for the first time a life died to cover human shame, pointing to the cross.
3. Driving them from Eden was mercy: not letting humanity live forever in its fallen state.
4. Job 5:17 and Revelation 3:19: “As many as I love” stands in front of discipline.
5. Picture: a broken bone needs alignment, immobilisation and time; the key word in Hebrews 12:11 is “afterward”.

Care for the person, then the matter
Say in action: I’ll walk with you as you change
Humbly accept God’s discipline
Go deeper with the eight stages
Key points:
1. Practice 1: when someone does wrong, practise making your first words about the person — “Are you all right?”
2. Practice 2: think of someone you have already given up on in your heart, and do one concrete thing for them this week.
3. Practice 3: ask the Holy Spirit, “What is the one thing you have kept saying to me lately that I keep dodging?” — and turn back today.
4. Go deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
5. Point to the 920 practice: patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness and self-control are exactly the fruit most needed when discipline is called for.

3. 321 insight: put the task above the person and you lose hearts; when the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong.
4. Point out the root is the self-centred life: I want my order, my face, my being right.
5. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan; let man be man and let God be God — it is the Holy Spirit who changes people, not me.

brief21.title: Point 2: I’ll Walk with You as You Change
notes: Slide text:
God doesn’t say, “Fix it yourself”
God says, “I’ll walk with you as you change”
“one who loves him is careful to discipline him”
(Proverbs 13:24)
Key points:
1. Contrast two sentences: “Fix it yourself” pushes people away; “I’ll walk with you as you change” catches them.
2. Emphasise “at all times” in Proverbs 13:24 (as the Chinese renders it): not showing up only when something goes wrong, not drawing near only when tempers flare.
3. Add the first half: “One who spares the rod hates his son” — not disciplining is actually giving up.
4. Quote Hebrews 12:7: this is the Heavenly Father’s heart.

brief21.title: The Three Cores of True Discipline
notes: Slide text:
1. Relationship: springing from love
2. Companionship: walking through change together
3. Restoration: bringing people back to their place
First “whom the Lord loves”, then “he disciplines”
Key points:
1. Relationship: the order of Hebrews 12:6 — first “whom the Lord loves”, then “he disciplines”.
2. Companionship: not demanding change but walking people through it; discipline can’t be done by remote control.
3. Restoration: John 8:11, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” — neither sentence can be left out.
4. Illustration: by the Sea of Tiberias Jesus lit a fire, invited Peter to breakfast and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17).

brief21.title: Restoring Is Mending Nets and Setting Bones
notes: Slide text:
“restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”
(Galatians 6:1)
The word also means mending nets and setting bones
Nets take time; bones take closeness
Key points:
1. The original katartizō: the same word as “mending their nets” in Matthew 4:21; in ancient medicine it also meant setting a dislocation.
2. Restoring is not throwing away a torn net and buying a new one, but mending the tear stitch by stitch.
3. “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” — the restorer’s greatest danger is pride; the moment pride comes in, restoring turns into judging.
4. 2 Corinthians 2:7–8: lest he be swallowed up with excessive sorrow; confirm your love toward him.
5. Psychology: Carl Rogers (1957), unconditional positive regard; people don’t change while being evaluated, but when they are accepted.

brief21.title: The Rod and Staff Became a Comfort
notes: Slide text:
“Your rod and your staff,
they comfort me.”
(Psalm 23:4)
When the relationship is right, discipline comforts
Key points:
1. Explain the rod and staff: the staff is a crook to hook back a sheep that wanders; the rod strikes wild animals and sets the right direction.
2. These are tools of discipline, yet David says “they comfort me”, because the one holding them is “my shepherd”.

3. Illustration: a father tells his son, “You have to take responsibility for this, but from tomorrow, every step you take, Dad will walk it with you.” Love does not cancel consequences; love refuses to let a person bear them alone.
4. John Gottman’s “magic ratio”: in stable relationships, positive to negative interactions are about five to one.
5. 321 insight: life, relationships, ministry; only when people are received in love do they have the strength to change.

brief21.title: Point 3: God First Asks, “Where Are You?”
notes: Slide text:
God did not ask, “What have you done?”
God first asked, “Where are you?”
It wasn’t God who hid; it was humanity
God still walks in the garden, still calls you
Key points:
1. Hebrew ayyekkah; the all-knowing God needed no information — he asked to restore the relationship.
2. Humanity covered itself with fig leaves and hid among the trees; God was still walking in the garden.
3. Ask: this morning, is there a corner inside you where a leaf-clad version of yourself is hiding too?
4. Reminder: you think God is angry with you, but in fact God is calling your name.

brief21.title: Three Things God Did for Fallen People
notes: Slide text:
He promised redemption (Genesis 3:15)
He made garments to cover shame (Genesis 3:21)
He drove them from Eden so sin would not last forever
His goodness leads you to repentance
Key points:
1. Genesis 3:15 is the “first gospel”: while humanity was still shifting the blame, God spoke the promise of salvation first.
2. Genesis 3:21: humanity used leaves, God used skins; for the first time a life died to cover human shame, pointing to the cross.
3. Driving them from Eden was mercy, not letting humanity live forever in its fallen state; sometimes the door God closes saves your life.
4. Romans 2:4: it isn’t that you repent first and then God is kind; God is kind first and leads you to repentance.

brief21.title: “Love” Stands in Front of Discipline
notes: Slide text:
“happy is the man whom God corrects”
“As many as I love, I reprove and chasten.”
(Revelation 3:19)
Key points:
1. The second half of Job 5:17: “Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.”
2. Revelation 3:19: in front of “reprove and chasten” stand the words “As many as I love”.
3. Lamentations 3:32–33: “For he does not afflict willingly” — when God disciplines, his own heart aches.
4. Hosea 11:8: “How can I give you up, Ephraim?” — a cry that almost breaks.

brief21.title: Remember the Word “Afterward”
notes: Slide text:
“not joyous but grievous;
yet afterward it yields
the peaceful fruit of righteousness”
(Hebrews 12:11)
Key points:
1. Picture: a broken bone needs three things to heal — alignment, immobilisation and time; miss one and it grows crooked.
2. The doctor is not punishing the patient but giving him the conditions for healing; so it is with God’s discipline.
3. Emphasise “afterward”: what you are going through now is not the end of the story.
4. 321 insight: humbly accept discipline and you receive grace; refuse discipline and you fall into pride (1 Peter 5:5).
5. Shift in perspective: from the human view, I am being suppressed; from God’s view, I am being sculpted; the temporary is bitter, the eternal is righteousness.

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Slide text:
Care for the person, then the matter
First words: “Are you all right?”
Say in action: I’ll walk with you as you change
I won’t give up on you
Key points:
1. Practice 1: when someone does wrong, don’t first think “How do I deal with this?” but ask “How can I help him get back into right relationship?”
2. Practical tip: this week practise making your first words about the person; each evening take three minutes to review the day’s first words.
3. Practice 2: let the Holy Spirit point out someone you have already given up on, and do one concrete thing for them this week.
4. Discern: the one who walks alongside asks, “How have you been lately?”; the supervisor asks, “Have you changed yet?”
5. Multiplication: when he is back on his feet, take him with you to walk alongside the next person who has fallen.

brief21.title: Practice 3 and the Eight Stages
notes: Slide text:
Humbly accept God’s discipline
Don’t run; don’t rationalise
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
1. Practice 3: quietly ask, “Lord, what is the one thing you have kept saying to me lately that I keep dodging?”
2. Discern: being sorry is an emotion; repentance is a turning — don’t let being sorry replace turning back.
3. Explain one by one how the eight stages of changing our mindset apply to this lesson.
4. Emphasise Repetition: a change of mindset is not a one-off decision but forty days, four hundred days of practice.
5. Memorise Hebrews 12:11 as the backbone of the practice.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Slide text:
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Humility beats pride; selflessness beats Satan
920: patience, kindness, gentleness
235: walking with them through change
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model (breakfast on the shore), the Bible is my standard (restore in a spirit of gentleness), the Holy Spirit is my guide (timing, tone, setting).
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — what I want is not “I’m right” but “he lives”; let Jesus receive all the glory.
3. The Goal: establish God’s system. A system of reward and punishment raises performers; the father–son system raises sons and daughters.
4. 920: of the ninefold fruit in Galatians 5:22–23, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness and self-control are the most needed when discipline is called for.
5. The priority of relationships: first with God, then ourselves, then others, and last with things; Galatians 2:20 — it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Discipline: from punishment to restoration
Focus: from the mistake to the relationship
God seeks people willing to turn back
This is the life of God’s system
Key points:
1. Two turnings: discipline from punishment to restoration; focus from the mistake to the relationship.
2. Call: you don’t have to become perfect before you dare to come to God; God is calling your name.
3. Luke 15:20: while he was still far off, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, and ran and embraced him.
4. Let Jesus be King in the family, in the church, in every moment of facing a mistake; all glory to Jesus.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, give me the Heavenly Father’s heart
Let me see the person before the matter
I am willing to be changed and shaped by you
All glory to Jesus. Amen
Key points:
1. Lead everyone in praying aloud together; keep the tone gentle and leave room for silence.
2. Three directions for prayer: forgiveness for putting tasks above people, the Heavenly Father’s heart, courage to accept discipline.
3. Invite each person to name someone in their heart and say to God, “I’ll walk with him as he changes; I won’t give up on him.”
4. Close with a blessing: may the Lord’s rod and staff be your comfort; may all the glory go to Jesus.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we come together to the third lesson on “Rectify the Priority”. The title is: Discipline Is for Restoration.
Our theme verses say, “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children” (Hebrews 12:6–7)
In the last two lessons God rectified our priority in “prayer”. Today God wants to rectify us in a place where it is even easier to go astray — in “discipline”.
Brothers and sisters, let me begin with a very ordinary scene.
A mother walks into the kitchen: the milk is spilled, a glass lies shattered across the floor, and her child is frozen in the middle of it.
At that moment, what would you say first?
For most of us, what slips out is: “How could you be so careless!” “Go and get a cloth, quickly!” Those sentences have one thing in common — every one of them is aimed at the “thing”.
But there is another kind of mother. She crouches down, looks her child in the eye and says, “Did you hurt yourself?”
The same mess on the floor; a different first sentence, and a completely different outcome. Our first words give away the real order inside our hearts.
When someone does wrong, our first reaction is usually: How do I correct it? How do I solve it? How do I get things back to normal?
But God doesn’t start there.
After the very first sin, the first words God spoke were these: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)
Brothers and sisters, did God need to ask? Of course not. He asked, not to gather information, but to restore a relationship.

And the root of the Greek word for “discipline” is the word for “child”; it means raising a child to maturity. So when God disciplines you, the picture is not of a judge banging his gavel, but of a father bending down and taking your hand.
Our first point: discipline centred on solving problems loses people’s hearts.
“You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5)
Notice — as a man disciplines his son.
But when discipline is only for solving problems, it turns into three things: controlling people with rules, forcing change with pressure, getting results with punishment.
In the short term it works very well, because things are brought under control.
But what about that person’s heart? He feels rejected, he feels negated, he feels he no longer has the strength to get up.
And so a vicious circle sets in: the problem brings punishment, punishment brings a backlash, the backlash brings harsher punishment, and in the end the relationship breaks and hearts are lost.

God rebuked this kind of discipline long ago: “You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.” (Ezekiel 34:4)
Brothers and sisters, God’s charge is clear: you did plenty of managing, but you lost the people.
The 321 insight reminds us: put the task above the person, and you will lose people’s hearts; when the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong.
When we put the task before the person, in the end even the task isn’t done well.
Our second point: discipline centred on love says, “I’ll walk with you as you change.”
God has never tossed out a “Fix it yourself!” and then turned and walked away.
“One who loves him is careful to discipline him” — or, as the Chinese puts it, “disciplines him at all times” (Proverbs 13:24).
Notice those words “at all times”. At all times means always there.

True discipline has three cores. First, relationship — not a reaction to sin, but something that springs from love. Second, companionship — not demanding change, but walking with people through change. Third, restoration — not condemnation, but bringing the person back to the right place.
David says, “Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4) The rod and staff are tools of discipline, yet they became a comfort, because the relationship was right.
“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1)
Brothers and sisters, the word “restore” here is the very word used for “mending nets” in the original, and it was also used for pushing a dislocated bone back into place.
Restoring is not throwing away a torn net and buying a new one; it is sitting down and, stitch by stitch, mending the tear.
Mending nets takes time. Setting a bone takes closeness. Neither can be done by remote control.
Only when people are received in love do they have the strength to change.
Our third point: God disciplines to restore people, not to punish them.
God did not ask, “What have you done?” God first asked, “Where are you?”
Brothers and sisters, on that day it was not God who hid; it was humanity. God was still walking in the garden; God was still calling out.
Let me ask you: this morning, is there some corner inside you where a leaf-clad version of yourself is hiding too?
You think God is angry with you, but in fact God is calling your name.
Then we see God do three things.
First, God promised redemption — the woman’s offspring would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). While humanity was still shifting the blame, God spoke salvation first.
Second, God made garments of skins for them (Genesis 3:21). Humanity used leaves; God used skins. A life had to shed its blood, and that points all the way to the cross.
Third, God drove them out of Eden, so that sin would not exist forever. The door God closed was saving your life.
So: humbly accept discipline and you receive grace; refuse discipline and you fall into pride.

“All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (Hebrews 12:11) Remember that word “afterward”.
Brothers and sisters, let’s practise three things.
First, care for the person first, then deal with the matter. When someone does wrong, practise making your first words: Are you all right?
Second, say through your actions: I’ll walk with you as you change; I won’t give up on you. This week, do one concrete thing for the person you have almost given up on.
Third, humbly accept God’s discipline. Don’t run, don’t rationalise; just say: Lord, I am willing to be changed by you.
Walk it out with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, this lesson can be distilled into two turnings.
When discipline turns from punishment to restoration, when our focus turns from the mistake to the relationship, life begins to be built up, and relationships begin to be restored.
God is not looking for perfect people; God is looking for people willing to turn back.
And when we ourselves have been restored like this, our hands become different. We no longer rush to correct; we learn first to ask: Are you all right?
We no longer say, “Fix it yourself”; we learn to say, “I’ll walk with you as you change.”
This is the life of God’s system.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that on the day humanity sinned, you first asked, “Where are you?”
Lord, I confess that I often put the task above the person. Please forgive me, and change the order in my heart.
Give me the Heavenly Father’s heart; let me see the person first and then deal with the matter; let me be able to say: I’ll walk with you as you change; I won’t give up on you.
I am also willing to accept your discipline humbly, and to let my life be renewed and shaped by you.
Reign as King in my home, and may the glory go to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s rod and staff be your comfort today. Brothers and sisters, see you tomorrow morning.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
This morning we come together to the third lesson on “Rectify the Priority”. The title is: Discipline Is for Restoration.
Our theme verses say, “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children” (Hebrews 12:6–7)
In the last two lessons God rectified our priority in “prayer”. Today God wants to rectify us in another place where it is even easier to go astray — in “discipline”.
Let me begin with a very ordinary early-morning scene.
A mother walks into the kitchen and finds the floor a wreck. The milk is spilled, a glass lies shattered everywhere, and her child is standing right in the middle of it, frozen stiff.
At that moment, what will the mother say?

For most of us, what slips out is: “How could you be so careless!” “Go and get a cloth, quickly!” Every one of those words is aimed at the “thing”. And the child, trembling inside — not one word is spoken to him.
But there is another kind of mother. She crouches down first, looks her child in the eye and says, “Did you hurt yourself?”
The same mess on the floor. A different first sentence, and a completely different outcome.
Brothers and sisters, our first words give away the real order inside our hearts.
When someone does wrong, our first reaction is usually three questions: How do I correct the mistake? How do I solve the problem? How do I get things back to normal?

None of these questions is bad; they are even very responsible. But God’s heart does not start there. What God cares about is not only “What have you done wrong?” but even more “Where are you, the person, right now?”
In this lesson God wants to lead us to see this: truly godly discipline is not for solving problems; it is for restoring relationships.
First, the background.

The church has always held different views on who wrote Hebrews. The third-century church father Origen made a very honest remark: as to who actually wrote this letter, God alone knows. It was written around AD 60–70.

The recipients were a group of believers from a Jewish background who had believed in Jesus, only to be thrown out of the synagogue and cut off by their families. A question sat in their hearts: if God loves us, why has life become harder since we started following the Lord?
Hebrews 12 is the answer. Verse 8 says that those without discipline are illegitimate, and not children.
Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: discipline is not the breaking off of a relationship; discipline is the very proof of it.

And the root of the Greek word for “discipline” is the word for “child”; it means raising a child into a complete person. So when God disciplines you, the picture is not of a judge banging his gavel, but of a father bending down and taking your hand.
Our first point: discipline centred on solving problems loses people’s hearts.
“You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5)

This was said when the forty years in the wilderness were about to end and the land of Canaan lay right before their eyes. To human eyes, forty years was punishment; to God’s eyes, forty years was upbringing — raising a crowd of slaves into a family of sons and daughters.
So notice where the weight falls: as a man disciplines his son. Not as a jailer manages a prisoner, not as a foreman manages a labourer, but as a father disciplines his son.
Brothers and sisters, which kind of God is the God in your heart?

Yet we very easily turn discipline into something else. When discipline is only for solving problems, it turns into three things: controlling people with rules, forcing change with pressure, getting results with punishment. In the short term it looks very effective: the child stops answering back, the co-worker stops coming in late, the figures are back on track.

I think of a fruit tree that has grown crooked. You can bind it tightly to an iron bar and force it straight; the tree is straight at once, but inside it has already snapped, and when you loosen the bar it will either fall over or never bear fruit again. Or you can set a stake beside it, gently support it, and give it time and sunshine; the process is slow, but that tree grows straight from the inside.
Brothers and sisters, forcing straight is management; patient support — that alone is discipline.
But for the person treated like this, what happens in his heart?

He feels rejected — so when I get it wrong, what you want is the result, not me. He feels negated — so in your eyes, I am nothing more than my mistake. He feels he no longer has the strength to get up — since nothing I do is ever good enough, I might as well not try.
And so a vicious circle sets in: the problem brings punishment, punishment brings a backlash, the backlash brings harsher punishment, and in the end the relationship breaks and hearts are lost.

Paul reminds fathers, “Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged.” (Colossians 3:21) That is the most frightening side effect of the wrong kind of discipline — it does not remove the mistake; it removes, along with it, the person’s strength to want to become better.

Between 1966 and 1971 the psychologist Diana Baumrind put forward her classification of parenting styles: authoritarian parents make high demands but are low in responsiveness, and their children are outwardly compliant but anxious and low in self-esteem inside; authoritative parents make equally high demands but are willing to explain and to listen, and their children do markedly better in self-control and mental health.
The Bible described this kind of discipline long ago.

“You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.” (Ezekiel 34:4)

Look at how it is built: the “things not done” are all about people; the last clause, the “thing done”, is about management. God’s charge is clear: you did plenty of managing, but you lost the people.

The 321 insight tells us: put the task above the person, and you will lose people’s hearts; when the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Put the task before the person, and the end result is often that even the task isn’t done well, because every task is done by people. And the root of putting the task above the person is the self-centred life. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
Our second point: discipline centred on love says, “I’ll walk with you as you change.”

Brothers and sisters, God’s discipline has never been to toss out a “Fix it yourself!” and then turn and walk away. God’s discipline is one sentence: I’ll walk with you as you change. That is the heart of the Heavenly Father.
“One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.” (Proverbs 13:24) The Chinese renders it “disciplines him at all times”.

Notice those words “at all times”. At all times means continually present. Not showing up only when something goes wrong, not drawing near only when tempers flare. A father who disciplines at all times is a father who is always there.
True discipline has three cores.

First, relationship — not a reaction to sin, but something that springs from love. Look at the order in Hebrews 12:6: first “whom the Lord loves”, then “he disciplines”. Love comes first; discipline follows.
Second, companionship — not demanding change, but walking with people through change. Third, restoration — not condemnation, but bringing the person back to the right place.

Facing the woman caught in adultery, Jesus said two things, and neither can be left out: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11) Only the first is indulgence; only the second is law. The two together — that is the gospel.
After Peter denied the Lord three times, Jesus didn’t rebuke him; he simply lit a fire on the shore, invited him to breakfast, and then asked him three times: Do you love me?
“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1)

Brothers and sisters, the Greek word for “restore” here is beautiful. The same word in Matthew 4:21 describes the sons of Zebedee “in the boat … mending their nets”. In ancient medical language it also meant setting a dislocated bone back in place.

Restoring is not throwing away a torn net and buying a new one; it is sitting down and, stitch by stitch, mending the tear. Mending nets takes time; setting a bone takes closeness. Neither can be done by remote control.

Paul adds one more line: looking to yourself. Because the greatest danger for the one who restores is pride — I am the one standing; you are the one who fell. Once that thought creeps in, restoring turns into judging.
David said something very strange: “Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4)

The staff is a crook, to hook back a sheep that has wandered off; the rod is a short club, to strike wild animals and set the right direction. These are tools of discipline! And yet David says: they comfort me. Why? Because the One holding them is “my shepherd”. When the relationship is right, discipline becomes comfort.

I once heard of a father whose son did something very serious in high school. That night he could hardly speak, and in the end he said only one thing: “Son, you have to take responsibility for this. Dad won’t shield you from it. But from tomorrow, every step you take, Dad will walk it with you.”
Notice that he didn’t cancel the consequences. Love does not cancel consequences; love refuses to let a person bear the consequences alone.
Only when people are received in love do they have the strength to change.
Our third point: God disciplines to restore people, not to punish them.
“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)
These are the first words God spoke after humanity sinned. Notice that God did not say, “What have you done?” What God said was, “Where are you?”
Did an all-knowing God need to ask? Of course not. He asked, not to gather information, but to restore a relationship.
And brothers and sisters, on that day it was not God who hid; it was humanity. God was still walking in the garden, still calling out.
Let me ask you: this morning, is there some corner inside you where a leaf-clad version of yourself is hiding too?
You think God is angry with you, but in fact God is calling your name.
Then we see God do three things.

First, God promised redemption. Genesis 3:15 says the woman’s offspring will bruise the serpent’s head; church history has called this the “first gospel”. Look at the timing: while humanity was still shifting the blame, God spoke the promise of salvation first. This is what Romans 2:4 means: the goodness of God leads you to repentance.

Second, God made them clothes. “Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.” (Genesis 3:21) Humanity used leaves; God used skins. Leaves wither; behind the skins, a life had to shed its blood. Those garments of skin point all the way to the cross.

Third, God drove them out of Eden. It looks like the harshest act of all, but hidden inside it is the deepest mercy: if humanity, in its fallen state, had eaten from the tree of life, it would have lived forever in sin.
Brothers and sisters, sometimes the door God closes is the door that saves your life.
So all of this reveals: God’s discipline carries love; God’s actions aim to restore relationship; God’s intention is to win people back.

“Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.” (Job 5:17) This is hard to accept, yet it is true. Because if God gave up on you, that would be the most frightening thing of all.
The Lord says to the church in Laodicea, “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten.” (Revelation 3:19) Look — standing in front of “reprove and chasten” are the words “As many as I love”.
Lamentations also says, “For he does not afflict willingly.” (Lamentations 3:33) Not willingly — when God disciplines you, God’s own heart aches too.
I think of a picture: a broken bone.

When a bone breaks, the first thing the doctor often has to do is push it back into place — and that hurts; then comes the cast, the immobilising, the order not to move. From the patient’s point of view, the doctor seems only to be adding to his pain. But the doctor is not punishing him; he is giving him the conditions for healing: alignment, immobilisation and time. Miss one, and it grows crooked.
God’s discipline is just like that. He pushes us back into place, he restricts us, he gives us a stretch of days that seem to go nowhere.
“All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (Hebrews 12:11)
Afterward. Brothers and sisters, remember that word “afterward”. What you are going through now is not the end of the story.

Humbly accept discipline and you receive grace; refuse discipline and you fall into pride. Seen from the human point of view, I am being suppressed; seen from God’s point of view, I am being sculpted.
Brothers and sisters, let’s practise. First, practise seeing mistakes with “relationship first”.

When someone does wrong, don’t jump straight to “How do I deal with this?” First ask: How can I help him get back into right relationship? This week, practise making your first words about the “person”: Are you all right?

Second, cultivate the attitude of “I’ll walk with you as you change”. Don’t just demand that the other person change; show through your actions: I’m willing to walk this road with you; I won’t give up on you.
Let the Holy Spirit point out someone you have already given up on in your heart, and this week do one concrete thing for him — don’t bring up his mistake; just let him know you’re still there.
The one who walks alongside asks, “How have you been lately?” The supervisor asks, “Have you changed yet?”
Third, practise humbly accepting God’s discipline. When God shines his light on us and rebukes us, don’t run, don’t rationalise; pray instead: Lord, I am willing to be changed by you.
Quietly ask one question: Lord, what is the one thing you have kept saying to me lately that I keep dodging? And learn to tell the difference — being sorry is an emotion; repentance is a turning.

We walk these three practices out with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. A change of mindset is not a one-off decision; it is practice repeated again and again.
Brothers and sisters, let’s put this lesson back into the 321 system.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he lit a fire on the shore and invited Peter to breakfast; the Bible is my standard — restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; the Holy Spirit is my guide — when to speak and what tone to use all depend on the Holy Spirit. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — if I am on the throne, what I want is “I’m right”; if Jesus is on the throne, what I want is “he lives”. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A system of reward and punishment raises “performers”, people who spend their whole lives proving they deserve to be loved; the father–son system raises “sons and daughters”, people who know they are already loved, and so have the strength to change.

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; with each of them we live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control — which of them isn’t most needed when someone has done wrong?
The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Most discipline that fails has the order upside down.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson can be distilled into two turnings. When discipline turns from “punishment” to “restoration”, when our focus turns from “the mistake” to “the relationship”, life begins to be built up, and relationships begin to be restored.
God is not looking for perfect people; God is looking for people willing to turn back.
You don’t have to become a perfect person before you dare to come to God. God is walking in the garden, calling your name: Where are you? He doesn’t want to condemn you; he wants to bring you back.

And when we ourselves have been restored like this, our hands become different. We no longer rush to correct; we learn first to ask: Are you all right? We no longer say, “Fix it yourself”; we learn to say, “I’ll walk with you as you change.”
Many people think strictness is what brings change, but God lets us see: love is the power that truly changes people. Discipline without love wounds people; discipline in love saves people.
This is — the life of God’s system.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father,
Thank you that on the day humanity first sinned, you first asked, “Where are you?”
Lord, I confess that I often put the task above the person. Please forgive me, and change the order in my heart.

Give me the Heavenly Father’s heart. When others fall, let me not stand up high passing judgement, but come down and restore them in a spirit of gentleness. Teach me to say these words: I’ll walk with you as you change; I won’t give up on you.
I am also willing to accept your discipline humbly, and simply say: Lord, I am willing to be changed by you.
Reign as King in my family, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord’s rod and staff be your comfort today. See you tomorrow morning.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Stone Held in Your Hand
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like you to do something first: hold out your hand and look at it — what are you holding in your hand right now?

There is an early-morning story in the Bible. John 8 opens by saying: “Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.” (John 8:2) That very morning a crowd dragged a woman caught in adultery into the temple courts, pushed her into the middle and made everyone look at her shame.

At that moment two things were present in the temple courts at once: a person who had fallen, and stones all over the ground. And every single person had to make a choice — when they bent down, was it to pick up a stone, or to write?

Brothers and sisters, that scene has never disappeared in two thousand years; it has just changed location: the church corridor, the small-group chat, the family dinner table, and those trials, one after another, that we hold in our hearts and never voice.

When a co-worker fails, when a brother’s marriage runs into trouble, when a sister’s child goes astray — what is our first reaction?

The lesson puts it with great precision: when someone falls, what best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but “how we respond.”

Because words can be dressed up; reactions can’t. Words are thought through before they’re spoken; reactions flow straight out from within. The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) Whatever a person is carrying inside comes out in its true colours the instant someone else falls.

So today there is only one question:

Throw a stone, or throw a rope? Condemn, or restore?

Brothers and sisters, notice that this is not just a matter of attitude, still less a matter of good manners. It is a matter of “priority.”

This is the fourth lesson on “rectifying the priority.” In the earlier lessons we learned: life first, then relationships, then ministry; first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today we put that order to the test in the hardest situation of all — when someone falls.

When the order is wrong, we put the “matter” in front of the “person,” and so we deal with the sin but lose the person.

When the order is right, we put the “person” in front of the “matter,” and so we restore the person and deal with the sin as well.

Brothers and sisters, a stone and a rope weigh about the same, and both are held in the same hand. The only difference is this: do you want him to go down, or do you want to pull him up?

Today God wants to teach us one thing — how to face a person who has fallen with God’s heart.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, One Father’s Heart
sections.html:
Before we come to the three key points, let’s get clear on the background of our theme passages. Cut off from its background, a passage easily becomes a stone in our hands; put back into its background, it becomes a rope.

First, Galatians.

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul, and it is the most fiery in tone of all his letters. If its recipients were the churches of south Galatia — the places Paul founded on his first missionary journey, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — it may have been written as early as AD 48 or 49, making it one of Paul’s earliest letters.

Why did Paul write with such urgency? Because a group of people had come into the Galatian churches teaching the Gentile believers that they had to be circumcised and keep the law to be saved. Paul says: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). The whole of Galatians fights for one thing: we are saved by grace, through faith, not by works.

Only once we understand this background are we struck by the turn in chapter 6: Paul spends five chapters firing on all cylinders against legalism, yet at the very start of chapter 6 he sets up another kind of law — “the law of Christ.”

He says: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:1–2)

In other words: a church that truly understands grace will always be a church that knows how to restore people. If you don’t know how to restore people, it proves you haven’t really understood grace yet.

More important still is the context. Just before Galatians 6:1 come 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? “Gentleness” is one of the nine graces of the fruit the Holy Spirit bears. When Paul says “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness,” he means that restoring a fallen person does not depend on technique; it depends on fruit. Only the life the Holy Spirit grows in you has what it takes to lift up a person who has fallen.

And 5:26 is even more direct: “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.” Being “conceited” is exactly the self-centred life; it is pride. Paul is saying: if you are still chasing empty glory, what you hold in your hand will certainly be a stone, never a rope.

Now look at Romans.

Paul wrote Romans to the church in Rome from Corinth, around AD 56–57. It is his most complete and most systematic account of the gospel. Romans 5:8 stands at a crucial point: Paul has just proved in chapters 1 to 3 that “There is no one righteous; no, not one” (Romans 3:10), and in chapter 4 has shown that Abraham was justified by faith; then in 5:8 he raises God’s love to its highest point:

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

“Commends” in Greek is συνίστημι (sunistēmi), meaning “to place side by side, to prove, to establish.” God does not just tell us in words that he loves us; he places the cross right beside our sin, sets the two side by side, to prove his love.

Brothers and sisters, remember the timing — “while we were yet sinners.” Not after we repented, not after we cleaned up our act, but when we were at our least lovable, when we most deserved to be stoned.

This is the foundation of today’s whole lesson. God’s order toward us is: love first, change after. If our order toward others is: change first, acceptance after — then we have turned the gospel upside down.

sections.heading: 1. God’s Heart: Hating Sin, Yet Loving the Sinner
sections.html:
1. God is clear about sin, and even clearer about people

Brothers and sisters, we first need to get one thing clear: God hates sin, and the Bible is never vague about that.

“You who have purer eyes than to see evil, and who cannot look on perversity, why do you tolerate those who deal treacherously” (Habakkuk 1:13). God’s holiness does not tolerate sin; that is not up for negotiation.

But God’s attitude toward “people” is even clearer.

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

“He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” (Psalm 103:10)

Psalm 103 is a psalm of David. Its greatness lies in the fact that David was not a man who had never fallen. He committed adultery, he committed murder, he counted the people. It was exactly such a man who wrote these words. And in the same psalm he explains why:

“Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:13–14)

“He remembers that we are dust” — God has never overestimated us. So God is never shocked by our failures either. The people who are shocked into fury by someone else’s failure are usually the ones who have overestimated themselves.

2. The order of the gospel: love first, change after

This is the heart of the gospel, and the most crucial order in today’s lesson:

God does not first demand that you change before he loves you; God loved you already, while you were still weak.

In Romans 2:4 Paul asks a stunning question: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?”

Notice the cause and effect: it isn’t “repentance brings goodness,” but “goodness leads people to repentance.”

Brothers and sisters, if this verse really got inside us, it would completely overturn the way we treat people. We tend to think: first he has to know how badly he’s gone wrong, and then he’ll change. God’s way is: first he has to know how deeply he is loved, and only then can he change.

A stone can knock a person down, but it has never once changed a person.

3. “Restore” in the original: the hands that mend nets

That is exactly why Paul gives the spiritual a command:

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

This verse has three key terms, and each deserves a close look.

The first is “caught in some fault.” The original is προλαμβάνω (prolambanō), meaning “to be seized before one can act,” “to be caught off guard.” Paul is not describing someone who sets out to do evil, but someone ambushed by sin, knocked down before he had time to react — like walking down the street and suddenly being tackled from behind. Brothers and sisters, any one of us could be the one who gets tackled.

The second is “restore.” The original is καταρτίζω (katartizō), meaning “to repair, to put in order, to make complete.” The word appears in Matthew 4:21: “Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets. He called them.” — “mending” is this very word. Commentators also point out that in the medical usage of classical Greek this word meant setting a dislocated bone back in place.

What a beautiful picture. Restoring someone who has fallen is like a fisherman mending his net — patiently, mesh by mesh, closing up the tear so the net can fish again; and it is like a doctor setting a bone — it hurts, but the aim is not punishment; it is putting things back in place.

Japan has an ancient craft called kintsugi, which repairs broken pottery with lacquer and gold powder. The craftsman doesn’t hide the cracks; instead he traces them with lines of gold, and the vessel ends up worth more than before it broke. God is that kind of craftsman: with the precious blood of his Son he traces our cracks into a testimony.

Orthopaedic medicine also tells us that when a fracture is correctly set and immobilised, then once the callus has formed and the bone has remodelled, the healed site can regain its original strength. A brother who has been well restored is often sturdier than someone who has never fallen, because he has truly come to know grace.

The third term is “gentleness.” The original is πραΰτης (prautēs) — not weakness, but “strength under control,” having power without abusing it. This is exactly one of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). When a wild horse is broken in, its strength is not reduced; that strength is simply under the rein from then on. Spiritual people are not people with no ability to point out others’ faults; their ability has been brought under the Holy Spirit’s rein.

4. That phrase, “looking to yourself”

Paul adds a phrase we most easily skip over: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”

Brothers and sisters, this phrase is a mirror. It reminds us: the person you’re lifting up today could be you tomorrow.

Psychology has a well-known phenomenon that the social psychologist Lee Ross named in 1977 the “fundamental attribution error”: when we explain “other people’s” failures, we tend to blame their character — he’s just that kind of person; when we explain “our own” failures, we tend to blame the situation — I was really exhausted that day.

The same event, two measuring sticks. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

The obedience-to-authority experiment that the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram published in 1963 reminds us further that, in certain situations and under the pressure of authority, many ordinary, decent people will do things they once thought they would never do. Don’t be too quick to believe, “I would never do that.”

Paul goes on in the same chapter: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” (Galatians 6:3)

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the self-centred life. The self-centred person stands on the ruins of someone else and feels like a mountain. He doesn’t realise that what’s under his feet is the very same ground.

5. A 321 Insight: only selflessness can love; the self-centred life is quick to condemn

The lesson gives us an exceedingly bright light:

Only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn.

When a person is full of himself, he passes judgment; when a person is full of Christ, he shows mercy.

Why is the self-centred person especially fond of condemning? Because condemning is the quickest, least effortful way to raise yourself up. I don’t need to become better; I only need to prove that you’re worse, and I look better by comparison. The instant the stone leaves his hand, the thrower has an illusion that he is standing on high ground.

But it is an illusion. That early morning, the Lord Jesus said to the crowd holding stones: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” (John 8:7)

Why did those words cut so deep? Because under the law of Deuteronomy 17:7: “The hands of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people.” The Lord Jesus did not abolish the law; he simply handed the law’s first stone back into the accusers’ hands.

And the result? “They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.” (John 8:9)

Beginning from the oldest. The oldest left first — because the longer you’ve lived, the better you know your own hands aren’t clean.

Then the Lord Jesus said two things that are precisely the perfect order of grace and truth: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11)

First, “Neither do I condemn you” — this is love, this is acceptance, this is the rope.

Then, “From now on, sin no more” — this is truth, this is the demand of holiness.

The order cannot be reversed. Had he said “sin no more” first, she would never have taken it in, because she was still on the ground, crushed under humiliation. Lift her up first, and only then does she have the strength to walk out.

“The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14) Brothers and sisters, it is “full of grace and truth,” not one or the other. Grace without truth is indulgence; truth without grace is a stone. The Lord Jesus is full of both.

So it should be with God’s people too: don’t strike people with stones; restore them with gentleness.

sections.heading: 2. Discernment: The Weak and the Wicked
sections.html:
1. God’s love is perfect; God’s principles are clear

Brothers and sisters, if we preached only the first point, we would swing to the other extreme — dealing with nothing, saying “God loves you” about everything, until the church becomes a place with no boundaries, where sin walks around freely and the wounded sheep have no one to protect them.

So the lesson goes on to give us a second key: discernment.

“Yahweh upholds the humble. He brings the wicked down to the ground.” (Psalm 147:6)

The same God, two responses. Not that God’s love is bigger or smaller, but that human hearts are soft or hard.

“Upholds” in Hebrew is עוֹדֵד (ʿôdēd), meaning “to make to stand, to lift up, to strengthen.” God stoops down and lifts up the one who has fallen. And the same God who stoops to lift people up will also bring down to the ground the one who stays hard to the end.

The Bible shows us two utterly different kinds of people.

2. The first kind: the weak

The weak have three marks: they fall; but they are willing to repent; and in their hearts they still fear God.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

“Confess” here is ὁμολογέω (homologeō) in Greek, made up of “same” and “speak” — literally, “to say the same thing.” Confession is not muttering to yourself “I’m no good”; it is saying “Amen” to God’s verdict — God says this is sin, and I say this is sin, and I no longer defend it.

Notice the astonishing wording of this verse: God forgives us because he is “faithful,” and also because he is “righteous.” Why is forgiveness righteous? Because sin has already been punished on the cross. God hasn’t simply written the debt off; God has paid the bill in full.

The classic example of the weak is Peter. He denied the Lord three times — an utter failure — but the Bible records one detail: “The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.’ He went out, and wept bitterly.” (Luke 22:61–62)

One look from the Lord, and he wept bitterly. That look was the rope.

David too. He committed a great sin, but when the prophet Nathan pointed it out, he said at once: “I have sinned against Yahweh.” (2 Samuel 12:13) He wrote: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

“For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16) Brothers and sisters, look closely: the Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says the righteous fall and “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not whether they fall, but whether they get up.

To people like this, God’s response is: uphold, forgive, restore.

3. The second kind: the wicked

The wicked also have three marks: no fear of God in their hearts; they keep on harming people; and they are unwilling to repent.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

James is quoting Proverbs 3:34: “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.”

“Resists” in Greek is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, what a solemn picture: God himself drawing up his battle lines, standing opposite the proud.

The classic example of the wicked is Saul. Saul “confessed” too, but look at what his confession said: “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel.” (1 Samuel 15:30) He confessed his sin, but cared about his face; what he wanted was not God’s forgiveness but people’s esteem. That is the self-centred life — even confession becomes a way to protect the self.

Judas too. He was filled with remorse, and he even said the right words: “I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood.” (Matthew 27:4) But the end was, “He went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5).

Peter and Judas both failed, and both were filled with regret. Where was the difference?

Paul says it all in one sentence: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” (2 Corinthians 7:10)

Godly sorrow — its focus is on God; it brings a turning back, leading to salvation.

The sorrow of the world — its focus is on the self; it brings despair, and produces death.

Psychological research happens to confirm this spiritual principle from another angle. The American psychologists June Tangney and Ronda Dearing, in their 2002 book Shame and Guilt, drew on long research distinguishing two emotions: “guilt” focuses on behaviour — “I did a bad thing” — and moves people to apologise, make amends and repair relationships; “shame” focuses on the self — “I am a bad person” — and instead makes people withdraw, hide, get defensive, and even lash out in anger at others.

Brothers and sisters, do you see now how dangerous that stone in our hand is? What a stone produces is shame, not repentance. And shame never brings anyone to the cross; it only drives them into deeper darkness.

What a rope produces is hope, and only hope has the strength to repent.

To those who stay hard to the end, God’s response is: resist, deal with, cut off.

But please be sure to remember: even when he deals with them, God’s heart does not change — “ ‘As I live,’ says the Lord Yahweh, ‘I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live.’ ” (Ezekiel 33:11)

God resists the proud not because he hates them, but because pride will kill them. God stands in their way to keep them from charging straight over the cliff.

4. A key: don’t treat everyone the same way

Here the lesson reminds us of something very important: don’t treat everyone the same way; follow the Holy Spirit and respond with wisdom.

This is not our invention; it is the plain teaching of the Bible.

“On some have compassion, making a distinction, and some save, snatching them out of the fire with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.” (Jude 22–23)

The Chinese Union Version reads these verses as three kinds of people with three approaches: on those who doubt, have mercy; those about to be burned, snatch out of the fire with all your strength; those already deep in lust, show mercy but stay on guard at the same time, lest you be stained yourself. That is spiritual discernment — love is not a formula; love is insight.

Paul says to Titus: “Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning” (Titus 3:10) — notice, it is after “a first and second warning,” not rejection the first time. God’s discipline always follows a process, and always gives a chance first.

And in 2 Thessalonians 3:15 Paul immediately adds: “Don’t count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.”

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the guardrail for all church discipline. Whatever stage things have reached, in our hearts the other person is never an enemy, but a brother.

5. A 321 Insight: humility receives grace; pride is resisted

The lesson’s second light is: humility receives grace; pride is resisted.

The core message of 321 puts it precisely: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: when we pick up a stone to strike someone, which seat are we sitting in? We’ve sat down on the judgment seat. And that seat, the Bible says, only One is qualified to occupy.

“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

Judging is leaving our originally intended position; discerning is returning to it.

Judging says, “I’ll decide his fate on God’s behalf”; discerning says, “I ask God to let me see, so I know how to love him right now.”

Judging uses my standards, my emotions, my past experience; discerning uses the standard of the Bible, the guidance of the Holy Spirit and the role model of Jesus — exactly the Three Foundations of 321.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Throw one stone, and the other person is sure to throw one back. And so the church becomes a quarry where everyone is wounded, everyone cries injustice, and not one person is restored.

Brothers and sisters, the discernment we’re learning this morning is not for sticking labels on people, but for knowing: this time, what should I hand out?

sections.heading: 3. Build the Relationship, but Don’t Indulge the Sin
sections.html:
1. The order the Lord Jesus himself set

Brothers and sisters, the third key point is a procedure the Lord Jesus laid down himself.

“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” (Matthew 18:15)

Notice the Lord Jesus’ words: “you have gained back your brother.” Not “you have won the argument,” not “you have proved you were right,” but “you have gained back your brother.”

On the scoreboard of the kingdom of heaven there is only one way to score: a person is won.

The Lord Jesus goes on: “But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” (Matthew 18:16–17)

This is a clear three-step path:

Step one, restore him privately first — relationship comes first.

Step two, then take one or two others along — testimony is established.

Step three, finally bring it to the church — spiritual authority.

Brothers and sisters, I want you to pay special attention to step one. The Lord Jesus said, “between you and him alone.”

The mistake we make most often today is skipping step one and jumping straight to step three — or even to a “step four”: telling everyone who has nothing to do with it. We pass it on in the group chat, we “name it for prayer” at the prayer meeting, we’re “just sharing” over dinner. Brothers and sisters, that is not step one; that is throwing stones, only with a label on the stone that says “concern.”

The Lord Jesus’ order always keeps the number of people who know about the wound as small as possible, and the chance of restoration as large as possible.

2. The context is the real key

Matthew 18:15–17 is often used as the rulebook for church discipline, but cut off from its context it becomes a knife.

Look at what comes before it. Matthew 18:12–14 is the parable of the lost sheep: “What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray?” (Matthew 18:12) And the conclusion: “Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” (Matthew 18:14)

Now look at what comes after it. In Matthew 18:21–22 Peter asks the Lord how many times he should forgive his brother — up to seven times? “Jesus said to him, ‘I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.’ ” (Matthew 18:22) And straight after that comes the parable of the unforgiving servant.

Brothers and sisters, see the order clearly: before it, God leaving the ninety-nine to look for the one; in the middle, the procedure for restoring a brother; after it, forgiving seventy times seven. The discipline of Matthew 18 is sandwiched between “seeking” and “forgiving.” Anyone unwilling to leave the ninety-nine to look for the one has no business carrying out 18:15; anyone unwilling to forgive seventy times seven has no business carrying out 18:17.

3. True love is not indulgence

But what if the other person never repents, all the way to the end?

The Lord Jesus said: “If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” (Matthew 18:17)

In 1 Corinthians Paul dealt with an extremely serious case. A man in the Corinthian church had taken his father’s wife, and the church not only failed to deal with it but was “arrogant” (1 Corinthians 5:2). Paul says they “are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” (1 Corinthians 5:5)

Brothers and sisters, please read the last clause of that verse three times: “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”

Even the severest discipline still has “salvation” as its aim.

And the story has a second half. In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8 Paul says: “This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one; so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him.”

Do you see it? The end point of discipline is not throwing someone out, but welcoming them back. Paul was even worried that too much punishment would make him be “swallowed up.” That is a father’s heart.

“For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives.” (Hebrews 12:6) “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (Hebrews 12:11)

The goal of discipline is “the peaceful fruit of righteousness,” not letting off steam.

Brothers and sisters, remember the lesson’s two sentences: true love is not indulgence; true love is for rescuing.

Paul says that love “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). Love and truth have never been enemies; they are the two hands of the same Lord.

“The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” (Proverbs 27:6) A true friend dares to say what you don’t want to hear; a false friend only says what is comfortable to hear.

“But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Love and truth-telling have to appear in the same sentence before they bring growth.

Love without truth-telling is staying down in the pit chatting with him.

Truth-telling without love is standing at the edge of the pit throwing stones at him.

Love plus truth-telling is letting the rope down, then planting your own feet firmly and pulling him up, bit by bit.

4. Examples from daily life: scaffolding and the throw rope

When the outer wall of a building is peeling, there are two ways to deal with it. One is to take photos, post them, tag them, and let everyone know how run-down the building is; the other is to put up scaffolding and repair the wall panel by panel. The first is called a commentator; the second is called a worker — the church has no shortage of commentators; the church is short of workers.

In swift-water rescue training there is a basic piece of equipment called a “throw bag.” When someone falls into the water, the most important principle is: the rescuer must not rashly jump in, but first get firm footing, and then throw out the rope.

That is the practical version of Galatians 6:1: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”

Brothers and sisters, if you want to save someone, you must first stand firm. Your devotional life, your relationship with God, your own repentance — that is the rock under your feet. Jump in before your feet are firm, and the result is often that both of you get swept away.

The psychologist John Gottman, who studied couples’ interactions for many years at the University of Washington, identified four patterns that destroy relationships, and the most damaging of them, the one that most strongly predicts a relationship breaking down, is “contempt” — belittling someone from a position of superiority.

Contempt is a look down from on high. It may never be spoken, but the person being looked at always feels it. And contempt is the most typical expression on the face of the self-centred life.

Can we point out someone’s sin without a trace of contempt? We can — so long as we truly remember who pulled us out, and from where.

5. A 321 Insight: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles

The lesson’s third light is: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles; loving people does not mean approving of sin.

When the order is right, two results follow: we build people up with love, and we protect the community with truth.

Notice that these two things must happen at the same time.

Build up the individual without protecting the community — and the wounded sheep will leave, because the church isn’t safe.

Protect the community without building up the individual — and the fallen sheep will be lost, because the church has no grace.

321 says: there is one Goal, and that is to establish God’s system.

What is God’s system? God’s system is a place where a person who has fallen still dares to come back, and at the same time a place where sin cannot stay.

Does that sound contradictory? Not at all. Because in God’s system, what makes it impossible for sin to stay is not our criticism but the presence of Jesus. We don’t need stones to drive sin away; we only need to let Jesus reign as King in this community, and sin will not be able to stay.

Brothers and sisters, this is the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Let life be restored first, then let relationships be built, and ministry will grow up naturally after. If we turn it the other way round — sacrificing relationships to protect the ministry, neglecting life to keep up relationships — we will lose both the people and the presence of God.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change from Stone to Rope
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we’ve learned today and look at it once more within the framework of 321.

1. The Three Foundations: on what basis do I lift people up?

Jesus is my role model — that early morning, the Lord Jesus didn’t pick up a stone; he stooped down and wrote on the ground. He was the only one qualified to throw the first stone, and the only one who didn’t.

The Bible is my standard — the way I lift people up doesn’t follow my temperament or my mood, but the order of Matthew 18, the gentleness of Galatians 6 and the discernment of Jude.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — discerning who is weak and who is hardened is beyond my ability. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies. (Zechariah 4:6)

2. The Two Core Values: who is sitting in that seat?

Let Jesus be King — when I pick up a stone, I am the king in that moment, deciding someone’s life or death. When I put down the stone and pick up a rope, I hand the throne back to Jesus. Brothers and sisters, judging is, at its core, usurping the throne.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when a fallen person is restored, who gets the glory? Not me, the one who “handled the matter so wisely,” but the Shepherd who left the ninety-nine to look for the one. If, in the course of restoring someone, I’m secretly enjoying my own nobility, what I hold in my hand is still a stone, wrapped in the outer skin of a rope.

3. The Goal: establish God’s system

Satan is building a system too, and his three steps are: make people fall, make people condemn, make people isolate one another. God’s system also has three steps: uphold, restore, build relationships.
