Every time someone falls, it is the moment when the two systems meet face to face. The stone or the rope in our hand decides which side we are standing on.

4. The self-centred life and selflessness

Galatians 6:3 says: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” This is the most precise definition of the self-centred life — treating what we don’t have as though we had it, treating what was grace as our own achievement.

When the self-centred person sees someone fall, his first reaction is comparison; when the selfless person sees someone fall, his first reaction is mercy.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When Christ lives in me, the way I see people is no longer my way of seeing, but the way of the One who prayed for his enemies on Calvary.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s name in Hebrew means “adversary, accuser,” and the Greek word for “devil,” διάβολος, originally means “slanderer, one who maligns.” Revelation 12:10 calls him the one “who accuses them before our God day and night.”

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when we condemn a brother, we are doing Satan’s work, just using church language.

5. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry

Today’s lesson is a complete fivefold change.

Change of mindset — from “the fallen person should be dealt with” to “the fallen person should be restored.”

Change of life — once the mindset changes, the “self” inside that loves to condemn is dealt with by the cross.

Change of daily living — no more passing things on in the group chat, no more commentary over dinner, praying for that person late at night.

Change of relationships — a relationship that was about to snap is joined up again by a rope.

Change of ministry — those who have been restored are, in time, the very best at restoring others. The Lord said to Peter: “You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” (Luke 22:32)

6. A change of perspective

From the human point of view to God’s point of view — people see “what he has done”; God sees “what he is going to become.”

From the earthly to the heavenly — seen from earth, this is a disgrace; seen from heaven, “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

From the temporary to the eternal — today’s embarrassment is temporary; a soul is eternal.

From the worldly to the godly — the worldly way is to weed out the failures; the godly way is to mend the torn net.

7. The 920 practice and the 235 relationships

The 920 practice is to treat everyone we are in a relationship with as our “2,” practising living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Look at those nine graces in Galatians 5:22–23, then look back at the “gentleness” in 6:1. Restoring a fallen person calls on almost all nine: accepting with love, sustaining with joy, defusing with peace, waiting with patience, softening with kindness, paying the price with goodness, persevering with faithfulness, speaking with gentleness, and holding our own tongues with self-control. So lifting a person up turns out to be the final inspection of all nine graces.

The 235 relationships are what the lesson’s “building relationships” concretely looks like. A person who has been restored doesn’t need a single conversation; he needs a “2” — a spiritual companion to walk with him; a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, someone ahead leading him and someone behind following him; and in the end, to enter the “5” — becoming comrades in a fivefold-ministry team.

That is why the lesson says “build relationships”: a rope can save someone once; only a team can save a whole life.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: Throw a rope, not a stone

When you see someone fall, don’t rush to criticise, judge or condemn; instead ask yourself two questions: How can I help him stand up? How can I become his support? Become his rope through encouragement, companionship and prayer.

Information — the “restore” of Galatians 6:1 is mending nets and setting bones; Romans 5:8 says God loved us while we were still sinners.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to show you a specific face. Whose name comes to mind right now? That is the person God wants you to lift up today.

Conviction — not “this is the more loving thing to do,” but “if I don’t do this, I am going against the gospel.”

Implementation — this week do three small things: don’t pass on a single word about him; pray for him specifically three times; reach out to him once, without mentioning what happened, just asking how he is.

Evaluation — at the weekend, get quiet and ask: this week, was I restoring, or collecting evidence?

Correction — if you find you’ve already thrown a stone, go and apologise. “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23–24)

Repetition — this isn’t a one-off good deed; it’s a new reflex, and reflexes are only trained through repetition.

Multiplication — take someone along with you. When you walk with a brother until he learns to throw a rope, one rope becomes two.

Practice 2: Train your spiritual discernment

Faced with different people, learn to discern: is he weak, or hardened? Is he willing to repent, or does he keep resisting? Don’t treat everyone the same way; follow the Holy Spirit and respond with wisdom.

Information — Jude 22–23: three kinds of people, three approaches; 2 Corinthians 7:10: two kinds of sorrow; the contrast between Peter and Judas.

Revelation — discernment isn’t something you analyse your way to; you pray your way to it. That is exactly what Solomon asked for: “Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9).

Conviction — I admit that my first instinct is often wrong; I will no longer draw conclusions from impressions or hearsay.

Implementation — when you run into a problem with someone, pray before you open your mouth, wait at least one night, and ask three questions: Does he fear God? Is he willing to face it? Is he continuing to hurt others?

Evaluation and Correction — look back on a time your judgment was off: what was I judging with — my emotions, my face, or the Holy Spirit? If you once treated a weak person as wicked, go and restore the relationship; if you once indulged a hardened person as though he were merely weak, add the missing step of truth.

Repetition and Multiplication — in time this becomes spiritual eyesight; and take this discernment into your small group, so the group gets used to asking first, “Is he weak or hardened?” rather than “Does he deserve a telling-off?”

Practice 3: Centre every choice on building relationships

In your daily See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, ask yourself: is this response building the relationship, or damaging it? Choose the actions that bring unity, restoration and connection.

See — when I look at someone, do I see his offences, or his worth?

Listen — when I hear about someone’s weakness, do I take it in and pray, or pass it on?

Think — what am I rehearsing in my mind: how to help him, or how to beat him?

Speak — is the sentence I’m about to say a rope or a stone?

Do — will what I’m about to do today bring the relationship closer, or push it further away?

Information — “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing all flow out of the heart; guard the heart, and you have guarded all five outlets.

Revelation and Conviction — relationships matter more than right and wrong; people matter more than things. I am convinced of this order.

Implementation and Evaluation — each evening take three minutes to run through the five outlets: today, whom did I draw closer? Whom did I push further away?

Correction — deal with it the same day; don’t let it sit overnight. “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26).

Repetition and Multiplication — keep it up for thirty days without a break, until it becomes a habit; and in your small group ask one another: “This week, who did you throw a rope to?”

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Two Systems, Two Kinds of Work
sections.html:
At the end the lesson gives us a vitally important reminder.

Satan’s work is: making people fall, making people condemn, making people isolate one another.

These three steps are a production line: Satan first tempts a person to fall, then turns around and accuses him, and finally gets that person isolated. Because a sheep on its own is the easiest to devour. “Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” (1 Peter 5:8)

And God’s work is: upholding, restoring, building relationships.

“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

So don’t be someone who throws stones; be someone who throws ropes.

The lesson’s last two sentences are worth memorising:

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and judgment comes.

Why? Because the “brain” only calculates: how many times he’s got it wrong, how much he owes me, whether doing this is worth it for me. But the “heart” sees: this is a created soul, bought back by the Lord with his precious blood.

Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Brothers and sisters, when we judge people, there is actually no joy in it at all; when we lift someone up, an inexpressible joy wells up inside instead. That is not a psychological effect; it is the Holy Spirit’s confirmation.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s read the lesson’s conclusion once more.

When we face people with God’s heart, three things happen: the weak are upheld, the hardened are awakened, and the community is protected.

Relationships are built, lives are restored, and the church moves toward true revival.

Notice: revival doesn’t start with a special conference; it starts with a rope.

James 5:19–20 says: “Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.”

“Will save a soul from death” — there is no greater ministry in this world than that.

Back to that early morning. When the crowd had all gone out one by one, beginning from the oldest, what was left on the temple floor? Stones that had never been thrown, all over the ground. And the woman was still standing.

Brothers and sisters, may the day come when the floors of our churches, our homes and our small groups are also covered with stones that were never thrown, because everyone chose to put them down.

From today, make a choice: no more stones, only ropes.

This is the life of those who belong to God.

Let Jesus reign as King in our responses, and let Jesus receive all the glory in every soul that is restored.

I will be someone who throws ropes, helping others stand up when they fall.
Give me wisdom to discern, and love to restore.
Let me live out the priority of relationships, and become someone who brings restoration and unity.

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you. Thank you that while I was still a sinner, you died for me. Thank you that you have not dealt with me according to my sins, nor repaid me for my iniquities.
Lord, forgive me. I confess that my hand is often clutching a stone, and that I even wrap it up in spiritual language. Let your precious blood wash my judging heart clean.

Open my eyes to see the person who is falling right now; give me the wisdom to discern, to know when to uphold and when to warn; give me a gentle heart, so that every word I say becomes a rope; and let me first stand firm on your rock, so that I can throw the rope out.
May my home, my small group and my church become a place where a person who has fallen dares to come back; may sin be unable to stay here, because you reign as King here.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
discussion: Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Think back to the last time someone fell in front of you. What was your first reaction? Does that reaction show that the self-centred life or selflessness is at work inside you? This week, how will you concretely throw a rope to this person?

Matthew 18:15: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” In your experience, which step is most easily skipped? Why? Share a time when “restoring privately first” led to a good outcome, or a time when getting the order wrong caused harm.

blog.title: Throw a Rope, Not a Stone

blocks.x: When someone near you falls, what are you holding in your hand?

Very early one morning, a crowd dragged a woman into the temple courts, pushed her into the middle of everyone and made them all look at her shame. At that moment there were two things on the ground: a person who had fallen, and stones everywhere.
Every single person there had to make a choice — when they bent down, was it to pick up a stone, or to write?

Two thousand years have passed and that scene has never disappeared; it has just changed location: the church corridor, the small-group chat, the family dinner table, and those trials, one after another, that we hold in our hearts and never voice.
When a co-worker fails, when a brother’s marriage runs into trouble — what is our first reaction?
What best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but how we respond. Because words can be dressed up; reactions can’t.
1. God’s order: love first, change after
The Bible says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Notice the timing — while we were yet sinners. Not after we had cleaned up our act, but when we were at our least lovable, when we most deserved to be stoned.

This is the order of the gospel: God does not first demand that you change before he loves you; God loved you already, while you were still weak. Paul also reminds us that it is the goodness of God that leads people to repentance (Romans 2:4). In other words: a stone can knock a person down, but it has never once changed a person.

That is why Paul gives the spiritual a command: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

The original word for “restore” is the very word the Gospels use for fishermen “mending” their nets, and in classical Greek it also meant setting a dislocated bone back in place. Restoring a person is like mending a net, like setting a bone — it hurts, but the aim is putting things back in place, not punishment.
And that phrase, “looking to yourself,” is more like a mirror: the person you’re lifting up today could be you tomorrow.
2. Love needs discernment, and boundaries too

Preaching only love is not enough. If nothing is ever dealt with, the church becomes a place with no boundaries, and the wounded sheep end up with no one to protect them. So the Bible says: “Yahweh upholds the humble. He brings the wicked down to the ground.” (Psalm 147:6) The same God, two responses. Not that God’s love is bigger or smaller, but that human hearts are soft or hard.

The weak fall, but they are willing to repent, and in their hearts they still fear God — Peter was that kind of man: one look from the Lord, and he went out and wept bitterly. The hardened have no fear of God in their hearts, keep on harming people and are unwilling to repent — Saul confessed his sin, but cared only about his face. Paul says it all in one sentence: godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death.

The psychologists Tangney and Dearing, in their 2002 research, also point out that “guilt” focuses on behaviour and moves people to apologise and repair relationships, while “shame” focuses on the self and instead makes people withdraw and get defensive.
That is exactly what makes a stone so dangerous — a stone produces shame, a rope produces hope; and only hope has the strength to repent.

The Lord Jesus also gave a clear order: restore privately first, then take one or two others along, and only finally bring it to the church (Matthew 18:15–17). The mistake we make most often is skipping step one and telling everyone who has nothing to do with it.
True love is not indulgence; true love is for rescuing.
3. Two systems, one choice

Satan’s work comes in three steps: making people fall, making people condemn, making people isolate one another — because a sheep on its own is the easiest to devour. God’s work also comes in three steps: upholding, restoring, building relationships.
Every time someone falls, it is the moment when the two systems meet face to face. The stone or the rope in our hand decides which side we are standing on.
Only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn. Judging is leaving our originally intended position; discerning is returning to it — let man be man and let God be God.

When we face people with God’s heart, the weak are upheld, the hardened are awakened, and the community is protected. Relationships are built, lives are restored, and the church moves toward true revival. Revival doesn’t start with a special conference; it starts with a rope.

Back to that early morning. When the crowd had all gone out one by one, beginning from the oldest, what was left on the ground were stones that had never been thrown — and the woman was still standing.
From today, make a choice: no more stones, only ropes.
This is the life of those who belong to God.
Reflection
Right now, has a face come to mind? This week, how will you specifically throw that person a rope instead of a stone?

brief12.title: Throw a Rope, Not a Stone
notes: Slide text:
Rectify the Priority (Part 4)
Facing the fallen with God’s heart
“Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”
(Galatians 6:1)
Key points:
1. Greet the congregation; announce the lesson title “Throw a Rope, Not a Stone” and the theme verse, Galatians 6:1.
2. Opening action: ask the brothers and sisters to hold out a hand and look at what they are holding.
3. Explain that this is the fourth lesson on “rectifying the priority”; the theme is facing those who fall with God’s heart.
4. Preview the three key points: God’s heart, spiritual discernment, building relationships without indulging sin.

brief12.title: Introduction: What Is in Your Hand?
notes: Slide text:
Throw a stone, or throw a rope?
Condemn, or restore?
This is not just a matter of attitude;
it is a matter of priority.
Key points:
1. Quote John 8:2 and describe the early-morning scene in the temple.
2. Key line: what best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but how we respond.
3. Words can be dressed up; reactions can’t — reactions flow straight out from within.
4. Point out that this is a matter of “priority,” not just of attitude.

brief12.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
“While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us”
(Romans 5:8)
Galatians: only a church that understands grace
knows how to restore those who fall.
Key points:
1. Read Romans 5:8, stressing the timing: “while we were yet sinners.”
2. “Commends” in the original means to place side by side, to prove: God places the cross right beside our sin.
3. Background to Galatians: one of Paul’s earliest letters, the whole book fighting for grace.
4. One line sets the tone: a church that understands grace will always know how to restore people.

brief12.title: 1. Hate the Sin, Love the Sinner
notes: Slide text:
God hates sin, and loves sinners even more.
“He has not dealt with us according to our sins”
God’s goodness leads you to repentance.
Key points:
1. Habakkuk 1:13 shows that God hates sin; God’s holiness does not tolerate sin.
2. Psalm 103:10; David, who wrote it, had fallen himself.
3. God knows how we are made; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14).
4. Romans 2:4: goodness leads people to repentance, not repentance bringing goodness.
5. Key line: a stone can knock a person down, but it has never once changed a person.

brief12.title: 1. Restore: Hands That Mend Nets
notes: Slide text:
“Restore” in the original: mending nets, setting bones.
Gentleness is fruit of the Holy Spirit.
“Looking to yourself”
321 Insight: only selflessness can love.
Key points:
1. “Caught in some fault” in the original: seized before one can act, caught off guard.
2. “Restore” in the original is the word for “mending” nets in Matthew 4:21, also used for setting a bone back in place.
3. Illustration: the Japanese craft of kintsugi traces the cracks in gold, and the vessel ends up worth more than before it broke.
4. “Gentleness” is one of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).
5. 321 Insight: only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn.

brief12.title: 2. The Weak
notes: Slide text:
They fall, but are willing to repent,
and still fear God in their hearts.
“If we confess our sins”
(1 John 1:9)
Key points:
1. Psalm 147:6: the same God, two responses.
2. Three marks of the weak: they fall, they are willing to repent, they still fear God in their hearts.
3. 1 John 1:9; “confess” in the original means “to say the same thing” — saying “Amen” to God’s verdict.
4. Example: Peter denied the Lord three times; one look from the Lord, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
5. Proverbs 24:16: a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.

brief12.title: 2. The Wicked
notes: Slide text:
No fear of God, unwilling to repent.
“God resists the proud”
(James 4:6)
321 Insight: humility receives grace.
Key points:
1. Three marks of the wicked: no fear of God in their hearts, keep on harming people, unwilling to repent.
2. James 4:6 quotes Proverbs 3:34; “resists” is a military term for drawing up in battle array against.
3. Contrast: Saul confessed only to save face (1 Samuel 15:30); Judas regretted, yet went to destruction.
4. 2 Corinthians 7:10: two kinds of sorrow — one leads to salvation, the other produces death.
5. Psychological support: Tangney and Dearing’s 2002 research — shame makes people withdraw; guilt moves them to repair.

brief12.title: 3. The Lord Jesus’ Three Steps
notes: Slide text:
Restore privately first: relationship comes first.
Then take others along: testimony is established.
Finally bring it to the church: spiritual authority.
“You have gained back your brother”
Key points:
1. Read Matthew 18:15, stressing “you have gained back your brother.”
2. The three steps: restore privately first, then take others along, finally bring it to the church.
3. Context: before it, the parable of the lost sheep; after it, forgiving seventy times seven.
4. Warning: the most common mistake is skipping step one and passing things on in group chats and over dinner.

brief12.title: 3. True Love Is Not Indulgence
notes: Slide text:
“Deliver such a one to Satan”
(1 Corinthians 5:5)
The aim is still that his spirit be saved.
321 Insight: loving people is not approving sin.
Key points:
1. 1 Corinthians 5:5 — the emphasis falls on the last clause, “that the spirit may be saved.”
2. The sequel: 2 Corinthians 2:6–7, you should rather forgive him and comfort him.
3. Hebrews 12:11: discipline aims to yield the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
4. Illustration: in swift-water rescue you get firm footing first, then throw the rope — the practical version of “looking to yourself.”
5. 321 Insight: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles; loving people does not mean approving of sin.

brief12.title: Practices
notes: Slide text:
Throw a rope, not a stone.
Train your spiritual discernment.
Centre every choice on relationships.
See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.
Key points:
1. Bring out the three practices one by one, and ask the brothers and sisters to fix a specific person in their hearts.
2. Three small things for Practice 1: don’t pass anything on, pray for him three times, reach out to him once.
3. Three questions for Practice 2: Does he fear God? Is he willing to face it? Is he continuing to hurt others?
4. Tie Practice 3 to Proverbs 4:23: out of the heart is the wellspring of life.
5. Mention the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
The weak are upheld,
the hardened awakened, the community protected.
No more stones, only ropes.
This is the life of those who belong to God.
Key points:
1. Contrast the two systems: Satan makes people fall, condemn and isolate; God upholds, restores and builds relationships.
2. 1 Peter 5:8: a sheep on its own is the easiest to devour.
3. Key line from the lesson: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and judgment comes.
4. Back to that early morning: stones never thrown, all over the ground.
5. Call: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, wash my judging heart clean,
give me wisdom to discern and love to restore,
let every word I say become a rope.
May Jesus reign as King among us.
Key points:
1. Lead the declaration of faith: I will be someone who throws ropes.
2. Prayer of response: ask the precious blood to wash the judging heart clean; ask for wisdom to discern and a gentle heart.
3. Pray for homes, small groups and churches to become places where those who fall dare to come back.
4. Close with the blessing of Numbers 6:24–26.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like you to do something first: hold out your hand and look at it. What are you holding in your hand right now? Today’s lesson is called “Throw a Rope, Not a Stone,” the fourth lesson on “rectifying the priority.” Our theme verse is Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Today God wants to teach us one thing — how to face a person who has fallen with God’s heart.

Brothers and sisters, when someone falls, what best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but how we respond. Because words can be dressed up; reactions can’t. Words are thought through before they’re spoken; reactions flow straight out from within. So ask yourself: throw a stone, or throw a rope? Condemn, or restore? This is not just a matter of attitude; it is a matter of priority. When the order is wrong, we treat people with judgment; when the order is right, we restore people with love.

Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the background first. Romans 5:8 says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Notice the timing — while we were yet sinners. Not after we had cleaned up our act, but when we most deserved to be stoned. And Galatians is a book that fights for grace from start to finish. Paul spends five chapters making it plain that we are saved by grace, and then in chapter 6 he says: a church that truly understands grace will always be a church that knows how to restore people.

The first key point: God hates sin, yet loves the sinner. God’s attitude toward sin is very clear — he hates it; but God’s attitude toward people is even clearer. Psalm 103:10 says: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” David, who wrote those words, had fallen himself. He also said that God knows how we are made; he remembers that we are dust. Brothers and sisters, remember the order of the gospel — God does not first demand that you change before he loves you; he loved you while you were still weak. Romans 2:4 says: “The goodness of God leads you to repentance.”

So Paul says: “You who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” The original word for “restore” is the word for mending torn nets, and it was also used for setting a dislocated bone back in place. Restoring a person is like a fisherman mending his net, mesh by mesh; like a doctor setting a bone — it hurts, but the aim is putting things back in place, not punishment. And “gentleness” is fruit that the Holy Spirit bears. Paul adds one more phrase: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Brothers and sisters, the person you’re lifting up today could be you tomorrow. A 321 Insight: only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn.

The second key point is discernment. Psalm 147:6 says: “Yahweh upholds the humble. He brings the wicked down to the ground.” The Bible shows us two kinds of people. The first kind is the weak: he falls, but he is willing to repent, and in his heart he still fears God. 1 John 1:9 says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” Peter was that kind of man. The Lord turned and looked at him, and he went out and wept bitterly. To people like this, God’s response is: uphold, forgive, restore.

The second kind is the wicked: no fear of God in their hearts, they keep on harming people, and they are unwilling to repent. James 4:6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Saul confessed his sin too, but cared only about his face; Judas regretted too, yet his end was destruction. Paul puts it plainly: godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death. Brothers and sisters, a stone produces shame, a rope produces hope; and only hope has the strength to repent. A 321 Insight: humility receives grace; pride is resisted.

The third key point: build the relationship, but don’t indulge the sin. In Matthew 18:15 the Lord Jesus says: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” Listen to the Lord’s order: step one, restore him privately first — relationship comes first; step two, then take one or two others along — testimony is established; step three, finally bring it to the church — spiritual authority. Brothers and sisters, the mistake we make most often is skipping step one and telling everyone who has nothing to do with it. That isn’t concern; that is throwing stones.

But what if the other person never repents? In 1 Corinthians 5:5 Paul says we “are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” Listen to the last clause — the aim is still salvation. Later Paul says: you should rather forgive him and comfort him. Brothers and sisters, the end point of discipline has never been throwing someone out, but welcoming them back. True love is not indulgence; true love is for rescuing. A 321 Insight: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles; loving people does not mean approving of sin.

Brothers and sisters, there are three practices today. First, throw a rope, not a stone: when you see someone fall, don’t criticise first; instead ask, how can I help him stand up? Become his rope through encouragement, companionship and prayer. Second, train your spiritual discernment: is he weak, or hardened? Don’t treat everyone the same way; follow the Holy Spirit. Third, centre every choice on building relationships: in your daily See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, ask yourself — is this response building the relationship, or damaging it?

Brothers and sisters, Satan’s work is making people fall, making people condemn, making people isolate one another; God’s work is upholding, restoring, building relationships. So don’t be someone who throws stones; be someone who throws ropes. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and judgment comes. When we face people with God’s heart, the weak are upheld, the hardened are awakened, the community is protected, relationships are built, lives are restored, and the church moves toward true revival. From today, make a choice: no more stones, only ropes. This is the life of those who belong to God.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that while I was still a sinner, you died for me. Lord, forgive me; I confess that my hand is often clutching a stone. Let your precious blood wash my judging heart clean; give me wisdom to discern, give me a gentle heart, so that every word I say becomes a rope. May my home, my small group and my church become a place where a person who has fallen dares to come back, because you reign as King here. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you, and give you peace.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today’s lesson is called “Throw a Rope, Not a Stone,” the fourth lesson on “rectifying the priority.” Our theme verse is Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Today God wants to help us learn a lesson that is very hard, yet very beautiful — how to face a person who has fallen with God’s heart.

I’d like you to do something first: hold out your hand and look at it. What are you holding in your hand right now? There is an early-morning story in the Bible. John 8:2 says: “Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.” That very morning a crowd dragged a woman caught in adultery into the temple courts and pushed her into the middle of everyone. At that moment two things were present in the temple courts at once: a person who had fallen, and stones all over the ground. And every single person had to make a choice — when they bent down, was it to pick up a stone, or to write?

Brothers and sisters, that scene has never disappeared in two thousand years; it has just changed location: the church corridor, the small-group chat, the family dinner table, and those trials, one after another, that we hold in our hearts and never voice. When a co-worker fails, when a brother’s marriage runs into trouble, what is our first reaction? The lesson puts it with great precision: what best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but how we respond. Because words can be dressed up; reactions can’t. So ask yourself: throw a stone, or throw a rope? Condemn, or restore? This is not just a matter of attitude; it is a matter of priority. When the order is wrong, we treat people with judgment; when the order is right, we restore people with love.

Let’s look at the background first. Paul wrote Romans around AD 56–57. In 5:8 he says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” The original word for “commends” means placing two things side by side to prove something. God does not just tell us in words that he loves us; God places the cross right beside our sin. Notice the timing — while we were yet sinners. Galatians, for its part, is one of Paul’s earliest letters, and the whole book fights for grace. He spends five chapters making it plain that we are saved by grace, through faith, and then in chapter 6 he says: a church that understands grace will always know how to restore people. If you don’t know how to restore people, it proves you haven’t really understood grace yet.

The first key point: God hates sin, yet loves the sinner. The Bible is never vague about God’s attitude toward sin. Habakkuk 1:13 says: “You who have purer eyes than to see evil, and who cannot look on perversity.” God’s holiness does not tolerate sin. But brothers and sisters, God’s attitude toward people is even clearer — the same God who hates sin gave his only Son for sinners. So never mix the two up: hating sin is hating the thing that harms people; loving sinners is loving the people who are harmed.

Psalm 103:10 says: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” The one who wrote this was David, a man who had committed adultery and murder. In the same psalm he explains why: God knows how we are made; he remembers that we are dust. Brothers and sisters, God has never overestimated us, so God is never shocked by our failures. Romans 2:4 goes further and asks: “Not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” Hear this order clearly: it isn’t repentance that brings goodness; it is goodness that leads people to repentance. A stone can knock a person down, but it has never once changed a person.

So Paul says: “You who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” There are three words here worth remembering. The first is “caught in some fault,” which in the original means seized before one can act, caught off guard. The second is “restore,” which in the original is the very word for “mending” nets in Matthew 4:21, and in classical Greek it also meant setting a dislocated bone back in place. Brothers and sisters, restoring a person is like a fisherman mending his net, like a doctor setting a bone — it hurts, but the aim is putting things back in place, not punishment. The third is “gentleness,” one of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit, meaning strength under control. Paul adds one more phrase: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” The person you’re lifting up today could be you tomorrow.

Brothers and sisters, here is a 321 Insight: only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn. When a person is full of himself, he passes judgment; when a person is full of Christ, he shows mercy. In 1977 the psychologist Lee Ross named the “fundamental attribution error”: when we explain other people’s failures, we blame their character; when we explain our own failures, we blame the situation. The same event, two measuring sticks. This is exactly what the Lord said: why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam in your own eye? That early morning, the Lord said to the crowd holding stones: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” And they went out one by one, beginning from the oldest. The oldest left first — because the longer you’ve lived, the better you know your own hands aren’t clean.

The second key point is discernment. Brothers and sisters, if we preached only the first point, we would swing to the other extreme: dealing with nothing, until the church becomes a place with no boundaries and the wounded sheep have no one to protect them. So Psalm 147:6 gives us a second key: “Yahweh upholds the humble. He brings the wicked down to the ground.” The same God, two responses. Not that God’s love is bigger or smaller, but that human hearts are soft or hard. “Upholds” in Hebrew means to make to stand, to strengthen. God stoops down and lifts up the one who has fallen; and the same God who stoops to lift people up will also bring down to the ground the one who stays hard to the end.

The first kind is the weak. He has three marks: he falls, but he is willing to repent, and in his heart he still fears God. 1 John 1:9 says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” The word “confess” in the original means “to say the same thing” — not muttering to yourself that you’re no good, but saying “Amen” to God’s verdict. The classic example is Peter. He denied the Lord three times — an utter failure — but the Lord turned and looked at him, and he went out and wept bitterly. Brothers and sisters, that one look from the Lord was a rope. Proverbs 24:16 says: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” The Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says the righteous fall and rise up again.

The second kind is the wicked. He also has three marks: no fear of God in his heart, he keeps on harming people, and he is unwilling to repent. James 4:6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” “Resists” is a military term, meaning to draw up in battle array against. Saul confessed his sin too, but cared only about his face. Judas regretted too, and even said the right words, yet in the end he went away and hanged himself. Paul says it all in one sentence: godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death. The psychologists Tangney and Dearing, in their 2002 research, also point out that guilt focuses on behaviour and moves people to repair relationships, while shame focuses on the self and instead makes people withdraw and get defensive. Brothers and sisters, a stone produces shame, a rope produces hope; only hope has the strength to repent.

Here is a second 321 Insight: humility receives grace; pride is resisted. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Brothers and sisters, when we pick up a stone, whose seat are we sitting in? Romans 14:4 says: “Who are you who judge another’s servant?” Judging is leaving our originally intended position; discerning is returning to it. Judging is me deciding his fate on God’s behalf; discerning is me asking God to let me see, so I know how to love him right now. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Jude 22–23 also says: on some have compassion, and some snatch out of the fire — don’t treat everyone the same way.

The third key point: build the relationship, but don’t indulge the sin. In Matthew 18:15 the Lord Jesus says: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” Notice the Lord’s words — you have gained back your brother. Not that you have won the argument, but that you have won a person. The Lord goes on: if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you; if he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. Brothers and sisters, this is a clear three-step path: restore privately first, then take others along, finally bring it to the church. The mistake we make most often is skipping step one and telling everyone who has nothing to do with it. Passing it on in the group chat, sharing it over dinner — that isn’t concern; that is a stone with a label stuck on it.

Brothers and sisters, cut off from its context, this passage becomes a knife. Before it comes the parable of the lost sheep in Matthew 18:12 — if a man has a hundred sheep and one goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine and go and look for that one? After it comes 18:22, where Peter asks how many times he should forgive his brother, and the Lord says not seven times, but seventy times seven. See the order clearly: before it, leaving the ninety-nine to look for the one; in the middle, the procedure for restoring; after it, forgiving seventy times seven. The discipline of Matthew 18 is sandwiched between seeking and forgiving. Anyone unwilling to go and look for the one has no business carrying out verse 15; anyone unwilling to forgive has no business carrying out verse 17.

But what if the other person never repents, all the way to the end? In 1 Corinthians 5:5 Paul says we “are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” Brothers and sisters, please read that last clause three times — even the severest discipline still has salvation as its aim. And the story has a second half: in 2 Corinthians 2:6–7 Paul says that the punishment inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one, and that you should rather forgive him and comfort him. The end point of discipline is not throwing someone out, but welcoming them back. Hebrews 12:11 also says that discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. True love is not indulgence; true love is for rescuing.

Here is a third 321 Insight: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles; loving people does not mean approving of sin. Ephesians 4:15 says: “But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.” Love without truth-telling is staying down in the pit chatting with him; truth-telling without love is standing at the edge of the pit throwing stones at him. In swift-water rescue training the most important principle is this: the rescuer must not rashly jump in, but first get firm footing, and then throw out the rope. Brothers and sisters, your relationship with God is the rock under your feet. When the order is right, we build people up with love and protect the community with truth.

Brothers and sisters, now let’s practise. The first practice: throw a rope, not a stone. When you see someone fall, don’t rush to criticise, judge or condemn; instead ask yourself: how can I help him stand up? How can I become his support? This week, please do three small things: don’t pass on a single word about him; pray for him specifically three times; reach out to him once, without mentioning what happened, just asking how he is. There are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Today you have received the information; now ask the Holy Spirit for revelation — whose name comes to mind right now? That is the person God wants you to lift up today.

The second practice: spiritual discernment. Faced with different people, learn to discern: is he weak, or hardened? When you run into a problem with someone, pray before you open your mouth, wait at least one night, and ask three questions: Does he fear God? Is he willing to face it? Is he continuing to hurt others? The third practice: centre every choice on building relationships. In your daily See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, ask yourself — when I look at someone, do I see his offences, or his worth? Is the sentence I’m about to say a rope or a stone? Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we’ve learned today and look at it once more within 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he was the only one qualified to throw the first stone, and the only one who didn’t; the Bible is my standard — the way I lift people up doesn’t follow my mood, but the order of Matthew 18; the Holy Spirit is my guide — discerning who is weak and who is hardened is beyond my ability. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; when I put down the stone, I hand the throne back to him, because judging is, at its core, usurping the throne. The Goal: establish God’s system — a place where a person who has fallen still dares to come back, and at the same time a place where sin cannot stay.

Brothers and sisters, Satan’s work comes in three steps: making people fall, making people condemn, making people isolate one another, because a sheep on its own is the easiest to devour. God’s work also comes in three steps: upholding, restoring, building relationships. So don’t be someone who throws stones; be someone who throws ropes. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and judgment comes. When we face people with God’s heart, the weak are upheld, the hardened are awakened, the community is protected, and the church moves toward true revival. Revival doesn’t start with a special conference; it starts with a rope. Back to that early morning — when the crowd had all gone out, what was left on the ground were stones that had never been thrown, and the woman was still standing. From today, make a choice: no more stones, only ropes. This is the life of those who belong to God.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that while I was still a sinner, you died for me. Lord, forgive me. I confess that my hand is often clutching a stone, and that I even wrap it up in spiritual language. Let your precious blood wash my judging heart clean; open my eyes to see the person who is falling right now; give me the wisdom to discern, to know when to uphold and when to warn; give me a gentle heart, so that every word I say becomes a rope. May my home, my small group and my church become a place where a person who has fallen dares to come back; may sin be unable to stay here, because you reign as King here. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
